3. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the respondent Abdul Salam Chowdhury, as plaintiff on 22.11.1979 instituted Other Suit No.182 of 1979 in the Second Court of Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chittagong. Subsequently, the said suit was transferred to the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Patia, District- Chittagong and renumbered as Other Suit No.223 of 1984, impleading petitioner Nos.1-6 as defendants on the averments that the land described in the schedule to the plaint belonged to Raj Chandra and Beni Mohan, who created Jote No.1 in respect of the suit land and settled the same with Osi Meah Chowdhury in Dar-raiyati right. Osi Meah Chowdhury had been in continuous peaceful and uninterrupted possession of the suit land on payment of rent to the landlord. The jote right was sold in auction for arrears of rent in 1938 and the same was purchased by the Government. The Dar-raiyati right in respect of the suit land was not cancelled. After the death of Osi Meah Chowdhury, his son Abdul Gani Chowdhury had been in continuous, peaceful and uninterrupted possession of the suit land on payment of rent to the Government. Interest of Abdul Gani Chowdhury remained intact but he had to apply for confirmation of settlement of the suit land. The relevant authorities concluded settlement in his favour and accordingly, he paid rent, Chowdhury in Dar-raiyati right. Osi Meah Chowdhury had been in continuous peaceful and uninterrupted possession of the suit land on payment of rent to the landlord. The jote right was sold in auction for arrears of rent in 1938 and the same was purchased by the Government. The Dar-raiyati right in respect of the suit land was not cancelled. After the death of Osi Meah Chowdhury, his son Abdul Gani Chowdhury had been in continuous, peaceful and uninterrupted possession of the suit land on payment of rent to the Government. Interest of Abdul Gani Chowdhury remained intact but he had to apply for confirmation of settlement of the suit land. The relevant authorities concluded settlement in his favour and accordingly, he paid rent, salami, back rent and other dues as required under the law. Since there was a bar for getting settlement of the suit land within 20 milies area from the Chittagong Court Building no agreement was executed. Abdul Gani Chowdhury continued to paying rents fixed by the authority on the strength of his riayati tenancy right as well as right created in his favour as per order passed in Settlement Case No.35 of 1946-47. Accordingly, Khatian has also been prepared and finally published in his name on the strength of his possession of the suit land as a tenant under the Government. Subsequently, a part of suit land was acquired by the Government under L.A. Case No.201 of 1961-62 and compensation was assessed on the basis of the S. A. Khatian in the name of Dar-raiyat Abdul Gani Chowdhury. 

 4. Thereafter, the Abdul Gani Chowdhury had filed an application before the A.D.C. (Rev.), Chittagong against the report of the R.D.C. which was recorded as Miscellaneous Case No.3 of 1972-73 and by order dated 22.08.1972 A.D.C. (Rev.) cancelled the S.A. Khatian no. 191 in respect of the suit land standing in the name of Abdul Gani Chowdhury on the finding that the Khatian was fraudulently prepared. Against the said cancellation order, Abdul Gani Chowdhury filed a revisional application being No.57 of 1972 before the Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong who transferred the case to the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration, Bangladesh and the said miscellaneous case was numbered as Miscellaneous Petition No.181 of 1973. After hearing, the said case was sent back on remand to the A.D.C. (Rev.), Chittagong, who by order dated 24.04.1975 decided against Abdul Gani Chowdhury. Against the aforesaid order, Abdul Gani Chowdhury filed a revisional application before the Secretary, Land Administration and Land Reforms, Dhaka but the petition was rejected on 05.08.1979. 

 6. The defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the suit by filing joint written statements denying the material allegations made in the plaint, contending, inter alia, that the suit land is out and out Government Khas land since long time. The plaintiffs and their predecessor being very influential men in the area always have/had an eagle’s eye over the suit land, with that end in view of the plaintiffs’ predecessor might have created some rent receipts and other papers without any basis. The Government did not recognize the plaintiffs or their predecessor as tenants at any stage. In all the proceedings in the revenue Courts the plaintiffs have lost as they and their predecessor always failed to produce any documents of their alleged title. The suit land is Government khas land for which they are not bound to pay any compensation from the Government as prayed for. The plaintiffs have no right and title on the suit land, but to grab the suit property, they have created some forged and fabricated papers by dint of which they cannot get any title in their favour against the Government, the rightful owner of the suit land. The collusive and fraudulent S.A. Khatian created by the plaintiffs’ predecessor having already been cancelled in accordance with law, the plaintiffs’ present suit for simple declaration is not maintainable. 

 15. Mr. Sheikh Mohammad Morshed, the learned Additional Attorney General appearing on behalf of the appellant Nos.1 and 2 in Civil Appeal No.253 of 2015 has submitted that the S.A. Khatian has no basis and by the said khatian Abdul Gani Chowdhuiy did not acquire any title in the suit land and the plaintiffs failed to establish their title, so they are not entitled to get a decree that they are raiyats under the Government and, as such, there is an error apparent on the face of record and, as such, considering the same, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. 

 16. The learned Additional Attorney General, at the time of review hearing, further pointed out that the judgment dated 02.03.2014 passed by this Division did not consider that the plaintiff-respondents have failed to prove the basis of their title. Because, exhibit-2 series submitted by the plaintiff respondents were not proved in accordance with law, by adducing any competent witness as required by the law. This aspect of the exhibit-2 series were not considered by this Division at the time of passing the judgment in affirming the judgment of the High Court Division. He added that this Division earlier opined that “… The High Court Division has elaborately discussed all the evidence and materials on record observing that the Jote land originally belonged to Raj Chandra and Beni Mohan who created Jote No.1 and gave settlement with Osi Meah Chowdhury in Dar-raiyati right. That jote right was sold in auction for arrears of rent and the same was purchased by the Government. The right, title and interest of the then dar-raiyati was not cancelled and the same remained intact under the law. After the state acquisition, relationship of landlord and tenant had been established between the Government and Abdul Gani Chowdhury by operation of law, some portion of the land was acquired by the Government under L.A. Case No.201 of 1961-62 and compensation assessment roll was rightly prepared in the name of Abdul Gani Chowdhury on the basis of S.A. Khatian, physical possession and continuous payment of rent. The High Court Division looked at Settlement Case No.35 of 1946-47, Exhibit-3(Ka) in consequence of which order was passed for settlement of the land in favour of Abdul Gani Chowdhury as evidenced by Exhibit-5. It was further observed that S.A. Khatian and R.S. Khatian were prepared correctly in the name of Abdul Gani Chowdhury, son of Osi Meah Chowdhury, which clearly proved established between the Government and Abdul Gani Chowdhury by operation of law, some portion of the land was acquired by the Government under L.A. Case No.201 of 1961-62 and compensation assessment roll was rightly prepared in the name of Abdul Gani Chowdhury on the basis of S.A. Khatian, physical possession and continuous payment of rent. The High Court Division looked at Settlement Case No.35 of 1946-47, Exhibit-3(Ka) in consequence of which order was passed for settlement of the land in favour of Abdul Gani Chowdhury as evidenced by Exhibit-5. It was further observed that S.A. Khatian and R.S. Khatian were prepared correctly in the name of Abdul Gani Chowdhury, son of Osi Meah Chowdhury, which clearly proved continuous and uninterrupted possession of the plaintiffs and their predecessor since 1939….” 

 18. The learned Additional Attorney General pointed out that the most pertinent question is that the plot numbers and khatian no. and quantum of land described in the schedule of the suit are quite different to that of exhibit-2 series which is abundantly clear on comparison of the schedule and the dakhilas. This pertinent question was not resolved by this Division. From which it is apparent that the judgment pronounced by this Division earlier has not occasioned to decide the title without resolving this point of the case under review. Such error is apparent on face of the record. 

 19. The learned Additional Attorney General has next submitted that it is admitted fact as per pleadings of the plaint that S.A. Khatian No.191 published in the names of the plaintiffs was cancelled by the ADC (Revenue), Chattogram against which the plaintiffs as petitioners fought upto last tire of the Government but lost. In the prayer of the suit, the plaintiff neither challenged the aforementioned order nor prayed for declaration that cancellation of the S.A. record was wrong. So, without seeking any redress against that order of cancellation, the plaintiffs cannot get any declaration of title for the suit land. 

 23. Mr. Probir Neogi, the learned Senior Counsel with Mrs. Anita Gazi Rahman, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the respondents in Civil Appeal No.253 of 2015, Civil Review Petition No.94 of 2014 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1311 of 2010 made submissions in support of the impugned judgment of the High Court Division as well as of this Division. He has submitted that in Chittagong S.A. and R.S. khatians are called P.S. and B.S. khatians respectively. P.S. khatian being S.A. khatian has no presumption of correctness of entry therein, but B.S. khatian being R.S. khatian has legal presumption of correctness of entry under section 144A of the State acquisition and Tenancy Act, and in the instant case, both P.S. and B.S. khatians having been prepared in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs, the ground of appeal in this respect is misconceived, and the High Court Division while allowing the first appeal and this Division in dismissing the leave petition rightly drew legal presumption of title in favour of the plaintiffs on the basis of B.S. khatian and, as such, considering the same, the instant appeal may kindly be dismissed. 

 25. He further submits that in view of the provisions of section 19 sub-section (3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 having contemplated- “ …… and the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly prepared or revised under this Chapter.”, in case of a dispute between private parties regarding genuineness of S.A. record, there will be no presumption of correctness of entry in the said record, but in a dispute between a citizen(s) and the Government, the Government is legally stopped from questioning the genuineness of a finally published S.A. record by operation of law. He next submits that the instant appeal arises out of leave granted on a civil review petition, so, the scope of review under Order XLVII, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Order XXVI, Rule 1 of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Appellate Division) Rules, 1988 is the scope of appeal in the instant case. It is further clear from the Rule 8, Order XXVI of the Appellate Division Rules, 1988. In Rule 8, “final disposal of the first application for review” means disposal of the appeal where leave is granted on review petition. Otherwise, the word “final” would bear no meaning. So, by the disposal of this appeal, “the final disposal” of the review petition upon which leave was granted will be made. There is no ground whatsoever to review the impugned judgment inasmuch as the Appellate Division found that the High Court Division on elaborate discussion of all the evidence and materials on record found that after the state acquisition, relationship of landlord and tenant had been established between the Government and Abdul Gani Chowdhury, predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs, by operation of law, some portion of the land was acquired by the Government under L.A. Case No.201 of 1961-62 and compensation assessment roll was rightly prepared in the name of Abdul Gani Chowdhury on the basis of S.A. Khatian, physical possession and continuous payment of rent. He also submit that the instant appeal is devoid of any merit inasmuch as in the impugned judgment the Appellate Division found –“the High Court Division looked at Settlement Case No.35 of 1946-47, Exhibt-3(Ka) in consequence of which order was passed for settlement of the land in favour of Abdul Gani Chowdhury as evidenced by Exhibt-5. It was further observed that S.A. khatian and R.S. khatian were prepared correctly in the name of Abdul Gani Chwodhury, son of Osi Meah Chowdhury, which clearly proved continuous and uninterrupted possession of the plaintiffs and their predecessors since 1939.” He further submits that the rent receipts/dakhilas (Exhibit-2 series) dating back to the month of Magh, 1926 B.S. and the Duplicate Carbon Receipt (Exhibit- 3 series) having been admitted into evidence and marked exhibits without any objection, the defendant-appellants cannot be allowed at this stage to contend ‘plaintiffs’ predecessors might have created some rent-receipts and other papers’, more so, when this submission of the appellant at the time of hearing of the leave petition was rejected by this Hon’ble Court finding – “ ……. we note that the defendants did not file any documentary evidence nor examined any witness to prove their case nor cross- examined any of the plaintiffs’ witnesses. The High Court Division found that the plaintiffs’ predecessor and thereafter, the plaintiffs were in continuous and uninterrupted possession of the suit land since settlement from the landlord in 1939. This is evidenced by the dakhilas and rent receipts issued by the Government, which have not been challenged. The petitioners took no step to substantiate their half-hearted contention that the plaintiffs’ predecessors might have created some rent receipts and other papers.” He further submits that the suit is not barred by limitation due to non-filing of the suit within 6 years from the cancellation of S.A./P.S. khatian as it is settled principle of law that the plaintiff is not bound to institute a suit for declaration that the cancellation of record is wrong. He can wait and when an invasion of his rights is made, he can come and sue for a declaration of the title on the ground that the record is wrong. Such a suit will be in time if brought within 6(six) years from the date of the threatened invasion. He finally submits that in view of the cumulative effect of the provisions of sections 101, 102, and 103 of the Evidence Act, it is well settled by a long line of decisions that unlike criminal proceedings, the fate of civil suits/proceedings is decided by the preponderance of evidence, in other words the comparative weight, worth and quality of evidence led by the parties, and, as such, no review of the judgment dated 02.03.2014 passed by the Appellate Division affirming the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division is warranted by the preponderance of evidence in the instant case. 

 31. It is apparent on the face of the record that, the quantum of land described in the schedule of the plaint and in the aforesaid exhibits-2(ga)-2(cha)are clearly distinguished, not only that, in exhibit-2(ka), there is no mention of the khatian or plot number, rather, mentioned only jomabondi No.191. In exhibit- 2(gha), it appears that, it is further improved by the plaintiff that, in the aforesaid exhibit, it has been written Jomabondi No.191. However, further improved the khatian No.200 and Mouja Gobadia of Towji No.133. Although, in exhibit-2(ga), there is no date of the rent receiving employee. However, in exhibit-2(ga), there is a date i.e. 13.04.1967 by the rent receiving employee of the Tohshil Office. It is apparent from the exhibit-2(uma) that, in this dakhila of rent receipt, there is further improvement wherein mentioned the Dag Nos.4, 5, 6 and 399 and the classification of the land is null. Although, earlier to rent receipt and exhibits-2(ka) and 2(ga), there is no mention of the nature of the suit land. In that view of the matter, we have gone through the plaint of the suit. On perusal of the averment of the plaint and description of the schedule land wherefrom it is apparent on the face of the record that there is quite different description which are as follows: “Schedule: Mouza Gobadia, P.S. Anwara, Chittagong, P.S. Khatian, Chittagong, R.S. Khatian No.66 Jote No.1 RS. Plots No.399/371/5/6 comprising of 115.41 acres. P.S. Kh.191/200-P.S. Khat-24/371/391/5 and 6 schedule-A-55.41 acres schedule-B 60.0 acres.” 

 35. It is further divulged from the Exts.3 and 3(ka), the copies of duplicate carbon receipt books, there is no plot number, khatian number of the suit land, rather, it has been written in Ext.3 in column from whom receipt name of Abdul Gani Chowdhury, in column on whose account, the P. Case No.85 of 46-47 and Ext.3(ka), it has been written that Case No.35 of 46-47 without describing any khatian number, plot number or quantum of land. So, it could not be concluded that those two exhibits were issued in respect of the suit plots. Although, at the judgment dated 02.03.2014 passed by this Division, this vital documents were not considered in its true perspective. Though, further mentioned the Settlement Case No.35/1946-47 as Ext.3(ka), showing that suit land was settled in favour of Abdul Gani Chowdhury. It appears, however, from Ext.5, it is an order sheet without mentioning any case number. However, on perusal of the context of the order sheet, it is apparent which quoted below: “The subject matter of the case was R.S. Plot Nos.399, 5 and 6, appertained to Khatian No.1, wherein, it has been written that, this jote was purchased by the Government in rent sale vide rent Suit No.1595 of 1934. R.S. Case No.78 of 1941/42 was started. But the case had to be dropped for want of suitable candidates since then the land has been lying in khas possession of the Government. Original rent of the said jote was Rs.40/- but the special Summary Officer reduced the rent by Rs. 8/- and the annual rent was fixed at Rs.32/- but the Jotedar even could not pay that amount. So, with the result was purchased. In my opinion, land now be settled with the applicant at the recorded rent of Rs.40/-, 1/4- E. Case No.2/3- Salami 10 times the rent. In all is to pay Rs. 443/7/-. After payment hang A. Notice inviting objection if any.” 

 37. In the impugned judgment, this Division also observed that the S.A. and R.S. khatians were prepared correctly in the name of Abdul Gani Chowdhry, son of Haji Osi Meah Chowdhury which was clearly proved continuous and uninterrupted possession of the plaintiffs and their predecessor since 1939. However, in the following paragraph, this Division opined that “the High Court Division observed that entries in the S.A. and B.S. records provides prima face evidence in regards to title. However, this Division observed that we cannot agree with this observation of law. Under Our law it can be said that R.S. Khatian provides evidence of possession and prima face evidence of title. But the same cannot be said about S.A. records.” So, we have to consider the S.A. and R.S. records which have been marked as Ext.1 wherein whether there is any error apparent on the face of the record. 

 38. On perusal of the Ext.1, it appears that under District-Chattogram, Mouza-Gobadia, J.L. No.7, Khatian No.66, Towji No.34611 have been written in the R.S. porcha wherein in the column of বিবরণ ও দখলকার, it has been clearly written that, khas mohal Potia and in the column অত্র স্বাত্বের বিস্তারিত দখল, namely-Ram Chandra, son of Loke Chandra Datta, Kali Mohon, Dokkhina Ranjan, both are sons of Jonnyochandra Datta, Norendra Lal, Femrendra Nath, both of sons of Monmohon Datta which do not support the possession and title of the plaintiffs and their predecessors, however, the name of Beni Mohon appears in the column. So, it is vividly clear that said Beni Mohon was not the sole owner of the suit jote. In the class of land, it has been written Khal, Baluchar and Plot Nos.56 and 3099, Bata-1. Such description in the exhibit-1 not in toto identical as of the schedule of the suit and specifically quantum of land written in the schedule and Ext.1 series are clearly distinguished. Moreover, it is apparent on the face of the record that, earlier findings and observations of this Division are not supporting the above mentioned exhibits. It is, therefore, apparent on the face of the record that there is an error in the exhibit-I which is apparent on the face of the record. 

 39. This Division earlier in the judgment dated 02.03.2014 opined that the respondents herein and their predecessors also in possession of the suit land which was clearly proved continuous and uninterrupted possession in the plaintiffs. However, in view of the such opinion, there is no discussion of evidence on record except S.A. and R.S. khatian. We have already discussed the S.A. and R.S. Khatians as exhibit-1 series, but we find that the documents produced before us through paper books are not identical to the suit property. Therefore, such opinion regarding the possession cannot be upheld; rather, it is required to be reviewed, because, in the earlier judgment, there is an error which is apparent on the face of the record. 

 47. In addition, the SA (PS) Khatian published in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs was duly cancelled and they turned no stone unturned to undo the said cancellation but failed.

lawyer:
Md Jamiruddin Sircar with AHM Abdul Wahab, Advocates -------- For the Petitioners. 
Bivash Chandra Biswas with Mrinal Kanti Biswas, Advocates -------- For the Opposite-Parties.
parties:
Azadul Islam and others -------- Defendant-Respondent-Petitioners
VS
Asis Bewa and others -------- Plaintiff-Appellant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
9. Mr Bivash Chandra Biswas along with Mr Mrinal Kanti Biswas, learned Advocates appeared for the opposite parties. Mr Bivash Chandra Biswas, on the contrary, submits that, this is a case for permanent injunction in which the question of proof of title does not at all arise. The learned Advocate submits that, the question of title may be looked into incidentally in a suit for permanent injunction. He submits that, the plaintiffs have filed RS khatian No. 147 showing 16 annas lands in the suit plot No. 796 and 830/1685, comprising 98 decimals of land, and the said khatian is in the name of predecessor of the plaintiffs, but the other side (defendants) did not challenge the said khatians and the presumption of the validity of the said khatians remains un-rebutted and this proves the prima-facie basis of the plaintiff's acquiring and remaining possession of the suit land. He next submits that, the schedule "Ka" to the plaint correctly described the land shown in the SA khatian No. 147 of Mouza Sathalia, PS Saghata, under District- Gaibanda. He further submits that, the plaintiffs have proved their case by adducing PW 1, who has deposed in support of the plaintiff's case and proved the documentary evidence including aforesaid khatian, to support their prima-facie case regarding the plaintiff's lawful possession in the suit land. PW 1 was then corroborated by PWs 2 and 3. He next submits, the defendants did not cross examine these PW Nos. 2 and 3, nor did the defendants adduce any witness to prove their positive case. He also submits that, the appellate court has pointed out all these aspects of this case and has rightly passed the impugned judgment and decree, which calls for no interference by this revisional Court. In support of his contention, he has referred to the decisions reported in 1986 BLD 155: between Pasharuddin Mir vs Ismail Mir, 4 BLD (AD) 285: between Manindar Nath Sen Sarma vs Bangladesh, 9 BLD 368 = 42 DLR 408: between Sheikh Ahmed vs Abdul Alim and also the decision reported in 56 DLR (AD) 53: between Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Gazipur vs AKM Abdul Hye. In these decisions, referred to above, the superior Court has confirmed the presumption of the validity attached to RS khatain as per section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, and also held that, failure to prove the title in a case for permanent injunction will not disentitle the plaintiff to get permanent injunction, if they prove their exclusive possession in the suit property. He proceeds on that, the impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate court suffers from no illegality or from any other lacuna, whatsoever, and this Rule has no merit and the same may be discharged. 

 12. I find that, RS khatian No. 147, shows 16 annas lands of the suit plot No. 796 and 830/1685, comprises 98 decimals of land, and that the said khatian is in the name of predecessors of the plaintiffs, but the other side (defendants) did not challenge the legality or correctness of the same and the presumption of the validity of these khatian remains un-rebutted. The schedule "Ka" to the plaint has correctly described the land shown in the SA khatian No. 147 of Mouza Sathalia, PS Saghata under District-Gaibanda. 

 13. I also find that, the plaintiffs have proved their case by adducing PW 1, who has deposed in support of the plaintiff's case and proved the documentary evidence including aforesaid khatians to support their prima-facie case regarding their lawful possession in the suit land and he was corroborated by PWs 2 and 3, but the defendants did not cross examine these PW Nos. 2 and 3, nor did they adduce witness to prove their positive case.

lawyer:
M Golam Rabbani with AKM Asaduzzaman, Advocates ----- For the Appellants.  
AY Salehuzzaman, DAG  ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Noor Mohammad Khan & ors ----- Appellants  
Vs. 
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh & ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The case of the plaintiffs, inter alia, was that the suit plot No. 5 measuring an area of 45.93 acres of land belonged to Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate as the recorded owner in the CS Khatian No. 1 of mouza Chowbaria under Police Station Savar, District Dhaka and the said Court of Wards Estate settled the said land in rayoti right to the plaintiff No. 1 on 20.6.1353 BS by granting Amalnama and rent receipt in his favour on receiving salami; that the plaintiff No. 1 settled part of the suit land to some tenants and he remained in possession of 28.79 acres of land after such settlement; that the plaintiff No. 1 subsequently gifted another portion of the suit land to his children, plaintiff Nos. 2-5 and thus all the plaintiffs remained in possession of the suit land; that at the initial stage of the SA settlement operation the suit land was recorded in the name of the plaintiff No. 1 but the defendant No. 2 most illegally and behind the back of the plaintiff No. 1 got the suit property recorded in SA khatian in the name of the defendant No. 2; that subsequently in RS khatian the same mistake was committed by recording the land in the name of the defendant No. 2; that the plaintiff No. 1 who was away from the country could not know about the wrong recording of the name of defendant No. 2 in the SA as well as RS Khatian; that the wrong recording of the suit land in the RS Khatian cast cloud over the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land giving rise to the cause of action of the suit. 

 3. Defendant Government of Bangladesh contested the suit by filing a written statement denying material allegations and stating, inter alia, that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and is not maintainable; that the defendant government further denied that the Dhaka Court of Wards Estate settled the suit plot to the plaintiff No. by granting amalnama or rent receipt on receipt of salami or that the plaintiff No. 1 leased out some portions of the suit plot to some tenants and the suit land remained in his possession or that the plaintiff No. 1 gifted some portion of the suit property to plaintiff Nos. 2-5 or that the plaintiffs have been owning and possessing the same peacefully. The further case of the defendant Government is that the suit plot was declared as reserved forest under Gazette Notification No. 3125 dated 13.4.55 published in the Dhaka Gazette on 5th May, 1965 and subsequently the Nowab Estate was acquired by the Government under the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Since the aforesaid Gazette Notification suit plot is in peaceful possession of the Forest Department. The Exlandlord of Dhaka Nawab Estate entered into an agreement with the Collector of Mymensingh and Dhaka on 26.1.1923 for the management of the forest and as such ex-landlord had no right to settle the suit plot to the plaintiff No. 1. The suit plot having been correctly recorded in the name of the Forest Department in the SA and RS Khatian, the suit is barred under section 144B of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The plaintiffs in order to grab the forest land of the Government have filed the suit on the basis of forged, fabricated, ante-dated and fraudulent papers. The plaintiffs did not acquire any right, title, interest or possession in the suit land on the basis of the alleged amalnama and rent receipt. 

 8. Mr. AY Salehuzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the defendant Government, submitted that in paragraph Nos. 5-7 of the plaint the plaintiff asserted that SA Khatian as well as RS Khatian in respect of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant Government. Under section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, there is presumption of correctness of the entry made in the RS Khatian and as such presumption of possession of the suit land is in favour of the defendant Government and the plaintiffs having failed to satisfactorily prove their possession in the suit land, the suit for mere declaration of title without prayer for consequential relief by way of either confirmation or recovery of possession of the suit land is barred under the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submitted that the plaintiffs asserted in the plaint that at the initial stage of preparation of record of rights the name of plaintiff No. 1 was re-corded in the S.A. khatian and subsequently the same was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant No. 2 and R.S. khatian is simply a copy of the S.A. khatian and that part of the suit plot was leased out by the plaintiff No.1 to some of the tenants and the same were recorded in their names but the plaintiffs failed to produce any khatian to show that part of the suit plot was recorded in the name of the alleged tenants of plaintiff No. 1 or compensation assessment roll for payment of compensation to the plaintiff No. 1 for the said tenanted land was prepared in the name of the plaintiff No. 1. Moreover, the plaintiffs could not produce any rent receipt granted either to them or to their tenants after the acquisition of Dhaka Court of Wards Estate by the Government. He further submitted that as the plaintiffs failed to prove their case there was no question of discharging onus by the defendant Government by adducing oral evidence or by producing counter-foils of rent receipts genuineness of which was challenged by the defendant Government. 

 10. We are to consider here whether the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title to the suit land. Ext. 1 is the receipt for payment of salami to the Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate. Ext. 2 is the alleged Amalnama granted by the said Estate settling the suit land to the plaintiff No. 1 and Ext 3 series are the rent receipts granted for the years 1353, 1354 and 1358 B.S. by the said Estate. The appellants have not included the said documents in the Paper Book though the Rules provide that part II of the Paper Book shall consist of exhibits and no finding or conclusion in the decision appealed from will be permitted to be challenged at the hearing of the appeal unless the materials on which such challenge is based is included in the Paper Book. As such we are not bound to consider the said documents. However, we have perused the said documents in the lower court records. The contents of Exts. 1 and 3 series were written with pencil and Ext. 2 with ink as pointed out by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. He also pointed out that the receipts were rubbed to make the same appear old and the same were written with pencil instead of ink so as to avoid the same from being checked. We have noticed from Ext. 1 that the amount of salami was received subject to the approval of the Chief Manager and from the remarks in the bottom of the said Ext No. 1 it appears that salami and rents received without approval of the Chief Manager will not have the effect of settling the land of the Estate to the person paying the same. We find from Ext. 2 that it is a form of proposal for settlement of the land of the said Estate and there was no approval of the Chief Manager. We have also noticed from Ext. 3 series, rent receipts that unless settlement is approved by the authorised officer of the Estate claim or settlement of land cannot be made on the basis of payment of rent. In Ext. 2 it has also been clearly written that the proposal for settlement of land will not be effective unless the tenant executes kabuliyat in favour of the landlord. The plaintiff No. 1 as PW 1 stated that the receipt for payment of salami was signed by Gobinda Chandra Roy, Cashier of Dhaka Nowab Estate in his presence and the said receipt was marked Ext. 1. The said witness further stated in his deposition that the suit land was leased out to him by the document of lease executed by the officers of Nowab Estate including Assistant Manager, Dhaka Nowab Estate by signing before him and the document was marked Ext. 2. He further stated that these are the signatures of the Head Assistant and Assistant Manager in the said document marked Exts. 2(i) and 2(ii). He further stated that he paid rent to the Nowab Estate afterwards and rent receipts were granted by the Dhaka Nowab Estate and the same were marked Ext. 3 series. From the cross-examination of this witness we find that he was a school student at the relevant time of taking lease and that he did not pay any rent from 1359 BS upto date. PW 5, who claimed himself to be an ex-employee of Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate as orderly of the then Assistant Manager, stated in his deposition that the Assistant Manager Abul Kashem executed Ext. 2 in his presence and proved his signature marked Ext. 2(ii). He further stated that receipt of salami Ext.1 and rent receipts were granted by Dhaka Nowab Estate. From his cross-examination, we find that he is an illiterate person and he could not satisfy the court that he ever worked as orderly of the said Estate. We are unable to place any reliance on the testimony of PW 5. He appears to be a procured witness who does not know how to sign his name and put his thumb impression in the deposition sheet. PW1 being the plaintiff and a school student at the relevant time on his own admission cannot also be relied on as he is interested in the result of the suit. The contents of the said documents were not even attempted to be proved by the PW1. Considering the evidence of the said witnesses we arc of the view that the said documents were not legally proved as writing of the said documents could not be proved by examining any witness. We are unable to appreciate the argument of the learned Advocate of the appellants that the said documents were legally proved. The decision referred to by the learned Advocate has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. From the very look the said documents appear to be spurious and manufactured for the purpose of the suit in collusion with the interested persons. Even if these documents are accepted as genuine the same could not create title in favour of the plaintiffs in the absence of the approval by the Chief Manager and execution of kabuliyat in compliance thereof. It appears that the alleged settlement by the said document were not acted upon as the plaintiffs failed to produce any rent receipts granted by the Government after the acquisition of rent receiving interest nor they could produce any khatian alleged to be prepared in the name of their alleged tenants in respect of part of the suit plot or any compensation assessment roll in the name of the plaintiffs or in respect of the said tenanted land or any khatian alleged to have been prepared in the name of the plaintiff No. 1 at the initial stage. Moreover, the PW 1 himself admitted that he did not pay rent from 1359 BS upto date. 

 11. Thus the plaintiffs having failed to prove their case there is no question of failure of the defendant Government to discharge any onus as the defendant Government did not admit plaintiffs' case of settlement of the suit land to the plaintiffs by setting up any counter case. In the trial Court the plaintiffs rightly began their case first and examined their witnesses in support of their case. In this case, we find that the defendant Govt. did not adduce any evidence except cross-examining the PWs. Order 18, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with order of production of evidence by the parties and not with onus which depends on the pleading of the parties. Plaintiffs' case having been totally denied by the defendant Government in the written statement, the onus to prove the case was entirely on the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs having failed to prove their case there was no onus on the defendant Government to discharge by producing either oral or documentary evidence. As the plaintiffs neither adduced any evidence to show that counterfoils of the rent receipts produced by them were in the custody of the defendant Govt. nor they called for any such counterfoils from the defendant Government, so we find no reason to form an adverse presumption against the defendant Government for non-production of any such documents existence of which were denied by the Government. 

 13. Though the Government did not examine any witness they produced copy of Dhaka Gazette dated May 5, 1955 publishing Notification No. 3125-For-13th April, 1955 under section 4 of the Forest Act, 1927 in respect of the suit plot No. 5 of Mouza Chowbaria. This Notification is a preliminary of vesting of the land contained in the said notification. The Government did not take any step to produce the Notification under section 20 of the Forest Act which is a natural culmination of a preliminary Notification under section 4 of the Forest Act. As we have already found that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title or possession in the suit land there is no necessity of deciding whether the suit land vested in the Government as reserved forest land. Admittedly SA khatian and subsequently prepared and published RS khatian are in the name of the defendant No. 2 Forest Department. RS khatian prepared under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has presumption of correctness under section 144A of the said Act. The plaintiffs having failed to displace the said presumption by proving their title and possession in the suit land the plaintiffs are not entitled to any decree and the learned Subordinate Judge rightly dismissed the suit.
justice_names: Mr. Justice A.R.M. Amirul Islam Chowdhury

lawyer:
Asrarul Hossain, Sr. Advocate, with Mozammel Huq Bhuiyan, Advocate Instructed by Md. Nurul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Appellants. 
Serajul Huq, Advocate, instructed by Aminul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Respondents No. 1-8, 10, 11 &13-20. 
Ex-parte-Respondent No. 9 Struck ------- off Respondent No. 12.
parties:
Ajufannessa @ Aji Bibi and others  ------- Appellants.
Vs.
Safar Miah and others  ------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff's case in brief is that the land in suit comprises a plot of land being C. S Plot No.310 measuring '80 acre, which was recorded, along with CS. Plot No.311 measuring .08 acre, as Koljote of one Mainuddin, the predecessor-in-interest of Defendants No.2 to 9, in Khatian No.83 of mouza Rajarbagh P.S. Tejgaon, under the Jote of one Mani Mohan Dutta, which was recorded in Khatian No.82 of the mouza under the superior interest of one Haladhar Dey Sarkar. The father's name of Mainuddin was wrongly mentioned to be Ainuddin in Khatian No.83 in place of his correct name of Amir. The jote of Mani Mohan Dutta was put to auction in execution of a decree for arrears of rent obtained by Haladhar Dey Sarker and purchased by the decree-holder on 6-7-38. The sale was confirmed on 11-8-38 and delivery of possession of the auction purchased property was taken through Court on 23-1-39. The decree-holder auction purchaser having possessed the land for sometime settled the land of C S Plot No.311, on which the homestead was situated, with Mainuddin, son of Amir, at an annual rent of Rs. 1/6/-annas on the basis of a Kabuliyat executed on 27-3-39 and registered on 1-4-39. The other plot, namely C S. Plot No.310, remained in the khas possession of the auction-purchaser till 15-1-41, when the same was settled with the predecessor of plaintiffs No.1 to 18, and plaintiff No.19 off behalf of himself and on behalf of plaintiff No.20, on the basis of a registered Kabuliyat of the said date. Taking advantage of the wrong recording of the father's name of Mainuddin in the record-of-right defendant No.10 who happened to be an Advocate of the Dacca High Court, along with his relative defendant No.11, created some Kabalas in collusion with the heirs of Mainuddin to grab a portion of the land which has become valuable in the meantime. A dispute having arisen as to the possession of the land, defendant No.3, initiated a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, in which possession having been found by the Magistrate, who was trying proceeding, in favour of the defendants, possession has been taken by the defendants from the receiver who had been appointed by the said Magistrate in the said proceeding. 

 3. Two sets of written statement were filed in this case, one by Defendants No.1 to 9 and the other by Defendants No.10 and 11 and the contentions raised therein are more or less the same. According to the contesting defendants, Mainuddin was a holder of an occupancy raiyati-right and was recorded as such in C.S. Khatian No.83 and his father's name also was correctly recorded therein as Ainuddin. The alleged auction sale of the interest of Mani Mohan Dutta, the landlord of Mainuddin is not true and, even if there had been any such auction-sale it did not affect the interest of Mainuddin, as it was a protected interest under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. In case, however, such an interest is held to be an encumbrance it had not been annulled by service of a notice, as required under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The story of granting settlement by the alleged auction purchaser of C.S. Plot No.311 to Mainuddin or of C.S. Plot No.310 to the plaintiffs is without any foundation and Mainuddin and his heirs, during the old age of Mainuddin, and after his death, during the minority of Defendants No.2 and 3, had all along been in possession of the disputed land through the plaintiffs and their predecessors as bargadars. 

 11. At the outset it may be pointed out that the view of the learned Judges of the High Court that the defendants had no locus standi to claim any interest in the suit land in the context of their allegation as to the father's name of Mainuddin being Ainuddin was misconceived. The father's name of Mainuddin was found to be Amir and not Ainuddin as wrongly stated in the C.S. Khatian No.83. The case of the plaintiffs in this regard was accepted and that of the defendant's was rejected, by the said courts. It was the plaintiff's case that defendants No.1-9 was successors-in-interest of Mainuddin who was the holder of the land recorded in Khatian No.83. The defence case on this question was also the same. The difference between the two cases was only in respect of the father's name of Mainuddin. According to the plaintiff, it was Amir, as was mentioned in the Kabuliyat Ext.3, and not Ainuddin as was mentioned in the Khatian Ext. 6, but according to the defence, it was Ainuddin and not Amir and it has been correctly stated in the Khatian Ext.6. The learned Judges of the High Court have observed that as defendants No.1-9 had admittedly no connection with Mainuddin, son of Amir, the Courts below ought to have held that these defendants had no locus standi to claim the suit land. It is not the case of the plaintiffs nor of the defendants that there were two Mainuddin, one being the son of Ainuddin and the other being the son of Amir and that the disputed land belonged either to Mainuddin son of Ainuddin or Maiauddin son of Amir. The findings of both the Courts below on this question were also that the defendants were the successors of Mainuddin, who was admittedly the holder of the land of Khatian No.83, but the father's name of the said Mainuddin was not Ainuddin, as claimed by the defendants, but was Amir, as asserted by the plaintiffs; So the observation of the learned Judges on this question that the Courts below ought to have held that the defendants had no locus standi to claim the suit land is based upon some misapprehension. 

 12. As has been indicated above, the learned Judges of the High Court disagreed with the concurrent finding of the two Courts below rejecting the plea of the settlement advanced by the plaintiffs. The plaintiff’s case of separate settlement of each of the two plots of land, appertaining to Khatian No.83 of Mouza Rajarbagh, after their auction purchase by the heirs of Haladhar Dey Sarker, one with Mainuddin by Ext.3 and the other with the plaintiffs by Ext. 3(a) was disbelieved by the learned Subordinate Judge on the grounds that the heir of Haladhar Dey Sarkar did not acquire any right, title and interest in the disputed lands and had, therefore, no authority to settle such land, that the case of surrender of the lands of Khatian No.83 by Maiauddin to the auction purchasers, which was not pleaded but was argued at the time of trial was very improbable and that the settlement by Ext.3 with Mainuddin of only C.S. Plot No.311 measuring .08 acre on which a part of his homestead was situated, the remaining part of the homestead, having been upon the other plot, was not acceptable in the facts and circumstances of the case. In the context of these findings the question of genuineness of the rent receipts, Ext. 4 series, which were produced by the plaintiffs in support of their case of settlement of C.S. Plot No.310 with them on the basis of the Kabuliyat, Ext.3(a) was examined by the trial Court as well as by the Court of first appeal who recorded the concurrent finding that those rent receipt were fabricated documents, The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have expressed disagreement with the aforesaid finding on the view that in judging this question the said Court had committed an error in regard to the burden of proof and that, as such, their finding was not tenable in law. We do not think that the learned Judges of the High Court were correct in their view that the findings of the Courts below on the question of the genuineness of the rent receipts had been vitiated by a wrong view of the burden of proof and were justified in rejecting the said finding for the purpose of the disposal of the appeal. 

 15. It will be found from the findings of the Courts below, as have been quoted above, that on an examination of the Dakhilas Ext. 4 series in the light of the circumstances, both of the Courts below arrived at the finding that those Dakhilas were fabricated documents Non-production of counterfoils was found to be circumstance indicating spuriousness of the-said papers. The said findings were not in any way based upon any presumption arising from any burden of proof. The learned Judges of the High Court, however, thought that the said findings had been vitiated by an error committed by the courts below as to the burden of proof applicable to the case. They have proceeded on the view that the Ext. 4 series had been disbelieved by the said Courts only on the ground of non-production of the counterfoils of the said Dakhilas and expressed the view that the primary onus of proving the rent receipts was discharged by the plaintiff as soon as tie rent receipts were produced in the Court from the proper custody and were proved and if the defendants chose to challenge the genuineness of the said Dakhilas, the onus shifted on them to prove their assertion. 

 18. In this case the plaintiffs have come to the court with the assertion that the disputed land was settled with them by the owners of the land on the basis of the Kabuliyat Ext.3 (a) and produced the Dakhilas Ext. 4 series in proof of the fact that the Kabuliyat was acted upon on subsequent payment of rent in pursuance of the said settlement. According to section 101 of the Act, as referred to above, it is for the plaintiffs to prove that as a matter of fact, settlement was granted by the owners of the land and the rent receipts Ext. 4 series were really genuine and represented the correct state of things, as the plaintiffs desire the Court to believe on the said assertion. The burden of proof as to the genuineness of the Dakhila Ext. 4 series is undoubtedly upon them in the absence of any legislative provision to the contrary. There having been no legislative enactment requiring the Dakhilas, Ext. 4 series, which had been formally proved at the trial of the suit, to be accepted as genuine documents, merely on proof thereof there is no question of shifting the onus upon the defendants. The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have been under a misapprehension as to the real effect of formal proof of a document in a Court of law. A private document cannot be taken notice of and marked as an Exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a per-son, as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There may be cases where the law requires that the content’s of particular document shall be presumed to be correct unless they are rebutted by adducing evidence by a party who disputes their correctness, as has been provided in Section 103B of the Beagal tenancy Act and Section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a land-lord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. The learned Judges of the High Court have apparently made a mistake in taking the view that as soon as the rent receipts have been proved the primary onus of the plaintiffs has been discharged and the defendants having failed to produce any rebutting evidence the said rent receipts should have been accepted as genuine and relied upon. The onus of the plaintiffs cannot be discharged until the court is persuaded to accept the position that there had been payment of rent by the tenant and acceptance thereof by the landlord, as a matter of fact, on the basis of the disputed rent receipts. In this case, both of the courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or procedure which had affected the merits of the case. The learned Judges of the High Court do not appear to pay much attention to the views of the Court below as to the several suspicious features which had been specifically referred to in the judgment of the said Courts but appear to have been influenced in their decision by a wrong view of the law as to the burden of proof. The learned Judges were not correct in the view that the lower appellant court discarded the said rent receipts only on the ground of non-production of counterfoils of the said rent receipts. The question whether a particular rent receipt, proved by a party may, be accepted without the production of the counterfoil of the said rent receipt is a question of fact and depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. Under the circumstances, the learned Judges of the High Court exceeded their jurisdiction wider section 100 of the Act in refusing to accept the concurrent finding of fact of the courts below as to the spurious character of the Dkahilas Ext. 4 series. 

 19. The finding of the two courts of fact that the plaintiffs were initially inducted upon the disputed land as bargadars under Mainuddin was dependent, to a certain extent, upon their finding on the question of the plaintiff's title, as sought to be established at the trial court by adducing evidence. The plaintiff's case is that the jote of Mani Mohan Dutta, as recorded in Khatian No.82, was auction purchased by the heirs of the decree-holders, Haladar Dey Sarkar, and was thereafter settled with the plaintiffs on 15.1.41 by a Kabuliyat Ext.13(a). The greatest hindrance, found by the Courts below, to the acceptance of the story of settlement as sought to be made out by the plaintiffs, was the character of Mainuddin's interest as recorded in Khatian No.83 of mouza Rajarbagh and the complete absence of any pleading as to how the said interest was extinguished. Both of the said Courts took the view that the entries in the Khatian clearly showed that the interest of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat which was protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and, therefore, by the auction sale of the superior right of his landlord, who was a tenure holder his interest as a raiyat was not affected at all. It was pointed out by the trial Court that even if it was held that the interest of Mainuddin was an under raiyati, not protected under section 160 of the Act, it would be an encumbrance which required a notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act for its annulment and that the service of any such notice having not been pleaded nor proved, the interest of Mainuddin could not be extinguished. At the time of the trial a new case as to the surrender by Mainuddin of his interest was sought to be established by proving a Kabuliyat Ext.3. In respect of C.S. plot No.311 and by adducing oral evidence to show that possession of plot No.311 was given up by Mainuddin in favour of the auction purchasers. The story of the surrender of the lands of C.S. Khatian No.83 and the giving up of possession of C.S plot No.310 was completely disbelieved by the said two Courts on an analysis of the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties in respect thereof and on a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. One of the points considered by the said Courts in this connection was that the homestead of Mainuddin was not confined to C.S. plot No.311 only but it spread over to a part of C.S. plot No.310 as well. 

 20. The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have expressed to view that the findings of the Courts below that the interest of Mainuddin was protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act having been reached without considering the provision contained in section 48G (3) of the Act which lays down that the right of occupancy enjoyed by an under raiyat should not be a protected interest under section 160 of the Act are not tenable in law. This view of the High Court is based upon the assumption that the interest of Mainuddin was that of an under raiyat, but there appears to be absolutely no basis for such an assumption. On a consideration of the entries of the Khatian No.82 and 83 of Mouza Rajarbagb, Ext. 6 and 6(a) both the Courts below came to the view that Mainuddin was a raiyat having a right of occupancy under Mani Mohan Dutta, who was a tenure holder. As a matter of fact, in the said Khatian the superior landlord of Mainuddin was specifically described as "Madhya Swatwadhlkary chiro-sthayee (i.e. parmanent tenure holder) and Mainuddin was stated to be a 'raiyat Sthitiban' i.e. settled raiyat of the village having regard to the said specific description as to Mainuddin being a settled ratyat having a right of occupancy there is hardly any scope for the court to conceive that Mainuddin was an under raiyat. 

 21. The learned Judges of the High Court seem to have been carried away by the term 'Kole jote’ which was stated to be the interest of Mainuddin in the said khatians, presumably on the assumption that the term 'Jote' invariably indicated the interest of a raiyat. This assumption of the learned Judges is obviously not correct because the term 'Jote' is a general term and sometimes used also to indicate the interest of a tenure holder and it is not necessarily equivalent to a raiyati jote, as was observed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Midnapore Zamindary Co. Vs. Naresb Narayan Singh L.R. 48 I.A. 49. I.L.R.48 Cal. 460 AIR 1922 P.C. 241. Similarly in the case of Krishna Nath Sarker Vs. Uani Kusam Kumar Das, AIR 1923 Cal.351 it was held by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court that the expression 'Jote' was a general term and did not necessarily mean a raiyati and in the facts of that case it was held to be a tenure. On the other hand in the case of Upendra Kishore Sarkar Vs. Sk Khalil, AIR. 1937 Cal. 568: 55 C.LJ, 170 it was held by another Division Bench of the said High Court that the word ‘Jote' might mean even an under raiyati. In the case of Sariatullah Vs. Joinuddin A.I.R 1935 Cal, 463; 39 C.W.N.454. Nasim Ali, J. of the Calcutta high Court in holding that the word 'Jote' did indicate in the facts of that case that it was a tenure made the following observation— 

 22. Even if the view that the term 'Jote' must neceesarily mean a raiyati Jote and 'Kol-jote' similarly would mean an under raiyat, both the Courts of fact having accepted the status of Mainuddin to be that of a raiyat on the basis of the specific description of such interest to be a raiyati and the jote of the superior landlord as a tenure, the learned Judges of the High Court were not justified in taking the said interest to be an under raiyati without properly coming to a finding that the description of Mainuddin to be a raiat and of his landlord to be a tenure holder in the Khatian was incorrect. The learned Judges of the High Court were not therefore correct in assuming the status of Mani Mohan Dutta the superior landlord of Mainuddin, as that of a raiyat and that of Mainuddin as an under raiyat simply from the description of their interest as Jote and koljote respectively in the C.S Khatian No.83. The term jote is a general expression and means a tenancy and the status of a holder of such a tenancy i.e. whether it is that of a tenure holder or of a raiyat will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. So far as the entries in Khatian No. 83 is concerned the specific nature of the tenancy as described in the terms 'Jote’ and 'Kol jot' were clearly spelt out by the use of expressions Chiro sthayee Madhya Swatwadhikary and sthitiban Raiyat in the Khatian itself, which give rise to statutory presumption as to the correctness of such description. No case as to the incorrectness of these entries in the Khatian was pleaded in the plaint nor any rebutting evidence was adduced by the plaintiffs at the time of the trial, although it was contended at the time of argument that the interest of Mainuddin was not that of raiyat and as such was not protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The learned Subordinate-Judge pointed out in his judgment that the term 'Jote' was ambiguous and might mean also tenure and also that it had been admitted by P.W.14, a relation and agent of Haladar Dey Sarkar, the superior landlord of Mani Mohan Dutta, that the status of Mani Mohan Dutta was that of a tenure holder. So the learned Subordinate Judge had no difficulty in coming to the finding that the interest of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. On appeal this view was affirmed by the Court of the Additional District Judge. It is significant, as it appears from the judgment of the said Court that no issue was joined on this question on behalf of the plaintiffs and that it was conceded by the learned lawyer appearing on behalf of the appellants in the said appeal that the status of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat. In the Second Appeal, however, this question appears to have been raised by the learned lawyer on behalf of the appellants in spite of their concession on this point in the last court of fact and the learned Judges of the High Court appear to have failed to take notice of the concurrent findings of the Courts below on this question and seem to have been carried away by the expression 'Koljote' as mentioned in the Khatian and assumed that such expression necessarily meant an under raiyati. The learned Judges appear to have held on the basis of such assumption that the provisions of section 48(G) 3 of the Act was attracted and as such the interest of Mainuddin was not a protected interest under section 160 of the Act. 

 23. It has been pointed out above that there is absolutely no basis for this assumption We have pointed out that the question whether Mainuddin was a raiyat or an under raiyat at is a question of fact and the entries in the C.S. Khatian raised a presumption in favour of the correctness of the entries made in the said khatian. In the absence of any rebutting evidence both the Courts below came to a concurrent finding as to the status of Mainuddin being that of a raiyat, relying upon the said entries and also upon the evidence and the facts and circumstances of the case. No error of law or procedure affecting the merits of the case were pointed out in regard to the said finding and as such the said finding was binding upon the High Court in the Second Appeal.
