2. Their claims are that the suit Jama recorded in C.S. Khatian Nos.  84, 69 and 47, described in schedule Nos.  1,3 and 4 was owned and possessed by Karful Bewa and the Jama in the C.S. Khatian Nos. 120, 53 and 16 of Mouza Jamalpur now Palisha Indrakuchi and Pakhalia described in schedule Nos. 2, 5 and 6 was owned and possessed by Karful Bewa and Barandi Mondal in equal share. Barandi Mondal died leaving 4 sons, the defendant No. 5 Azijatullah Mondal, Shahed Ali Mondal, Alimuddin Mondal and Jabbar Mondal and 4 daughters, Nekjan, Sokina, Sakiran and Atarjan. Shahed Ali died leaving behind one son Baitullah and 3 daughters, the defendant No. 7, Most. Hinduri, Zahiran and Ahiran. Zahiran died leaving her husband the defendant No. 8. Ohiran died leaving 4 sons, defendant Nos. 9-12. Alimuddin died leaving the defendant No. 13 and 3 sons, the defendant Nos. 17-19 and Haziran. Haziran died leaving her only son, the defendant No. 20. Abdul Jabber died leaving Sons and daughters, the defendant Nos. 21-31, Nekjan Bewa died after the promulgation of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance,1961 leaving son Khamir Master and the defendant Nos. 24- 31 and son Jasim Uddin. Khamir Master died Leaving 3 sons, the defendant Nos. 25-27 and 3 daughters, the defendant Nos. 38-30. Jasimuddin died leaving behind wife, the defendant Nos. 30 and 3 sons, the defendant Nos. 33-35 and 2 daughters, the defendant Nos. 36 and 37, Sakina died leaving 2 sons, the defendant Nos. 38 and 39 and 2 daughters, Sahera and Rahima and husband Nazar Master Ralunan and the defendant No. 50. Naser Master died leaving daughter, the defendant No. 41. Atarjan died leaving behind her husband, the defendant No. 42 and 2 sons, the defendant Nos. 43 and 44, and 4 daughters, the defendant Nos. 45-48. Julekha died leaving the defendant No. 49. Karpul Bewa died leaving 2 brothers, Samir Mondal and Sadar Mondal. Samir Mondal died leaving wife Asimon and son Abdul Mondal. Sadar Mondal died leaving son Taison Ali and daughter Tambiton Bewa. Ahdul Mondal sold 2.76 acres of land by Kabala deed dated 11th September, 1961 to the plaintiff No. 1. Taison and Asimon sold 3.30 acres of land to the plaintiff No. 2 by Kabala dated 1st September, 1961. Taison, Abdul and Asimon Bewa transferred 2.85½ acres of land to Fulzan by deed of exchange. Fulzan died leaving behind her son the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 daughters, the defendant Nos. 2-4, Plaintiff No. 2 sold .30 acre and .45 acre of land out of his purchased and inherited land to the plaintiff No. 1 by two Kabalas. Plaintiff No. 2 transferred some land to his wife, Keni Bibi, and Rahimuddin sold .75 acres of land to the plaintiff No. 3. Thus plaintiffs possessed 7.32 acres of land in the suit Jama and claimed saham in respect of the same on the ground that the suit Jams was never partitioned. The defendants refused to partition the suit land. 

 3. Some of the appellants who are defendant Nos. 6-12 and their predecessors contested the suit jointly. Their case in short is that the suit land under C.S. Khatian Nos. 84 and 120 belonged to Barundi Mondal alone. Karful Bewa had no share in the same. The name of Karful Bewa was wrongly recorded in the Khatians. Neither she nor her heirs ever possessed the suit land. The heirs of Borundi Mondal were in possession of the land in CS, Khatians exclusively. The suit jama which was recorded in c.s. Khatian Nos. 69, 47, 53 and 16 of Mouza Pathatia was under possession of Sadi Mondal, who died leaving widow Karful Bewa and brother Barundi Mondal. His widow Karful Bewa inherited 4 annas share in the property left by Sadi Mondal. Borundi possessed 12 annas share. After his death the heirs have been in possession of the property. Karful Bewa had no issue, she had adopted Naimuddin, predecessor of the plaintiff Nos. 1-2 and she made a Hiba-bil-ewaz in respect of some property out of the suit khatians to him. There arose dispute between the sons of Borundi Mondal and Naimuddin. Thereafter on 2nd Paush 1337 a deed of relinquishment was executed in respect of the said lands. Tasirudden, the only son of Sadar Mondal executed a Nadabi Patra on 17th January, 1935 in favour of the sons of Borundi Mondal. 

 6. Question that calls for consideration is whether the presumptive value that the C.S. khatian can be rebuttable by the S.A, khatian prepared under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in the absence of any other evidence. Mr. Bhuiyan submitted that since the S.A, khatian was prepared after hearing objections of the plaintiffs, the High Court,. Division has committed fundamental error in giving the presumptive value to the S.A. Khatians over the S.A. Khatian. In support of his contention he has referred the case of Pramatha Nath Vs. Kamir Mondal, 17 DLR(SC) 392. The second point raised by the learned counsel is that the High Court Division erred in law in interfering with the judgment of the court of appeal below without reversing the findings of fact arrived at by the final court of fact on the question of record of rights. 

 7. There is no dispute that out of 6 khatians, 4 khatians were prepared showing Sadi Mondal's jote and in respect to two khatians Borundi Mondal's jote was recorded. Of the 6 khatians, Karful Bewa was shown to have exclusive possession in respect of 3 khatians and in respect of other 3 khatians, Karful Bewa had 8 annas share and Borundi Mondal 8 annas share. This Borundi Mondal is the brother of Sadi Mondal. In paragraph 7 of the written statement the defendant Nos. 6 and 21 admitted that Karful Bewa had sixteen annas possession in respect of C.S. Khatian No. 84 and that she had 8 annas share in respect of C.S. Khatian No. 120. It was held in Promatha Nath (supro) that The presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is only this that the entry in the record-of-right represents the correct state of affairs on the date it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs is continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is its presumptive value. This is a matter, therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive proof." 

 8. With due respect I am unable to endorse the above views that after a presumption attaches to a record of right under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 such presumption diminishes progressively with the lapse of time and that the older the record the less is its presumptive value. H, Rahman, J, did not cite any authority basing upon which he has arrived at such conclusion. An entry in a record-of-rights under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act is presumed to be correct until the contrary is shown. (Anup Mahto V. Mite Dusadh, 59 CLG 147 (PC). It was concluded by the judicial committee that 'therefore all the courts have to do with the Record is to apply this presumption as directed by the section. It is because such record-of-rights was prepared with considerable formality and the proceedings of the Revenue Offices were conducted with publicity after hearing objections against draft record. The Revenue Officers heard and decided disputes following the procedure of the Code of Civil Procedure, It is true that no finality attached to them and it was open to the parties to reopen the questions decided in the ordinary civil courts. Until a civil court decides the dispute, a presumption of correctness shall continue. This presumption being statutory one is not taken away merely by an allegation by a party that the entry was not correct. The presumption under this section may be rebutted by either evidence external to the settlement proceedings or evidence of matters apparent on the face of those proceedings. 

 9. A presumption is a rule of law that courts shall draw a particular inference from a particular fact or from particular evidence unless and until the truth of such inference is disproved. A presumption of law is a rule of law that a particular inference shall be drawn by a court from a particular circumstance. A presumption of law is always obligatory being expressed in the, form of an imperative rule of law and therefore, the court is bound to act according to the rule and cannot refuse to draw the presumption. This presumption may or may not be rebuttable. When rebutted it is called rebuttable presumption of law and is indicated in the Evidence Act by the expression 'shall presume'. This presumption occurs in sections 79-85, 89 and 105. When not rebuttable it is called "irrebuttable presumptions of law" or "conclusive proof". Three instances of such presumptions are mentioned in sections 41 and 112. Presumptions are rebuttable, as their evidentiary effect may be negative by contrary proof. They are indicated in the Evidence Act by the expression 'may presume' and are mentioned in sections 86-88, 90 and 114. When a presumption operates in favour of a party, the burden of proof is on the opponent. It is true, a presumption of law in favour of the accuracy of the entry in the record-of-rights cannot arise when the point in issue has already been decided on evidence between the parties by a decision of the civil court. 

 10. To rebut such presumption the defendants have filed only a khatian, the record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act, 1950. Except the said khatian, they have failed to produce any other evidence. The court of appeal below held that since the record-of-rights was prepared in the name of the defendants after a contested hearing before the Revenue Officer under section 19(3), the defendants have been able to prove their title in the suit land. There is fallacy in the opinion. The court of appeal below erred in holding the above view for, a record-of-rights prepared under Section 19(3) of the Act of 1950 cannot confer title upon person in whose favour it was prepared. Even the record-of-rights prepared   under the repealed section 143A cannot be the basis of title to the land. It may be used for collateral purpose of possession.   If the views taken by the court of appeal view are accepted, no litigant will be required to take shelter to the civil court for establishing the right, title and interest in the suit land. 

 12. Section 18 says, the particulars should be recorded in the record-of-rights. When a draft record-of-rights prepared or revised under section 19(1) containing particulars referred to in section 18, the publication of the draft is with a view to receive and consider any objection that may be made as regards any entry in the record-of-rights. The finality referred to in sub-section (3) of section 19 which shall have conclusive evidence is for the purpose of payment of compensation and the court cannot draw any presumption other than that There is no presumption of possession of land in respect of record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) like the one under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Reference in this connection are the cases of Halima Begum V. Syed Ahmed, 21 DLR 854, Chan Mahmood (Md) V. Md. Hossain Ali, 3 BLC 364, Abdul Kader Bari V. Kaiser Ahmed Howlader, 4 BLC 17, Ahmed Meah V. Abdul Majid, BLD 1985 (HCD)47, Md. Naimuddin Sarder V. Abdul Kalam Biswas, 39 DLR(AD) 237. In Halima Begum the preemptor claimed pre-emption as co-sharer on the strength of record-an-right prepared under the Act of 1950. It was observed that record-of-right indicates certain right of certain parties but that right is certainly dependent on some material evidence, oral and documentary so as to establish title in favour of persons who claim under the said record of right. The presumption of correctness as to C.S. record of right is not certainly available with regard to State Acquisition Khatians, There is no presumption of correctness in respect of the State Acquisition Khatians.... I add here that certainly there will he presumption of the correctness of the B.S. Khatians prepared or to he prepared after a thorough survey which is under process. 

 13. In Akrab Ali V. Zahiruddin, 30 DLR(SC) 81 relates to presumption as to the entries in the settlement records. The settlement khatian was recorded as 'jote Aftab Uddin Sarkar occupant Faizuddin Haji by purchase at Rs. 50'; In the column of the tenancy it has been described as the and  right of a settled raiyat d in the column 'rent', a remark has been made to the effect 'fit for rent but no transaction The C.S record-of-rights was finally published in the district of Dhaka before the amendment   of Bengal Tenancy Act, when any transfer of an occupancy raiyoti holding or a part thereof was compulsorily registerable, irrespective of the fact whether the consideration was above or below Rs 100 Before such amendment, in view of section 17 of the Registration Act, only those transfers which were for Rs 100 and above were compulsorily registerable The purchase of the land appertaining to C S Plot No 1873 by Foizuddin Haji from Aftab Uddin Sarkar for Rs 50 did not require under the law a registered instrument It was made orally Faizuddin Haji got into occupation of the land by virtue of his purchase from Aftab Uddin, who was a settled raiyat of the village but no rent appeared to have been fixed The name of Faizuddin Haji was recorded as an occupant by purchase arid the class of tenancy was stated to be that of a settled raiyat and in the remark column for rent, it was assessable to rent but no amount of rent was mentioned as there was no transaction The question which was raised was whether from such entries a presumption of the recorded person can be made. This Division held that the presumption as the correctness of the said entries necessarily arose by virtue of subsection (5) of section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act. 

 15. Under the repealed provision it was provided in sub-section (2) that an application filed under subsection (1) shall be deemed to he a plaint and order passed thereon shall have the force of a decree under Code of Civil Procedure No such language is used in section 19(3) or in section 143B of the Act of 1950. Even a record-of-rights prepared under section 143A which has presumptive value does not confer any title to a litigant on the basis of such record because it is not a suit for declaration of title but it is a proceeding for rectification of mistake of the record-of-rights prepared on the basis of possession in the land in question. So the scheme of the section showed that if a record-of-rights was prepared in pursuance of a decree of a civil court in exercise of powers under section 143A, there is presumption as regards possession of the said land. Reference in this connection are the cases of Assistant Custodian V. Bholanath Ghua and 36 DLR (AD) 79, Riazuddin V. Jatindra Kishore, 37 DLR (AD) 202. Therefore, under no stretch of imagination it can be inferred that by reasons of the record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) the defendant have acquired title in the land as held by the court of appeal below. 

 16. Next question is whether there was extinguishment of title of the plaintiffs' predecessors in pursuance of the deed of relinquishment (মুক্তিপত্র) exhibit A(1) The court of appeal below held that since Naimuddin admitted in this deed as the adopted son of Karful Bewa and relinquished his right, the plaintiffs could not claim title by way of inheritance and purchase of the property of Karful Bewa and that admittedly Naimuddin was not the legal heir of Karful Bewa. The defendants failed to adduce any legal evidence to prove the C.S. record-of-rights prepared in favour of Karful Bewa other than the record-of-rights prepared under section 19(3) of the Act of 1950. As observed earlier by this record-of-rights no presumption of title can be drawn as is available under section 103B. More so, the suit was remanded to the trial court enabling the defendants to prove মুক্তিপত্র dated 18th December, 1930, exhibit:-A(1) and the A deed dated 17th January, 1935 exhibit-A(2) a deed executed by Toisor Ali in favour of Alimuddin Mondal arid Jamir Ali Mondal. In this deed the executant admitted that the recipients were in possession of the lands over statutory period. The court of appeal below held that Naimuddin extinguished his title by executing these two deeds and therefore the plaintiffs cannot claim any title as heirs of Naimuddin. It misread ext-A(2) for, Naimuddin did not relinquish his title in the lands covered by the deed. This finding is self contradictory with its earlier finding, inasmuch as, Naimuddin being the adopted son of Karful Bewa, he did not inherit her property. More so, after the remand of the suit, the trial court held that though exhibit-B(1) (wrongly mentioned as ext-B(1). It would be ext-A(2) was exhibited but the contents of the deed having not been proved by the defendants in accordance with law, the contents couldn't be looked into; that in proof of exhibit-A (2), the defendants did not produce any in dependent witness and that despite giving opportunity to the defendants, they failed to prove enforceability of exhibit-A(2). It was further observed that the plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 have been able to prove their title and. possession in the suit land, The court of appeal below has totally over-looked those findings and illegally took exhibits-A(1) and A(2) as the basis of title of the defendants and illegally held that the title of the plaintiffs' predecessor extinguished. In view of the above, the judgment of the court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal. 

 17. As observed above, in the C.S. khatian Karful Bewa's 16 annas possession in Schedule, 1, 3 and 6 had been recorded. Though the jote was shown in the name of Sadi Mondal, since this record has presumptive value in the absence of rebuttal evidence by the defendants that despite showing 16 annas possession of Karful Bewa the defendants' predecessor continued   possession in the said land have not established by them and also in respect of exhibit 1(a) she had 8 annas possession. What's more, in the absence of any evidence either oral or documentary that though Sadi Mondal's jote was noted in exts 1-1(b), whether the legal heirs of Sadi Mondal ever exercised the title and possession in the lands covered by those deeds, it is difficult to accept the defendants claim of ownership in those lands. There is no finding either in their regard. The onus lies upon the defendants to prove that despite such recording, Karful Bewa had no possession therein and that they have been continuing possession from the time of predecessors have not been established. 

 22. The plaintiff-respondents, claiming 7.23 acres out of 11.28 acres of land under partition, instituted in the instant suit. The land measuring .38 acre, of plot No. 425 and 436 of C.S. khatian No. 84, 1.01 acres of plot No. 430, 431, 434 and 433 of C.S. khatian No. 120 of Kampur Mouza, 6.00 acres of plot Nos.  62, 71, .63 and 164 of C.S. khatian No. 69 of Mouza Nawbhadanga, .39 acre of plot No.  637 of C.S. Khatian No. 47, .32 acre of plot No.  336 of C.S. khatian No.  53 of Mouza Polisha and 3.12 acres of plots No. 1, 8, 9, 30, 35, 282, 288, 171 and 296 of Mouza Pathalia are the scheduled properties of the suit for effecting partition. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, was that one Karpul Bewa was the owner of the lands' described in schedules No. 1, 3 and 4 to the plaint, that is the land recorded in C.S. Khatian Nos.  84, 69 and 47 respectively to the extent of 16 annas and the lands as described in schedules No. 2, 5 and 6 to the plaint, that is the lands recorded in C.S. khatians No. 120, 53 and 16 respectively to the extent of 8 annas share, Rest 8 annas share of khatians No. 120, 53 and 16 belonged to Baramdi Mondal. Karpuli Bewa died leaving behind two brothers Samir Mondal and Sadar Mondal. Samir Mondal died leaving his widow Asiman @ Aliman and son Abdul Mandal @ Abdul Sheikh. Sadar Mondal died leaving died leaving his son Taison Ali arid daugh-ter Ambijan Nessa. Abdul Mondal transferred 2.76 acres of land to plaintiff No. 1 by a deed dated 01.09.61. Asiman @ Aliman and Taison Ali transferred 3.30 acres of land to plaintiff No. 2 by a deed dated 01.9.1961. Taison Ali, Abdul Sheikh @ Abdul Mondal and Asimon @ Alimon transferred 2.85½ acres of land by exchange to Fulzan who died leaving three sons, the plaintiff No. 1, 2 and defendant No. 1 and three daughters, the defendant No. 2-4. The plaintiff No. 2 transferred 1.50 acres of land to plaintiff No. 1 by two separate sale deeds. The plaintiff No. 2 transferred some lands to his wife Keni Bibi. The plaintiff No. 2 and Keni Bibi, then, transferred .75 acre of land to plaintiff No. 3. By this way, the plaintiffs acquired title in 7.32 acres of land. 

 23. The contesting defendant-petitioners in their written statement contended that the Lands described in schedules 1 and 2, that is, land recorded in khatian No. 84 and 120 belonged to Baramdi Mondal inasmuch as it was erroneously mentioned in those two khatians that Karpuli Bewa was the possessor of 16 annas and 8 annas shares respectively. Their further case was that the lands as described in schedule Nos. 3, 4, 5 and 6, that is, the land recorded in C.S. Khatians No. 69, 47, 53 and 16 originally belonged to Sadi Mondal. Though name of Korpul Bewa was shown as possessor in the entire land of khatians No.  69 and 47 and also with the Baramdi Mondal in C.S. khatians No. 53 and 16 but such endorsement was erroneous. The fact was that Sadi Mondal, while owning and possessing his shares in the land of those khatians, died leaving his widow Karpul Bewa and full brother Baramdi Mondal. In C-S. operation, the name of Sadi Mondal was recorded as owner of the "Jote" but name of Karpul Bewa was erroneously shown as possessor. These defendants are the successive heirs of Sadi Mondal and Baramdi Mondal who have been possessing their respective shares. The names of the plaintiffs along with the names of defendants were recorded in S.A. operation in respect of lands as described in schedule 3 of the plaint. Karpul Bewa had no issue. She adopted one Noimuddin, father of plaintiffs No. 1 to 3 as her son. They, creating some deeds, have brought the suit. In S.A. operation, the lands of other Khatians were duly recorded in the names of these defendants rejecting the objections raised by the plaintiffs. 

 25. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants, submits that Sadi Mondal was the Jote owner of the land of C.S. khatian Nos. 69, 47 , 53 and 16 and after his death his wife Karpul Bewa and brother Baramdi Mondal inherited his property. Similarly Baramdi Mondal was the owner of Jote of C.S. khatian Nos.  84 and 120. At the time of preparation of S.A. record of right, the Revenue authority, rejecting the objections, recorded the names of these defendants in the khatians finding them in possession. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that though in C.S, operation, name of Korpul Bewa was mentioned as possessor but same had no basis and by adducing sufficient evidence, these defendants had rebutted the presumption so far the possession is concerned.   He submits that the High Court Division committed error of law in giving much importance regarding endorsement i as to possession in C.S. khatians. Mr. Quamrul Haque Siddiuqe, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs respondents, submits that as per provision of Section 103(B) (5) Bengal Tenancy Act the entry made in C. S. khatian in presumed to be correct, the defendant appellants failed to rebut the presumption of CS, khatians, the High Court Division rightly held that the plaintiffs have acquired valid title in 7.32 acres of land. 

 26. On perusal of the C.S. khatians, exhibits 1 to 1(E), it appears that the land described in schedule 1 measuring .38 acre of C.S. khatian No. 84 (exhibit, 1-B) was recorded as "Jote" of Baramdi Mondal and possessor was Korpul Bewa; the land described in schedule-2 measuring 1.01 acre of C.S. khatian No. 120 (exhibit-1-C), was the "Jote" of Baramdi Mondal and said Baramdi Mondal and Korpul Bewa were the possessors to the extent of 8 annas share each; the land described in schedule 3 of C.S. khatian No. 69, (exhibit-i) was the "Jote" of Sadi Mondal and possessor was Korpul Bewa, the land described in schedule 4 of C.S.. khatian No.  47, exhibit 1(E), was Jote of Sadi Mondal and possessor was Korpul Bewa, the land as described in schedule 5 of the plaint recorded in C.S. khatian No. 53 (exhibit-1-D) was the "Jote" of Sadi Mondal and possessors were Baramdi Mondal and Korpul Bewa to the extent of 8 annas share each and the land described in schedule 6 of the plaint, that is, the land recorded in C.S. khatian No. 16 (exhibit 1-A) was the "Jote" of Sadi Mondal and possessors were Korpul Bewa and Barumdi Mondal to the extent of 8 annas share each. The plaintiffs claimed that Korpul had ownership in 16 annas shares in the lands as described in schedule No, 1, 3 and 4 of the plaint since in C.S. khatians name of Korpul Bewa appeared as possessor. They also claimed that Korpul had 8 annas shares in the land as described in schedule No.  2, 5 and 6 since in these C.S. khatians name of Korpul Bewa appeared as possessor to the extent of 8 annas shares. The status of Korpul should be determined with reference to the other evidence. As per provision of Section 103(B) (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, every entry in a record of right finally published shall be evidence of the mater referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it proved to be incorrect. The entry can be regarded as presumptive evidence of the matter referred to in the entry; as also of the condition things which existed at the time of record of right was prepared. The entry in the record of rights has only a probative value. We have seen that the lands of C.S. khatian No. 84 and 120 were of the Jote of Baramdi Monda and land recorded in C.S. khatian No. 69, 47, 53 and 16 were the Tote of Sadi Mondal. The term 'Dote" ordinarily means "holding" and a tenancy is described as 'jote' in general. In the case of Narendra Chandra Vs. Rajendra Chandra Chanda reported in AIR 1941 Cal 506 it was observed that 'Jote' is a perfectly general expression to mean tenancy of any kind. In the case of Sariatullah V. Joyenuddin AIR 1935 cal 462 it was held that the "jute simply means a tenancy". In the case of Upendra Kishore Sarker Vs. Khalii Fakir reported in 139 I.C. page 544 it was observed that "Jote may mean a raiyat, under raiyoti, or any sort of holding for the purpose bf cultivation. The "জোত" of Baramdi Mondal and Sadi Mondal indicated that they were tenants of the holdings, that is, they held those lands as recorded in C.S. khatihns under the landlords. In other words, they were the raiyats who acquired right to hold those lands for the purpose of cultivating by themselves or by the members of their family or by servant or labour or with other partner. c.s. khatians attach presumption that Korpul Bewa was in possession of the land at the time of preparation of record of rights exclusively in the lands of some khatains and with Barumdi with other khatians. The court is always justified in looking into the history of proceedings which have resulted in a particular entry in order to test its validity. The presumption as to the correctness of an entry may be rebutted by the surrounding circumstances. Here, from the entries in C.S. khatians it appears that all the lands are rented lands but no where in plaint the plaintiffs claimed that Korpul paid any rent to the landlords. Presumption of title from possession can arise only where facts disclose no title to other party. In the instant case, possessor Korpul Bewa was wife of Jote owner Sadi Mondal who was full brother of co-possessor and Jote owner of some khatians Baramdi Mondal. There is no averment in the plaint or any evidence that the interest of the holders of Jotes or, in other words, rayoti interest of raiyots had been, in any way, extinguished or entire raiyoti interest of Sadi Mondal had been devolved upon Karpuli Bewa. Mr. Bhuiyan cited the case of Promotha Nath Vs. Kamir Mondal reported in 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 392. In the cited case it has been observed that the presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103 B of the Bangla Tenancy Act is only this that the entry in the record of right represents the correct state of affairs on the date that it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs is continued even after-wards is not a presumption which arises under this section but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is its presumptive value. Admittedly Korpul and Sadi Mondal had no issue Korpul adopted one Naimuddin as her son who did not inherit the property left by Korpul. The plaintiffs are the heirs of said Naimuddin. They claimed that they had purchased their claimed land from the heirs of Korpul in 1961.  From the period of publication of C.S. record of rights to 1961 the plaintiffs' predecessors did not pay any rent to the landlords or the Government. After losing in the objection case filed against the contesting defendants, wherein the Revenue authority held possession of the defendants, they remained silent till 1980, that was the year of filing suit. 

 27. On the other hand, the contesting defendants produced ext. B, "Muktipatra" executed by the father of the plaintiffs No. 1 and 2 on 8.12.1930 in respect of the some lands of khatians No. 36, 47 arid 120 in favour of Alimuddin Mondal and others wherein he Stated,  ------ তাহা আপনেরা মালীকান হওয়ায় কর আদায়ে আপনাদের নিজ স্বত্ব ভুগ দখল করিতেছেন। It is true that "Muktipatra" is not a deed of transfer but recital of this more than 30 years old document, produced from proper custody is admissible in evidence against the parties who made it, Similarly, Taison Ali, from whom, the plaintiffs purchased, executed as "স্বত্ব ত্যাগ পত্র" (Ext. B-1) on 17.01.1935 in favour of Alimuddin and others sons of Barumdi Mondal in respect of land of khatian 16 and 69 reciting ‘‘উক্ত জোত জমি আপনারা দ্বাদশ বৎসরে উদ্ধকাল যাবত ভোগ দখল করিতেছেন।” The contesting defendants produced exhibit-C series, the rent receipts and the S.A. khatians exhibit A series which are evidence of possession. The revenue authority while rejecting the objection under section 19(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in 1962 held that the objectors (the plaintiffs) admitted the possession of the contesting defendants. Where the evidence of possession is found to be equal weight on both sides, the presumption as to possession is said to have been rebutted.

AKM Shafiqur Rahman with Mostafa Kamal Pasha and Shahabuddin Faiz ----- For the Petitioners.

Lal Meah & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. The plaintiff's case in short is that the disputed tank belonged to Bakar Ali, Gul Banu and Bhagyabati Gul Banu and Bhagyabati had no heir except Bakar Ali. Bakar Ali was great grandfather of plaintiff No. 1. Maghi survey was made in the names of Bakar Ali, Gul Banu and Bhagyabati. CS Khatian stands recorded in the name of Uzir Ali who was son of Baker Ali. MS plot No. 6998 corresponding to CS plot No. 7190 was in possession of Md Waresh Ali who was in Chasha (cultivator) under plaintiffs predecessors. RS Khatian was wrongly prepared in respect of the disputed tank and it was recorded as RS plot 8746. Recording of 7/9th share in the names of defendants predecessors was wrong. Uzir Ali died leaving sons Asmat Ali, Ismat Ali and Hamdu Meah. The plaintiff No. 2 and proforma defendant 43 are the heirs of Hamdu Meah. lsmat Ali died leaving sons, plaintiff No. 1 and proforma defendant No. 42. The plaintiffs are possessing the disputed tank for generations. PS and BS khatian also are wrongly recorded. The plaintiffs transferred 2 gondas of land to Gura Meah and 2 gondas of land to Yakub Ali. The defendants have no share in the disputed tank. 

 4. The defendants 2 and 8 contested the suit by filing joint written statement contending, inter-alia, that the suit is not maintainable and it barred by limitation. The defendants are the heirs of Gut Banu and Bhagyabati. Gul Banu and Bhagyabati were not related to Baker Ali Md Zaman was the husband of Gul Banu and Hari Chand was the husband of Bhagyabati. Gul Banu died leaving son Abdul. Abdul died leaving two sons namely, Mohsen Ali and Malekazzaman. Mohsen Ali died leaving two sons namely, Torab Ali and Amjad Ali. Torab Ali died leaving three sons namely, Chunnu Meah, Sultan Ahmed and Lal Meah. Sultan Ahmed died leaving widow Abeda Khatun and daughter defendant No. 1 Gul Safa Khatun. Lal Mueah died leaving widow Sanwara Begum and brother Chunnu Meah. Chunnu Meah transferred his share to defendant No. 2 Lal Meah Amjad Ali died leaving three namely, Chunnu Meah Yakub Ali and Akmal Ali. The defendants Nos. 6 to 11 are the heirs of Yakub Ali, Abdul Sobhan purchased the share of Malekazzaman for his heirs. Bhagyabati died leaving Md. Waresh Md. Waresh died leaving Mubarak Ali Mubarak Ali died leaving daughter Amirun Nessa who sold her share to Abdul Malek. CS. Khatian was recorded in the names of predecessors of the plaintiffs, and the defendants. RS. Khatian was recorded correctly. PS. Khatian and BS Khatian are prepared in the names of defendants. The principal defendants (1-10) are in possession of 7/9the share of the disputed tank. The principal defendants have graveyard on the eastern and western banks of the disputed tank. The principal defendants have cowshed and haystack on the western bank of the disputed tank. They have 4 outer houses on the western bank of the disputed tank. The Plaintiffs and proforma defendants (41-56) got 2/9th share of the disputed tank. 

 5. The learned Munsif found that the plaintiffs having paid the advalorem court fees as per Courts Direction in the plaintiff’s prayer "for declaration that the recording of 7/9th share in the disputed tank in RS. Plot No. 8746 is wrong and also for declaration that in spite of that wrong recording the plaintiff's right and interest has not been affected" the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and, as such, the suit as framed was maintainable. The learned Munsif further found that Maghi Chitta is a document of title, that Gul Banu and Bhagyabati were the predecessors of the plaintiffs 41-56, that the defendants suggestion that Md. Waresh Ali, the predecessor of defendants 23-29, 33-35 and 37-40, was the son of Bhagyabati was disproved by CS Khatian Exhibit 1(f) and a and that the descendants of Chasa Md. Waresh Ali got their names recorded with their masters' descendants. He also found that the recording of the 7/9th share in the names of the defendants' predecessors during the RS. Operation was wrong and the plaintiffs are entitled to get a declaration to that effect and that the suit having been filed within 6 years from 15-5-74 on which date defendants threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession on the basis of wrong entry in the RS Khatian, the suit was not barred by limitation or adverse possession. Accordingly the learned Munsif decreed the suit in part declaring that the recording of RS Khatian, Exhibit A (1) and A (2) to the extent of 7/9th share in the names of the defendants' predecessors was wrong and that the right of the plaintiffs and proforma defendants Nos. 41 to 56 to the extent of 16 annas share in the disputed tank has not been affected by RS. Khatians in dispute and further declaring that the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants joint possession with defendants who had purchased 4 gandas of land out of the disputed tank appertaining to RS Plot No. 8746 from the plaintiff No 1 be confirmed. Against the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif the contesting defendants 2 and 8 prepared the appeal and the plaintiffs-respondents in the appeal filed cross-objection for cost of suit. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge found that in the plaint there is no clear mention of declaration of title in the disputed property, that two negative prayers in prayer (kha) make it affirmative i.e. it tantamount to the position that the principal defendants have got right to disturb in the possession of the entire disputed tank of schedules 1-2 of the plaint, that from the prayer portion of the plaint it appears that schedule 1 property is disputed i.e. 7/9 th share and schedule 2 i.e. 2/9th share is not disputed and thus it creates contradiction in the prayer (kha) and that the negative specific relief of permanent injunction in prayer (ga) is a vague term. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge further found that the recording of RS Khatian in the names of principal defendants is correct, that the principal defendants have possession in the disputed tank, that the Maghi Chitta cannot alone create title in favour or the plaintiffs for the disputed tank and that the plaintiffs side having not rectified the recording of the RS Khatian by filing any suit/case the question of limitation for challenging the RS Khatian also arises, that the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants have joint possession in the disputed tank along with the principal defendants, that the RS Khatian cannot be rectified as the plaintiffs did not take to correct it within the period of limitation, that in the absence of direct evidence the presumption of RS Khatian cannot be rebutted that there is no clear claim by the plaintiff's side that they have title in the entire disputed tank, that the suit is not maintainable and it is barred by limitation. Accordingly he allowed the appeal and rejected the cross-objection and dismissed the suit in reversal of the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif. Against the judgment and decree of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge the plaintiffs have obtained the present Rule. 

 11. In support of the finding of the Sub-ordinate Judge that the Maghi chitta does not create title, Mr. SC Das, the learned Advocate for the opposite-parties 1-2 refers the case of Fazlur Rahim vs Nabendra Krishna Roy and others 17 CWN 151 and the case of Prodyot Kumar Sen Gupta vs Nagendra Kumar Chowdhury, 52 CWN 72. In 17 CWN 151 it was held that a chitta prepared by the Government when interested as a proprietor of the estate concerned could not be said to be a public document and that no special presumption attached to these chittas. In 52 CWN 72 it was held:-It is not necessary for us to hold that Maghi Chitta is wrong. Each record must be presumed to be correct at its date, and since the position indicated by the entries in the chittas could, during the interval, well change into the position indicated by the cadastral and revisional survey records, the latter position is not shown to be impossible or invalid in law, as the learned Sub-ordinate Judge erroneously supposed." In the light of the above cases reported in 17 CWN 151 and 52 CWN 72 it can safely be held that Maghi chitta did not create title in favour of the plaintiff in the disputed tank as has been correctly found by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge and the latter position indicated by the RS record is valid in law. As to the presumption of RS khatian and its rebuttal the learned Advocate for the opposite-parties 1-2, has referred to the case of Akrab Ali vs Zahiruddin Kari, 30 DLR (AD) 81 and the case of Meherjan Bibi vs Naimuddin Dhali being dead Raisuddin and others 33 DLR 127 in the case reported in 30 DLR (AD) 81 it is held that according to section 103B(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in a record of right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. In 33 DLR 126 it is held that the presumption of correction as available on the strength of section 103 B (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it. In the light of the proposition of law enunciated in the Appellate Division case reported in 30 DLR (AD) 81 the RS Khatian in the present case raises a presumption of its correctness until proved to be incorrect and in view of the decisions in 33 DLR 126 the onus is on the plaintiffs to rebut the presumption of the correctness of the RS khatian in the present case in as, much as, the plaintiffs have alleged that the entry of the RS khatian is wrong. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge has correctly found that there is no direct evidence in the case to rebut presumption of the RS khatian. As such the correctness of the entry of the RS Khatian is not rebutted in the present case.

4. One of the points urged in the Trial Court was with respect to the interest of the Chanda brothels. The plaintiff contended relying upon the C. S. Khatian No. 517 (Ext. 2(C) and Khatian No. 414 Ext. 2 (d) Jogendra Chanda alone was the owner of the land under whom Zarip Khan was an occupancy raiyati whereas the defense case was that the land belonged to Kashi Chanda, the father of Jogendra and therefore all the Chanda brothers who were the sons of Kashi had interest in the land. The Trial Court on a consideration of the evidence on record came to the finding that the suit had originally belonged to Jogendra father and as such after Kashi's death, all of his six sous got the land by right of inheritance The 'la 'al Court a took the view that no presumption could be attached to the entry of the C. S. Khatian Ext. 2(h) as into evidence has been adduced to show the has of the entry of the said Khatian. Thereafter on an analysis of the evidence of both parties and the documentary evidence adduced in this case the learned Munsif held that the plaintiff did not acquire any title to the suit of his alleged purchase and that his allegation as to possession was not true. He came to the conclusion that the plaintiff also failed to prove his allegation of dispossession in the middle of Poush, 1370 B.S and Monoranjan was the real owner of the land and as such the plaintiff having had no valid title to the suit land was not entitled to get khas possession of the suit land. 

 5. On an appeal being taken by the plaintiff, it was heard by the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge Dacca and the learned Subordinate judge held that the learned Munsiff was not justified in rejecting the C. S. Khatian as evidence of title and possession of Zarip Khan in respect of the disputed land. According to the learned Subordinate Judge the plaintiff and accreted good title by virtue of the registered executed by the successor in interest of Zarip Khan He dis-believed the defense case of Monoranjan the owner of the land on the ground that the Kabala Ext. D evidences sale of rent-receiving interest only and that no documentary  fahdeaceead been adduced to prove the alleged oral sentiment of the refraining share of the disputed land by Upendra Kumar in favour of Monoranjan He referred to the evidence given by the witnesses of both parties and on a consideration of the same accepted the plaintiff's ease and held that the plaintiff's case of title and possession and dispossession had been sufficiently proved and that the earned Munsif was not justified in dismissing the suit The appeal was allowed and the plaintiff's suit was decreed on the basis of the aforesaid findings. 

 7. Mr. S M. Haque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents at the very outset pointed out that the view which has been taken by the learned Munsiff on the question of presumptive value of the C. S. Khatian Ext 2(VI) is not correct and this submission of the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents appears to be justified. Any party who relies upon the entries of a Settlement Khatian is not under any obligation to adduce evidence to prove the basis of the said entry. Of course, if on a production of some evidence it can be shown that there was no basis for the entry in the C. S Khatian to say that the said entry is contrary to or not supported by the basic document which may have been referred to in the Khatian itself, in  case it can be rightly argued that the Khatian has no basis and therefore no presumptive value can be attached to the same but ordinarily the entries in the C. S. Khatian shall have statutory  presumption of correct news in respect the stale of tutus indicated by the said entries. irrespective of the fact whether the person relying upon the said entries adduce any evidence in support thereof or not la this case the entries in the said C. S. Khatian shall raise a presumption in favour of the occupancy tenancy right of Zarip Khan as shown in the said C S Khatian It is for other side who chooses to dispute the correctness of the said entries to adduced evidence to show the contrary. In that view of the matter the learned Munsif ought to have approached the consideration of the evidence on record from the standpoint It is however, found that there are materials on record which can be taken onto consideration for the purpose of examining the question whether the presumption raised by the entries in the Khatian have been sufficiently rebutted by the said materials or not and although the learned Munsif made an error in attaching the proper presumptive value to the entries in the C. S. Khatian he had applied his mind to the other evidence on record on the question of title and possession of the land. 

 8. As regards the first point urged by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the learned Subordinate Judge has misconstrued the Kabala Ext. (1), I find that this contention has some justification. The learned Subordinate Judge is not correct in holding that the Kabala was merely a deed for the purpose of transfer of the rent-receiving-interest of the vendors. Rather, it appears from an examination of the contents of the document that was purported to have been demised by the said deed was the land itself, which was alleged to have been in actual possession of the vendors. As regards the second point also I find that the learned Subordinate Judge has not given any consideration to the documents Ext. Nos. 8, 13(1 ) and C series for the purpose of ascertaining the actual position with regard to possession of the &sported land. Ext. B is a copy of the Order sheet in a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, Est. B 1) is a carotids copy of an order in a Criminal case brought by the plaintiff as against the defendant No 1 whereby the case under section 379 P.P.C. was dismissed and Ext. C series are the rent-receipts in respect of payment rent on behalf of Monoranjan in respect of Khatian No. 446/1 which included the disputed C.S. plot No 196 till the record was corrected by subsequent order of the Revenue authority. These rent-receipts also have some bearing upon the question of possession. With regard to the third point also find that the learned Advocate for the appellant is right in his contention that the discrepancies in the testimony of the plaintiff's witness as have been noticed by the learned Munsif and also certain admission made P W. 2 which weighed with the learned Munsif for his conclusion have not at all been taken notice of by the appellate Court. In my opinion, the failure of the learned Subordinate Judge to advert to the documents and also to the discrepancies and other points mentioned above have vitiated the judgment of the lower appellate Court and therefore the said Judgment is not sustainable in law One of the questions involved in this case pertains to a claim of a right of tenancy by a bargadar and the position of bargadar under the old system was anomalous. There was no bar against a bargadar having a right of tenancy under the Bengal Tenancy Act, and although in 1929 by an amendment of provision relating to the definition of a tenant, a legal presumption that a bargadar is not tenant was sought to he introduced, but by adding a proviso to the amending legislation it was made clear it could still he shown by producing evidence in a court that the bargadar had a right of tenancy and was not merely an agricultural labourer engaged for cultivation of land and growing crops thereon. The same definition has been adopted in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The legal import of this definition was considered and explained in a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Kumir Mandal and others Vs Pramatha Nath Chowdhury and others, reported in 14 DLR 830 and by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in an appeal from the said decision in the case of Pramatha Nath Chowdhury and others Vs Kumir Mandal and others, reported in 17 DLR (SC) 392 same case PLD 1965 (Supreme Court) 434. In a Division Bench decision of this court in the case of Sona Mia and others Vs. Momraj Bhuiyan and others, (Second Appeal No. 920 of 966 decided on 8 3.7 to which I was party it has been pointed out that it is ultimate a Civil Court which will have to decide the question as to a bargadar having a right of tenancy, if such a question is raised, on the basis of the materials on record after paying due regard to the presumption which mar be raised by some entries in a Settlement Khatian.

lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Attorney-General with Khademul Islam Chowdhury, Deputy Attorney-General and SM Rezaul Karim Assistant Attorney-General —For the Petitioners.

full_judgment:
2. The short facts, giving rise to the issuance of this Rule, are that the plaintiff opposite party Nos.1-5 instituted the above suit against the petitioners and other opposite party Nos. 6-18, for permanent injunction restraining the petitioners from entering into the lands described in the schedule of the plaint. The plaintiffs'' case is that, the suit lands originally belonged to Bhawal Courts of Wards Estate as Khas Khamar and the same were recorded as such in the Khatians of the said Estate during CS Operation. The plaintiffs thereafter took settlement of the suit lands from the aforesaid Estate by two Amalnama dated 4-5-49; that on payment of a salami they were granted rent receipts and since then the plaintiffs have been possessing the land peacefully and adversely to all. It is further stated that the record was duly prepared in the name of the plaintiffs in the SA and RS Khatian on the basis of title and possession. But against the said record of right the principal defendants filed an objection under section 30 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the objection was allowed. Against the said order allowing objection the plaintiffs preferred appeal under section 31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the appellate revenue officer set aside the order and passed an order for recording the suit land in the names of the plaintiffs. After the order of the appellate officer the plaintiffs started paying rent to the defendant No.1 Government and obtained rent receipts. It is further stated that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land by constructing dwelling huts, cultivating the land, growing seasonal crops and planting various fruit bearing trees. The lands have been classified as Chala Bari, pond and sail, etc. The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants gave out threat to dispossess them from the suit land and hence the suit. 

 4. The trial Court on consideration of both oral and documentary evidence on record decreed the suit against the principal defendants and they were restrained permanently from entering into the suit land. 

 5. The petitioners preferred appeal against the decree of the trial Court and the appellate Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the trial Court''s decree. 

 6. The petitioners being aggrieved by the aforesaid decree of the courts below moved this court and obtained the present Rule. 

 7. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Attorney-General appearing for the petitioners, has firstly submitted that a simple suit of the plaintiff opposite parties for permanent injunction is not maintainable inasmuch as the dispute involves complicated question of title. The courts below having failed to consider that the plaintiff must establish their title by filing a regular suit for declaration of title committed error of law in decreeing the suit which has resulted in an error in the decision causing failure of justice, In support of his above contention he has referred to a decision in the case of Rafizuddin Ahmed vs Mongla Barman and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 215 wherein it has been held as follows: 

 "In a simple suit for permanent injunction with regard to disputed landed property the relief is available to a person who is in possession. The court may enquire incidentally into the respective claims of the parties to the suit for determining whether the plaintiff has got a prima facie case, i.e. whether he is in possession of the disputed property and entitled to the specific relief of permanent injunction. If the dispute involves complicated question of title the plaintiff must establish title by filing a regular suit for declaration of title. A simple suit for permanent injunction should not be allowed to be used as a testing device for ascertainment of title. 

 8. Mr Attorney-General has next submitted that the Gazette notifications vide Exhibits A, A(1) and A(2) declared the suit land along with other lands a protected forest and reserved forest and those lands vested in the government under the provisions of Forest Act. The courts below having misread and misconstrued the said exhibits, committed error of law in not dismissing the plaintiffs'' suit by holding that the suit lands vested in the government and this has resulted in an error in the decision causing failure of justice. 

 9. It has been further submitted that Exhibit B, a sale notice for auction of the Gazari trees by the Forest Department and the Exhibits D and D(1) showed that the record of the suit land stood in the name of the Zaminders during the CS operation but the courts below having failed to consider those documents in their proper perspective committed error of law which has led to an error in the decision causing failure of justice. 

 10. Mr Attorney-General has lastly, submitted that the plaintiffs having not possessed the suit land for more than 60 years acquired no title and, as such, the decree for permanent injunction granted by court below cannot be sustained in law and the same is liable to be set aside. 

 11. Mr Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties, has filed counter affidavit to oppose the Rule. Repelling the above submissions of the learned Attorney-General it is contended by Mr Mahbubuddin Ahmed that the opposite parties had already acquired title in the suit land because of the facts that the suit land originally belonged to Bhawal Courts of Wards Estate as their Khas Khamar land and the plaintiffs along with others took settlement of the suit land from the said Estate by Amalnama on payment of salami on 4-5-49 and they were granted rent receipts by the said Estate. It has been further submitted that suit lands were subsequently recorded in the name of the plaintiffs and they (opposite party) paid rent to the government. Mr Mahbubuddin. Ahmed therefore contends that both the courts below having rightly considered the oral and documentary evidences found plaintiffs'' possession in the suit lands and prima facie title in their favour quite legally. It is therefore urged before me that in a suit for permanent injunction, the question of title is not that material to be looked into but incidentally the court can look into it. 

 16. I have heard the learned Counsels of both sides, perused the connected papers and the judgments of the courts below. 

 17. The learned Attorney-General has questioned the very maintainability of the suit of the plaintiffs and referred the decision reported in 43 DLR (AD) 225 as noticed above. Now with regard to the maintainability of the suit, I am of the view that the above cited decision is not applicable in the facts that in the above cited case the plaintiff filed the suit for permanent injunction for restraining the defendants from entering into CS plot Nos. 784 and 802 appertaining to CS khatian No. 125 of mouza Galtoir PS Chirirbandar District Dinajpur. The trial Court upon consideration of materials on record found that Dinomoni inherited the land of CS khatian No. 125 from her husband and that her son-in-law Janaki looked after her properties and there was no basis of noting of the alleged exchange in the CS khatian, the trial Court held that Janaki got his son Lalit''s name included in the CS khatian fraudulently, that Dinomoni had title in all the lands including plot No. 784 and that the presumption of correctness of the record of right was rebutted. The trial Court further found that in the kabala dated 18-1-1938 executed by Dinomoni in favour of Janaki, there was a reference to two other plots besides the two suit plots: that Janaki asserted his title and possession in the suit lands and executed Ext.1 the kabala dated 1-4-1957 in favour of the plaintiff who after purchase got his name mutated and got rent receipts. The trial Court also accepted the evidence of PWs 2 and 3 in support of the plaintiffs'' case and rejected the evidence of the defendants'' witneses. The appellate Court upheld the trial Courts, decree with regard to plot No. 802 but dismissed the plaintiffs'' prayer with regard to the other plot namely, the plot No. 784 after finding that the plaintiff failed to prove his prima facie title and exclusive possession there. In the above cited case the plaintiff assailed the presumption of CS khatian but in the instant case the plaintiffs have not assailed the presumption of khatian as the SA and RS khatians already stood in the name of the plaintiffs. Furthermore, the plaintiffs in the instant case proved this prima facie case and both the courts below having considered the materials on record found exclusive possession of the plaintiffs in disputed plots. 

 19. In view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case, the whole argument of Mr Ahmed is that when the possession is proved in respect of the disputed property the title is not that, material in a suit for permanent injunction and even if the plaintiff is in possession of the property without any title, he is entitled to an order of injunction from the court of law. In support of his above contention learned Advocate has referred to a decision in the case of Kaimuddin Sheikh alias Kimu Sheikh vs Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi reported in 3 Bangladesh Law Chronicles 1998 at page 410 wherein a Single Bench of this Division having considered the various decisions on the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court held as follows: 

 "In the face of payment of rent of mutation and taxes in respect of the suit land and possession thereof, the question of title is not that material in a suit for permanent injunction and even if the plaintiff is in possession without any title he is entitled to an order of injunction from the court of law. The aggrieved party may however get his title declared and recover possession of the suit land from the plaintiff in a proper proceeding." 

 21. On scrutiny of the records of the case and upon perusal of the judgments of the courts below, I find that both the courts below discussed the basic documents of prima facie title of the plaintiffs namely, the two Amalnamas the Exts. 1, 1-A(i.e. settlement taken by the plaintiffs from the Bhawal Court's of Ward Estate) that two rent receipt Exts. 2 and 2 A two khatians Exhibits 3 and 3(a) standing in the names of the plaintiffs and preformat defendants. It further appears that during RS operation, the suit lands have been recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and preformat defendants and the plaintiff filed three rent receipts Ext. 5, 5(a) and 5(b) to show their payment of rent for the suit lands for year 1379 to 1382 BS. It further appears that during RS operation the lands were recorded wrongly in the name of the government and against that initial record the plaintiffs preferred appeals and their appeals were allowed vide Ext.6. The trial Court also considered the notifications of the government Ext. A. A(1) and A(2) and other documentary evidence namely Ext. B, C, D and D(1) in their proper perspective. 

 22. In a suit for injunction the materials issues are prima facie case and possession. Both the courts below concurrently held that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their prima facie case and possession in the suit lands. Considering the material evidence on record and in such view of the matter I do not find that there has been a non consideration of material evidence which is specifically essential for determination of material issue. I therefore hold that the plaintiffs are entitled to get a decree for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with the peaceful possession of the suit lands and from taking possession thereof except in due process of law. 

 23. Having regard to the above discussions and in view of the facts and circumstances of the case I do not find that any illegality has been committed by the courts below in decreeing the suit for permanent injunction and no interferences is called for. 

 24. In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree passed by the courts below are hereby affirmed. The order of injunction granted in this Rule on 4-3-97 and 30-10-97 is hereby vacated.

full_judgment:
(a) 8 annas share as to 'Ka' schedule property of CS khatian No.70 comprising 23 decimals of land, 

 (b) 202.50 decimals of land as to Kha schedule property of CS khatian No.280 (94 decimals of land in Plot Nos. 3443, 3450 and 3480 as exclusive possessor and 108.50 decimals of land in rest of the plots in 8 annas share, total (94 + 108.50) = 202.50 decimals of land), 

 (c) 16 annas share as to `Gha' schedule property of CS khatian No.678 comprising 94 decimals of land, and 

 (d) 8 annas share as to `Gha' schedule property of CS khatian No.813 comprising 78 decimals of land. 

 3. The properties situate at mouza Sreepatirchar, Police Station-Homna, District-Cumilla. The basis of the abovementioned claim of the plaintiffs, as stated in the plaint, is that CS khatian No. 70 was recorded in the names of the plaintiffs' predecessor Uzir and the defendants' predecessor Wahed Ali in equal shares. Plot Nos. 3443, 3450 and 3480 of CS khatian No. 280 were recorded in the name of Uzir Ali as exclusive possessor and the rest of the plots were recorded in the names of Uzir Ali and Wahed All in equal shares. CS khatian No.678 was recorded exclusively in the name of plaintiffs' predecessor Uzir Ali. CS khatian No. 813 was recorded in the names of Uzir Ali and Wahed Ali in equal shares. Uzir Ali died leaving behind the plaintiff No. 1 Montaz Uddin alias Momtaz Uddin as only son and two daughters namely, Sabaner Nessa (plaintiff No. 2) and Moina Bibi. While the son and two daughters of Uzir Ali had been possessing the scheduled property as owner through succession, Moina Bibi died leaving behind Toyfol Nessa (plaintiff No.3) as only successor. The plaintiffs have been possessing the land in ejmali by erecting houses and growing crops. The schedule mentioned properties were not partitioned which have resulted in misunderstanding and quarrel between the parties. On 19-4-2008, the defendants refused to partition the property amicably and hence, the suit for partition. 

 5. In respect of CS khatian No.70 (Ka Schedule) and CS khatian No.813 (Gha schedule), the defendants do not dispute the plaintiffs' case that these-khatians were recorded in the names of Uzir All (plaintiffs' predecessor) and Wahed All (defendants' predecessor) in equal shares. 

 6. In respect of CS khatian No. 280 (Kha schedule), the defendants claim that the said khatian was prepared in the names of Uzir Ali and Wahed Ali in equal shares. Subsequently, Uzir Ali sold and handed over possession of 17 decimals of land in plot No. 3443 and 14 decimals of land in plot No. 3450, both of CS khatian No 280, total 31 decimals of land to Wahed Ali, but no registered sale deed was executed. On 21-11-1944, Wahed Ali transferred the said 31 decimals of land to his wife-Arabia Khatun through a registered deed of hiba-bil-ewaj. 

 7. In respect of CS khatian No. 678 (Ga schedule), the defendants' case is that although 94 decimals of land of the said khatian were owned and possessed by Uzir Ali and Wahed Ali in equal shares, but during the CS operation the same was wrongly recorded in the name of Uzir Ali. During the SA operation, the land was correctly recorded in the corresponding SA khatian No. 815 in the names of plaintiff No. 1, who is the son of Uzir Ali and these defendants as successors of Wahed Ali in equal shares. 

 10. The trial Court held that out of 397.50 decimals of land of the four khatians as claimed by the plaintiffs, they are entitled to saham of 303.50 decimals of land in the following manner: 

 from CS khatian No. 70 in 8 annas share = 23 decimals 

 from CS khatian No. 813 in 8 annas share = 78 decimals 

 from CS khatian No. 280 in 8 annas share = 155.50 decimals 

 from CS khatian No. 678 in 8 annas share = 0.47 decimals 

 11. The plaintiffs preferred an appeal which was allowed in part. The appellate Court below modified the decree passed by the trial Court by enhancing the saham of the plaintiffs from 303.50 decimals of land to 350.50 decimals of land. In so doing, the appellate Court allotted the entire land of CS khatian No. 678 (94 decimals) to the plaintiffs while maintaining equal shares in respect of the rest three khatians to the plaintiffs and the defendants respectively as allotted by the trial Court. 

 13. Mr Md Mostafa, the learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent-petitioners, submits that he has no objection as to allocation of saham to the parties in respect of CS khatian Nos. 70, 813 and 280 by the appellate Court below. The learned Advocate, however, submits that the appellate Court below committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice by allotting the entire share of CS khatian No. 678 to the plaintiffs inasmuch as in the corresponding SA khatian No. 815 the names of the plaintiff No. 1 and these defendants were recorded in equal Shares which cast cloud upon the title of the plaintiffs so far as entire share of CS khatian No. 678 is concerned and therefore, until and unless the plaintiffs' title in the entire share of CS khatian No. 678 is declared by a competent Court or the corresponding SA khatian is not declared wrong by a Civil Court, the suit for partition simpliciter is not maintainable. In support of the argument, the learned Advocate refers to the case of Rezaul Karim and others vs Shamsuzzoha and others, 49 DLR (AD) 68. 

 14. Mr Sikder Mahmudur Razi, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party Nos.1-16, on the other hand, submits that it now settled principle of law through judicial pronouncement that in a suit for partition, the Court can determine each conflicting claims incidental to partition. In support of the argument, the learned Advocate refers to the cases of Shashi Kumar vs Nagendra Nath, 1982 BLD 36 and Cinmoy Chowdhury and another vs Mridul Chowdhury and others, 55 DLR (AD) 115. The learned Advocate next submits that order VII, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers the Court to give relief to the plaintiff as he is found entitled to but omits to pray. The learned Advocate refers to the case of Dhaka City Corporation and others vs Shamsur Rahman and others, 59 DLR 207 in support of the argument. The learned Advocate further submits that the appellate Court below rightly allotted the entire share of the land of the CS khatian No. 678 to the plaintiffs as the same was recorded in 16 annas share in the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor and that there is no basis of recording 8 annas share of the same in the defendants' name in the corresponding SA khatian. In this regard the learned Advocate submits that the presumption of correctness as to CS khatian is not available with regard to the SA khatian. In support of the argument, the learned Advocate refers to the cases of Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Kuri and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81, Hindu Devi Lakshmi Gobinda Jew vs Deputy Custodian Enemy Property (now vested property) Government of Bangladesh and others, 7 BLT 133 = 51 DLR 300, Hriday Ranjan Dey and another vs Niranjan Dey being dead his heirs, Probate Dey and others, 10 

 16. In the instant suit for partition, the plaintiffs prayed for saham of land in respect of four CS khatians. Both the trial Court and the appellate Court below allotted 8 annas shares of land of three khatians to the plaintiffs. The bone of contention arises in respect of CS khatian No. 678. Plaintiffs claimed 16 annas share of land of CS khatian No.678, but the trial Court gave 8 annas share to them which, on appeal filed by the plaintiffs, was modified and the appellate Court gave 16 annas share of land of CS khatian No. 678 to the plaintiffs. Now, the defendants are the petitioners before me. 

 17. Admittedly, 16 annas share of CS khatian No. 678 was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor Uzir Ali. Defendants claim that the land of CS khatian No.678 was owned and possessed in equal shares by the respective predecessors of the plaintiffs and the defendants. So, the CS khatian No. 678 was wrong which was corrected in the corresponding SA khatian No. 815 which was recorded in equal shares in the names of the plaintiffs and the defendants. 

 18. The trial Court observed the plaintiffs failed to prove that neither their predecessor nor the plaintiffs are the owner, and possessor of the entire land of CS khatian No. 678. The trial Court further observed that in the corresponding SA and BS khatians, the land has been recorded in equal shares in the names of the plaintiffs and defendants which prove that the defendants own and possess 8 annas share of land of CS khatian No. 678 as successors of their predecessor. However, the trial Court did not elaborate its findings with reference to any oral or documentary evidence. The appellate Court below reversed the finding of the trial Court holding, 

 “এই সম্পত্তিতে (referring to CS khatian No. 678) বিবাদীর মালিকানা অজর্নের কোন প্রমাণ বিবাদী উপস্থাপন করেনি । এস, এ, খতিয়ান কোন ভাবেই মালিকানার প্রমাণ বহন করেনা । ... স্বীকৃত মতে বি, এস, খতিয়ান এখনও চূড়ান্ত হয়নি। ...সুতরাং সাক্ষ্য বিশ্লেষণে এটাই প্রতীয়মান হয় যে, ৮১৫ নং এস, এ, খতিয়ানে ভুল রেকর্ডের সুযোগে ওয়াহেদ আলীর ওয়ারিশগণ (বিবাদী-রেসপনডেন্ট) ৬৭৮ নং সি, এস, খতিয়ানের মালিক উজির আলীর সম্পত্তিতে ভিত্তিহীন হিস্যা দাবী করছেন। এই ৬৭৮ নং সি, এস, খতিয়ানে বিবাদীর কোনরূপ মালিকানা নেই। অর্থাৎ সি, এস, ৬৭৮ খতিয়ানের সম্পূর্ণ ৯৮ শতক সম্পত্তিতে ওয়ারিশসূত্রে উজির আলীর ওয়ারিশগণ (বাদী-আ্পীলকারী) একক মালিক মর্মে প্রমাণিত হয়। বিজ্ঞ নি্ন আদালত কোন ধরনের প্রমাণ ব্যতিরেকে এই খতিয়ানের অর্ধেক যা ৪৭ শতক ভূমিতে বিবাদী রেসপনডেন্ট এর মালিকানা আছে মর্মে যে সিদ্ধান্ত দিয়েছেন তা সঠিক হয়নি ।” 

 19. The learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners could not show that the findings of the appellate Court are perverse or that appellate Court misread the evidence or that it failed to consider the evidence, which if considered, the findings would have been otherwise. In Halima Begum and others vs Syed Ahmed and others, 21 DLR 854, it was argued that SA khatian having recorded the disputed land in the name of the pre-emptor it should be presumed that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in respect of the said disputed land. It was held, 

 "It is true that record of right indicates certain right of certain parties but that right is certainly dependent on some material evidence, oral and documentary so as to establish title in favour of persons who claim under the said record of right. The presumption of correctness as to CS record of right is not certainly available with regard to the State Acquisition Khatians. There is no presumption of correctness in respect of the State Acquisition Khatians as it is to be found in case of CS Khatians in pursuance of the provision under section 103-B of the Bengal Tenancy Act." 

 "The presumption of the CS Khatian under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is that every entry in a record of rights finally published shall be the evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to he incorrect. Reference may be made in this regard to the case of Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Kari and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81." 

 21. Reverting back to the case in hand, the defendants could not show as to how their predecessor became owner of 8 annas share in the land of CS khatian No. 678. The entire land was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor alone. Therefore, I am of the view that the appellate Court below rightly held that the plaintiffs are the owners of 16 annas share in the land of CS khatian No. 678 as successors of the CS recorded owner Uzir Ali. 

 22. I have already noted that the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners has. argued that the instant suit for partition is not maintainable due to the fact the SA khatian No. 815, which is corresponding to CS khatian No. 678, has been recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and the defendants in equal shares as owners. Thus, a determination of the respective title of parties is required which cannot be adjudicated in the suit for partition simpliciter. The learned Advocate has relied upon the case of Rezaul Karim and others vs Shamsuzzoha and others, 49 DLR (AD) 68. In the reported case, it has been held as under: 

 26. In the instant case, the plaintiffs proved their title in respect of 16 annas share in the land recorded in CS khatian No. 678. The appellate Court below categorically found that the defendants failed to prove their title in respect of 8 annas share in CS khatian No. 678. Therefore, the instant partition suit is maintainable inasmuch as no dispute emerges as to the title of the plaintiffs to the partible property and that the title of the parties can formally be determined to effect partition. 

 27. The trial Court found that earlier the plaintiffs filed objection case under section 30 of the Bengal Tenancy Act in respect of plot Nos. 2934 and 3042 of CS khatian No. 678 which was rejected. This finding is a total misreading of documentary evidence. Records show that the said objection case was filed in respect of plot Nos. 3443 and 3450 of CS khatian No. 280. Therefore, this finding, which is wrong on the face of the records, does not assist the defendants.
