Chan Mahmood (Md) & others  ------ Petitioners
Vs
Md Hossain Ali being dead his heirs (Ka) Md Sekander Ali & ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. The suit of the plaintiff, in short, is that, Gowhar Sheikh was the original Raiyot having his 16 annas ownership over 12.42 acres land including the suit land comprising an area of 8.47 acres. The CS Khatian was correctly prepared in the name of said Gowhar Sk Plaintiffs are the successive heirs of Gowhar Sk According to them, the suit land devolved on them and they are in possession. The suit land is part of the land of CS Khatian 31(Ext). The CS Khatian has also been proved and exhibited by the defendants as Ext. C and by the plaintiff as Ext.1 

 3. Plaintiffs'' specific case is that, the land of CS Khatian 31 was divided into three ROR Khatians, that is SA Khatians being 28, 29 and 30. ROR Khatians 28 and 29 were wrongly prepared in the name of the defendants. Despite the same, the plaintiffs were in possession of the entire suit land of the said three ROR Khatians. Because of the preparation of said two Khatians 28 and 29 in respect of post of the suit land in favour of the defendants the title of the plaintiffs has been clouded. Therefore, they have filed the suit for declaration of their title alleging that in the month of Agrahayan, 1393 BS when they went to the local Tahsil office to pay rent they found that the said ROR Khatians have been wrongly prepared in the name of the defendants. 

 4. Defendants 1-4 contested. Defendants admitted the original rayoti right of Gowhar Sk in the suit land under the CS Khatian. Defendants also admitted the plaintiffs as successive heirs of said Gowhar Sk. Their specific case is that the suit land was auctioned sold in 1930 AD in Rent Realisation case No. 1051C of 1930. The original Zaminder of the suit Khatian Abdul Hamid Chowdhury of the Nagbari Estate, purchased the suit land in auction vide Ext. B, the sale certificate. He possessed and held the land for stipulated period for more than two years and thereafter the defendants took pattan of the suit land from said Abdul Hamid Chowdhury. Accordingly, the defendants, as alleged, have acquired their ownership in the suit land and are in possession on payment of land revenue althrough both to the Zamindar and to the Government. 

 5. Defendants denied the possession of the plaintiffs since alleged auction sale. They also assert that ROR Khatians were correctly prepared in their favour in consideration of their ownerships and possession of the suit land. 

 7. Plaintiffs' exhibits are 1-1(a), 1(b), 1 (c), 2 part, 2(a)2 and 2(a), Defendants exhibits are A series, which are rent receipts showing payment of rent by them to the Zaminder and to the Government after state acquisition. Ext B is the Bainama (Sale Certificate) and Ext. C is the CS Khatian and C(2) is the ROR Khatian. These are the material exhibits from the side of both parties. Defendants could not file the pattannama or any documentary evidence as to their taking pattan from Abdul Hamid Chowdhury So also defendants failed to produce or file in the court the letter of delivery of possession to complete the alleged auction purchase of the suit auction by Abdul Hamid Chowdhury. The defendants also could not produce any paper or document to show that the suit land originally belonged to Nagbari Estate of Abdul Hamid Chowdhury. 

 12. Mr Halder, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff petitioners, reads the contents of Ext 1 vis-a-vis Ext.0 which is the CS Khatian to me which shows that the property originally did not belong to Abdul Hamid Chowdhury, rather, it belonged to one Shayam Chand Singh and under him Gowhar Sk was in possession as Raiyot. So, the specific case of the defendants as stated above is belied by the contents of Ext. 1 of the plaintiffs which is at the same time Ext. C of the defendants. Thus the plaintiffs succeeded in proving their moot case as to title and the defendants'' case cuts at the root of it. 

 13. The trial Court dismissed the suit finding, inter alia, that the auction sale was valid and the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession. Trial Court held that the defendants could prove that the suit land along with other lands of the said Khatian belonged to Nagbari estate and the suit land was auction sold and was legally purchased by said Abdul Hamid Chowdhury as the Original landlord and later on settled the same to the defendants. This finding of the trial Court is totally beyond the admitted basic title deed namely, the CS Khatian. Therefore, these findings of the trial Court are the result of misreading of evidence, it has been rightly rebutted by the appellate Court. 

 14. Appellate Court has decided the dispute in a very slipshod manner. Appellate Court believed the possession of the plaintiffs and disbelieved the possession of the defendants as the last and final court of fact, considering the evidence both oral and documentary. Appellate Court rightly found that the defendants could not produce any paper as to the rent suit or execution case thereof and also admittedly the defendants could not file letter of delivery of possession. Although SA Khatian has been prepared in the name of the defendants, but the same cannot extinguish the title of the plaintiffs who are admittedly the heirs of the original owner said Gowhar Sk. Appellate Court also found that the defendants could not prove their pattan which is the anchor sheet of their case of title from said Abdul Hamid Chowdhury. 

 16. Mr Ramzan Ali Khan, the learned Counsel for the defendant opposite parties, submits that the rent receipt of the defendants although are many in number, but the same were manufactured by forgery by the defendants to grab the suit land although they have no title or possession in the same. Defendants could not show payment of rent of the period from the years 1934-1943, 1945-46, 1950-52 and for the years 1976-87 which also destroys the case of the defendants that they paid rent for all the years from 1930, the alleged years of taking pattan of the suit land by them. Preparation of SA or ROR Khatian and payment of the rent does not create any title in favour of the defendants when the plaintiffs could prove their possession as well, in the suit land. 

 Here in this case, there is nothing to show that the delivery of possession was taken by the auction purchasers namely, the zaminder. Lacking of delivery of possession has upset at the very root of the case of the defendants. Ext. 1 of plaintiffs is the Exts of the defendants which is the CS Khatian wherein there is nothing to show that Abdul Hamid Chowdhury was at all the previous zaminder having rent receiving interest in any portion of the suit land. 

 Mr Halder relies on the decision in the case of Abdul Hamid and others vs. Abul Hossain Mir and others reported in 35 DLR 295 and submits that latter record of right will prevail over the earlier one and in that view, he submits that SA Khatian having been prepared in the name of the defendants it will prevail upon the CS Khatian. But his submission cannot be accepted because of the more important observation made in the same decision which is as follows : 

 "Presumption of the CS Khatian did not lose its weight because of absence of evidence as to its basis." 

 SA Khatian can create presumption of possession but not of title which the CS Khatian can. Both parties adduced oral evidence to prove possession. The appellate Court on appreciation of the same as the last and final court of fact has found the same in favour of the plaintiffs.

full_judgment:
5. On examination of the record, it reveals that initially the preemption case was disallowed by the Trial Court by order dated 31.12.1973 mainly on the ground that there were 11 persons recorded in R.S khatian no. 156, Exhibit. B(1), Hot no. 485 lying to the north of one of the case plot no. 486 namely Kishore Mohan Nath and the others who were not impleaded as parties although names and particulars were supplied by the pre-emptee. 

 10. Mr. Mostafa Neaz Mohammad, the learned Advocate along with Dr. Mohammad Abul Basher has taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and during the argument, the learned Advocate also has taken me through the preemption application and evidence of the parties and submitted having regard to the judgments of courts below that the pre-emptor-petitioner as of necessity has to prove his own case and he can not succeed on the weakness of the pre-emptee opposite party. Then, Mr. Neaz referring to the exhibits of the pre-emptor has submitted that the preemptor has failed to prove his title as being owner of the land contiguous to the case land but the courts below without adverting to the materials have allowed the preemption which is an error of saw and as such, the judgments are liable to be set aside. He further submitted that the courts below had to decide the title of the preemptor Over his own land in as much as the preemptor has not filed any documents of his tittle but he sought the preemption only submitting S.A. Khatian which has got no evidentiary value though C.S. and R.S. Khatian has evidentiary value and failing to consider those aspects of the case and allowing the preemption committed fundamental error of law. He submitted further the Courts below relying merely on S.A. Khatian without prove of title on the basis of any legal documents have allowed the pre-emption case and thus committed error of law. Mr. Mostafa Neaz Mohammad then referring to the evidence of PW. 1 submitted that one Kalu has not been impleaded in the preemption proceeding and as such, the preemption proceeding suffers from defect of parties and in spite of such materials on record the courts below allowing preemption have committed error of law and thereby, judgments are liable to be set aside. 

 ‘‘5. Mr. Md. Jani Alam, leaned Advocate appearing on behalf of the pre-emptor opposite party no. 1 submits that the State Acquisition Khatian having recorded the disputed land in the name of the pre-emptor it should be presumed that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in respect of the said disputed land. After what we have stated above with regard to the documentary as well as oral evidence we are unable to attach any importance to the said record of right. It is true that record of right indicates certain right of certain parties but that right is certainly dependent on some material evidence, oral and documentary so as to establish title in favour or persons who claim under the said record of right. The presumption of correctness as to C.S. record of right is not certainly available with regard to the State Acquisition Khatians. There is no. presumption of correctness in respect of the State Acquisition Khatians as it is to be found in case of C.S. Khatians in pursuance of the provision under section 103-B of the Bangal Tenancy Act." 

 ‘‘নালিশী ৪৮৬/৫১০ দাগের জমির লাগ উত্তরে দরখাস্ত কারীর সত্য দখলীয় ৮১নং সমসপুর মৌজার ঝ.অ. ২০৪ নং খতিয়ানের ১। আনা জমার অন্তর্গত ৪৮৭ দাগের ২৯ শতাংশ জমি এবং ঐ মৌজার ঝ.অ. ২০২ নং খতিয়ান ॥. আনা জমার অন্তর্গত ৪৪৮ দাগের .২৫ শতাংশ জমি থাকায় দরখাস্তকারী লাগ পাশাইলা হিসাবে" on such statement filed this pre-emption case but not a scrap of paper showing his title filed before the courts but only filed S.A. Khatian in as much as he submitted that the S.A. Khatian is not a deed of title but only such Khatian proves the possession and that S.A. Khatian has no presumption in evidence but the courts below having not recorded any findings as to the title of the pre-emptor have allowed the pre-emption on the basis of S.A. Khatian and allowing pre-emption have committed error of law. 

 "9. Admittedly, both the S.A. Khatians as well as RS Khatians in respect of the suit land stand in the names of the predecessor-in interest of the plaintiff-opposite parties and also in some of their names It is true that the SA records, in view of section 19(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act do not provide conclusive evidence as regards title but it provides conclusive evidence as regards their preparation and revision. But entries in the SA records; in my opinion, provide a prima facie evidence as regards title. In order to maintain a suit for declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff is required to have prima facie evidence showing that he has a legal character or right to a property in respect of the subject matter of the suit and granting or refusal to grant a decree in such suit shall always depend on final adjudication thereof on evidence. Since the SA records vide Exts. 3 and 3(ka) stand in the names of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff opposite parties and also in some of their names it should be taken to be a prima facie evidence of title of the plaintiff-opposite parties in respect of the suit land and, as such, the plaintiff-opposite parties were competent to file the present suit. I do not dispute the legal principles deduced in the aforesaid cases cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners. Since the present suit was not for a declaration of title but for a declaration of the act of the revenue authority namely, the order of mutation outside the purview of law as illegal the same is certainly maintainable. Reference may be made in this connection to the case reported in 16 DLR 298." 

 17. I have perused the judgment of both the courts, Admittedly, the judgment of the Appellate Court is in the affirmation of the Trial Court and the courts below held that the preemption case is maintainable and that the preemptor is a holder of land contiguous to the land transferred and the courts below have arrived at such findings and decisions upon consideration of the materials on record. Be that as it may. I have considered the section 96 and sub-section 1 and 2 and upon close consideration of the provisions of the aforesaid section, it appears to me that the court has to decide only upon inquiry whether the applicant is a co-sharer tenant of the holding and in this case, the courts below have found on the basis of the S.A. Khatian that the preemptor is holding land contiguous to the land transferred. It appears further that From the records that the name of the predecessor Sonaullah Molla of the petitioner appears in R.S. Khatian which has been exhibited by the preemptee as exhibit-B(2) and so also the name of the petitioner Hachan Kha appears in exhibit-B(3). R.S. Khatian has got evidentiary value and considering the exhibits along with S.A. Khatians, exhibits 2 and 2(a) the courts below held that the pre-emptor is a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, taking as a prima facie evidence of title of the preemptor and the courts below allowing pre-emption on the basis of such evidence on record committed no error of law. 

 18. In deciding the case under section 96 of the SA&T Act the courts need not make inquiry in respect of the title of the preemptor but only require to consider incidentally whether the pre-emptor is a co sharer tenant by inheritance, by purchase and tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred and in this case the courts below were satisfied that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer holding land contiguous to the land transferred on the basis of S.A. Khatians exhibit-2 and 2(a) along with the R. S. Khatian exhibit-B(2) and B(3) the courts below have committed no error of law. I find no substance in the submissions of Mr. Neaz Mohammad.

Abdul Aziz ------ Appellant
Vs.
Hindu Deity Luxmi Gobinda Jew and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
4. The case of defendant No. 2, is that the suit property became enemy property and, as such, vested in the defendant Government. The plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit property and, as such, it has no locus standi to bring the suit. The case of the defendant No.4, on the other hand, is that the suit is barred by limitation and the plaintiff has no locus standi to file the suit as he is neither the shebayet nor the suit property is a debuttor property, that the suit land and other lands of mouza Daulatpur and Kirtibashdi were taken in its possession by the Government under section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and were accordingly recorded in the newly prepared khatian No.1 as khas land and the said land was settled with him and one Shafiuddin Ahmed in Settlement Case Nos. 173 of 1966-67 and 176 of 1966-67 on 3-4-1967. 

 9. It is undisputed that the suit land was recorded in the CS Khatian Exhibits 1 and 1(a) as debuttar property in the name of the plaintiff deity Luxmi Gobinda Jew Bigraha but the SA Khatian in respect of the suit land was prepared in the name of Suresh Chandra Roy. The definite case of the plaintiff is that one Debendra Chandra Bhattachatjee was the shebayet of the deity and before him Sharat Chandra Bhattachatjee was the shebayet of the plaintiff deity. But the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of Suresh Chandra Roy who had no title and possession the rein, it appears that the High Court Division discussed the evidence of PW 1 Prafulla Chandra Bhattacharjee the present Shebayet and other plaintiffs witness. PW 1, Prafulla Chandra Bhattacharjee in his evidence stated that the deity was installed long ago. He further stated that before him, his father was the shebayet. He also stated that he himself cultivated a portion of the suit property and his bargadars cultivated the remaining portion. He also stated that he did not receive any notice for treating the suit property as enemy property. He further stated that the property has not been declared as abandoned property and the plaintiff was never dispossessed from the suit land. He further stated that his father Debendra Chandra Bhattachatjee and others did not file. Miscellaneous Appeal No. 395 of 1965 before the Commissioner of Dhaka Division, PW 2, Jogesh Chandra Dey aged about 70 years. PW 3 Md Ali. aged about 59 years and other PWs stated that the deity was installed in a portion of the suit land long ago and the shebayet of the deity possesses the suit land. 

 11. The High Court Division held that the suit land was recorded in the name of the deity Luxmi Gobinda Jew Bigraha in the CS Khatian as a rent free jote. It also appears that there is no evidence on record that the deity ever migrated to India at any point of time or that the deity was taken to India by the shebayet. It may be pointed out that the suit property was once treated as an abandoned property and subsequently as an enemy (now vested) property. The High Court Division held once the property became an abandoned property and vested in the Government the same cannot be treated as enemy property and, therefore, such action of the defendants in treating the suit property as enemy property is evidently illegal and without jurisdiction. 

 13. We have already pointed out that undisputedly the suit land was recorded in the name of the deity in the CS Khatian Exhibits 1 and 1(a). The CS Khatian has a presumption of correctness under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act but the SA Khatian has no such presumptive value, it is true that presumption of correctness of entry in the CS Khatian is rebuttable by adducing cogent and reliable evidence, in the instant case there is no attempt even to rebut the correctness of entry ill the CS Khatian prepared in the name of the deity. The High Court Division relying on the case of Sukumar Bose and others vs Abani Kumar Halder and others reported in 60 CWN 778 observed that in that case it was held that a debuttor property can never be turned into a secular property, in view of the proposition that once a property becomes a property of the deity which is immortal, it continues to be a property of the deity for all times to come. The dedication of the property to an idol may take place at the time of installation of the idol or may precede it or it may take place after the installation of the deity and after the dedication in all cases it remains the property of the idol and ceases to be the property of the donor. Even if a particular image may be destroyed, the deity whose visible form the image continues for ever and its property as debuttor property remains totally unaffected. 

 14. In view of our above discussion, that the CS Khatian Exhibits 1 and 1(a) were correctly prepared in the name of the plaintiff deity, the title of the suit land remained with the deity and the deity possessed through shebayet and preparation of the SA Khatian in the name of Suresh Chandra was apparently without any basis. The High Court Division it appears, on analysis of evidence on record, found possession of the plaintiffs shebayet in the suit land, Moreover, if according to defence case the property was once taken over as abandoned property, as claimed by the defendant, the same cannot be treated as enemy property again.

Md. Zahangir Alam and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Ziaul Haque and others ------ opposite parties
full_judgment:
2. Facts in short are that the opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted above suit to the Land Survey Tribunal Chandpur for declaration that B.S. khatian Nos.1359 and 439 in the names of the defendants are unlawful and for creation of a new khatian for 19 decimal land in the names of the plaintiffs out of 31 decimal land of above two B.S. khatians. It was alleged that above property belonged to Ramjan Ali @ Ranjon Ali, Alemjan and Nekjan in whose names C.S. khatian No.1046 was correctly prepared. Above Ramjan Ali died leaving three sons Ansar Ali, Monsur Ali and Golam Mohammad and two daughters Taramon and Paktunnessa as heirs. Above Golam Mohammad acquired the shares of Taramon and Paktunnessa and was in possession in 19 decimal land which he transferred to his daughter Zinnatunnessa by registered deed of gift dated 29.12.1970. Above Zinnatunnessa died leaving the plaintiffs as heirs who are processing above land by constructing dwelling house. But above land has been erroneously recorded in the names of the defendants in above two B.S. khatians. 

 3. Defendant Nos.1-32 contested above suit by filing a joint written statement alleging that Ansar Ali and Monsur Ali two sons and heirs of Ramjan Ali transferred 31 decimal land to Shomsher Ali by registered deed of exchange dated 27.01.1932 who in his turn transferred the same to Abdur Rahman and Abdul Jabbar by two registered deeds of exchange dated 08.03.1932 and their names were rightly recorded in S.A. khatian No.824. Defendants are successive heirs of above Abdur Rahman and Jobbar and they are in possession in the dwelling house in above land and B.S. khatians No.1539 and 439 were correctly prepared. 

 8. Mr. Md. Harun Al Kaioum learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that undisputedly defendants are heirs of S.A. recorded tenant Abdur Rahman and Abdul Jobbar. Above Rahman and Jobbar acquired 31 decimal land by registered deed of exchange dated 08.03.1932 from Samser Ali who acquired the same from Ansar Ali and Monsur Ali two sons of C.S. recorded tenant Ramjan Ali. Above Rahman and Jobbar were in possession in above land by constructing dwelling house and above two B.S. khatians were correctly prepared in the names of the defendants. But the learned Judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal totally failed to understand the facts and circumstances of the case and affirmed the unlawful judgment and decree of the Land Survey Tribunal which is not tenable in law. As far as maintainability of this civil revision under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is concerned the learned Advocate submits that the Judge of the Land Survey Tribunal has been appointed from among the Joint District Judges and proceedings before above Tribunal has been designated as suit and a decree is drawn from the judgment of the Land Survey Tribunal and the Tribunal records evidence and determines title and possession in immovable property and makes correction of B.S. khatian on the basis of title and possession. The impugned judgment and decree has been passed by a District Judge as the Judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal. All above facts show that above Land Survey Tribunal and Land Survey Appellate Tribunal are, in fact, civil courts whose judgment and decree is subject to revisional jurisdiction of this court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. 

 9. On the other hand Mr. Humayun Kabir learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that Golam Mohammad a Malik of S.A. khatian No.824 transferred 19 decimal land to his daughter Zinatunnessa by registered deed of gift dated 29.12.1970. Above Zinatunnessa possessed above land by constructing dwelling house and after her demise the defendants as her heirs are in possession in above house. But the Surveyors most illegally recorded above land in the names of the defendants in above two B.S. khatians. On consideration of above facts and circumstances of the case and materials on record the learned Judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal rightly dismissed the appeal and affirmed the lawful judgment and decree of the Tribunal and directed for creation of a new khatian for the plaintiffs for 19 decimal land out of above two B.S. khatians which calls for no interference. 

 11. After final publication in official Gazette a huge number of errors in the entry or omission in entry in B.S. khatians were found. The Revenue Officer having no jurisdiction for correction of above errors or omissions legislature for the sole purpose of correction of above errors, mistakes or omissions in BS khatians introduced Act No.IX of 2004 to the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and established the Land Survey Tribunal and the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal. Above Tribunals are not civil courts and they have no jurisdiction to determine title or possession in immovable property. Section 145E of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 gives finality to the judgment and decree passed by the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal. This court needs to employ its valuable time for hearing of civil revisions involving legal disputes as to right to office or right to property instead of examining errors or omissions in the entry of BS khatians. 

 15. It is admitted that above property originally belonged to Ramjan Ali who died leaving three sons, Ansar Ali, Monsur Ali and Golam Mohammad and two daughters Taramon and Paktunnessa. Admittedly plaintiffs are heirs of Zinatunnessa, a daughter of Golam Mahammad and defendants are heirs of Abdur Rahman and Abdul Jobbar in whose names S.A. khatian No.824 was recorded. Plaintiffs claim that Zinatunnessa acquired 19 decimal land from her father Golam Mohammad by registered deed of gift dated 29.12.1970. Defendants, on the other hand, claim that Ansar Ali and Monsur Ali two sons of Ramjan Ali transferred 31 decimal land to Shomsher Ali by two registered deed of exchange dated 27.01.1932 who in his turn transferred above land to Abdur Rahman and Abdur Jobbar, predecessors of the defendants by registered deed of exchange dated 08.03.1932. 

 16. It turns out that disputed two B.S. khatians were prepared in the names of the defendants on the basis of S.A. khatian No.824 and registered deed of exchange dated 08.03.1932 and the plaintiffs do not dispute correctness of above khatians and defendants title and possession in 12 decimal land. Plaintiffs claim 19 decimal land out of 31 decimal of above two BS khatians. 

 17. The learned Judge of the Land Survey Tribunal framed an issue whether the plaintiffs have succeeded to prove their title and possession in above land and on consideration of oral and documentary evidence held that the plaintiffs title and possession in 19 decimal land out of 31 decimal was proved and on the basis of above findings ordered for deduction of 19 decimal land out of 31 decimal of above two BS khatians. The learned Judge of the Tribunal also held that S.A. khatian No.824 was erroneous. 

 19. A civil court is empowered to try all suits of civil nature unless its jurisdiction is specifically barred. A suit of civil nature means any suit involving disputes relating to right to property or right to office and right to property includes right to ownership and possession in immobile property. The jurisdiction for determination of title and possession in immovable property falls in the exclusive domain of civil court. On the other hand a Tribunal is a judicial or quasi judicial body established by law to hear and determine claims or disputes of specific class or type. Section 145A of the Act mentions that sole jurisdiction of the Land Survey Tribunal is to deal with the suits arising out of final publication of the last revised record of rights under section 114 of the Act, which is B.S. khatians. The Land Survey Appellate Tribunal is empowered only to hear appeals from the judgment and decree of the Land Survey Tribunal. The Land Survey Tribunal being not a civil court it has no jurisdiction to entertain a suit involving dispute as to title and possession in immovable property. 

 20. The purpose of land survey is to prepare a public record as to the location, nature, area, ownership and quantity of rent of each and every piece of land so that the land may be identified, owners may be recognized, land disputes minimized, rents may be smoothly realized and above record of rights may be used for other official works. After promulgation of the Bengle Tenancy Act, 1885 a comprehensive and physical land survey under above Act was started in 1887 and concluded in 1940. The record of rights prepared though above survey was designated as cadastral survey khatian or C.S. khatian. After the state acquisition of rent receiving interest in 1950 a revision of above record of rights was held under section 17 of the Act not by field survey but by desk works in the revenue office. The objectives of above revision of record of rights were to prepare a compensation rent roll, recognize the tenants as maliks and fixation of equitable rents. The record of rights or khatian prepared through above survey is called State Acquisition khatian or S.A. Khatian. After final publication of above khatian in the official gazette huge errors in entry and omissions in entry of S.A. khatians were found. The Government for correction of above errors in S.A. khatians inserted section 143A to the Act by Ordinance No.IIX of 1967. Above provision empowered all civil courts having jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession to order necessary corrections of S.A. khatians through a summary procedure. All District Judges were authorized to hear appeals from the judgment of above civil Judges. After disposal of nearly all cases seeking correction of S.A. khatians section 143A of the Act was deleted by Ordinance No.54 of 1975. 

 21. The Bangladesh survey was started in 1970 by physical field survey of each and every piece of land and a record of rights namely B.S. Khatian was prepared and finally published in the official gazette under section 144 of the Act. Despite preparation through physical field survey a huge number of allegations as to errors in entry or omission in entry in BS khatians emerged and to redress above grievances Section 145A to 145I were inserted in the Act by Act No.IX of 2004. The Land Survey Tribunal was established for “disposing of suits arising out of the final publication of last revised record of rights”. While section 145B of the Act established the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal to hear and dispose of appeals from the judgment and decree of the Land Survey Tribunal. Section 145A of the Act did not empower the civil court for correction of errors in entry or omission in entry of the B.S. khatians as was done by now deleted section 143A of the Act nor the Land Survey Tribunal or Land Survey Appellate Tribunal were declared as civil court. 

 23. The Land Survey Tribunal has no jurisdiction to entertain any suit involving any dispute as to the legality or correctness of S.A. khatian. On the contrary the Land Survey Tribunal is required to accept the S.A. Khatian as flawless previous record of rights in view of deletion of section 143A by Act No.54 of 1975. The B.S. khatian was prepared on revision of previous record of rights or S.A khatians on the basis of field survey and outcome of objection case and appeal against the draft B.S. khatian under Rules 32 and 33 of the State Acquisition Rules, 1951. 

 24. The Tribunal needs to accept the S.A Khatian as baseline and examine the allegation of errors or omission in entry in B.S khatian on the basis of the S.A. khatian. The B.S. khatian must be referable to the S.A. khatian and should have been prepared in the names of the malik or heirs of the Malik of S.A. khatian or transferees from above Malik or his heirs. If any entry in B.S khatian fails to pass above test the same be declared as erroneous and unlawful and the Tribunal shall pass a decree for correction of above khatian. 

 25. Any person still aggrieved by an entry or omission of entry in the S.A. khatian needs to realize that after gazette publication of B.S. khatian the S.A. khatian has become a previous or past record of rights and there is no provision for correction of erroneous S.A. khatian by a civil court after deletion of section 143A of the Act by Ordinance No.54 of 1975. But if the title or possession of any person in immoveable property is denied or threatened on the basis of erroneous S.A. khatian or any other erroneous document the aggrieved person is entitled to move to the relevant civil court with an appropriate suit for title and possession. 

 26. The Land Survey Tribunal should emphasis on disposing of suits relating to erroneous entry or omission of entry in the B.S. khatian on the basis of evidence on affidavit. The lengthy examination and cross examination of four witnesses and analysis of a series of documents by the Land Survey Tribunal for determination of title of the plaintiff was unnecessary and caused wastage of court time. 

 27. A khatian or record of rights is not a deed of title. A khatian or record of rights carries a presumption as to possession of the person whose name stands in the khatian. But above presumption as to possession is not static nor a record of rights or khatian is conclusive prove of possession. In fact mere erroneous record of rights does not require the rightful owner to move to the court unless his title or possession is threatened on the basis of erroneous record of rights or khatian. 

 29. The amendment of section 145C of the Act for stopping appeal to the Appellate Division and giving finality to the judgment of the Land Appellate Tribunal show that the legislature did not want to bring the disputes involving error in entry or omission in entry of B.S. khatian to the Supreme Court. This court has no jurisdiction to entertain a civil revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure challenging the legality and proprietary of a judgment and decree passed by the learned Judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal. 

 30. In above view of the facts and circumstances of the case and materials son record I hold that the learned Judge of the Land Survey Tribunal clearly usurped the jurisdiction of civil court and most illegally adjudged the B.S. and S.A. khatians of the defendants as erroneous on the basis of erroneous determination of title and possession of the plaintiffs in 19 decimal land and the learned Judge of the Land Appellate Tribunal most illegally affirmed above unlawful judgment and decree of the Land Survey Tribunal and this court has no jurisdiction to entertain the instant civil revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against above judgment and decree of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal. 

 31. The learned Judges of the Land Survey Tribunal and the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal shall keep in mind and follow the directions mentioned below while disposing of suits or appeals arising out of the last revised record of rights or B.S. khatians: 

 (2) The sole jurisdiction of the Land Survey Tribunal is to detect errors in entry or omission in entry in the last revised record of rights prepared under section 144 of the Act or BS khatians and pass an appropriate order; 

 (3) S. A. khatian is the immediately past or previous record of rights prepared and published under Chapter IV, section 17 of the Act and the Land Survey Tribunal has no jurisdiction to entertain any suit challenging the legality or correctness of S.A kahtian; 

 (4) If title and possession of any person is threatened on the basis of erroneous entry or omission in entry of previous S.A. khatian he is at liberty to move to the competent civil court with an appropriate civil suit for declaration of title and confirmation or recovery of possession or partition. 

 (5) The Land Survey Tribunal and Land Survey Appellate Tribunal shall accept the S.A. khatian as flawless past record of right and use S.A. khatian as baseline for detection of error in entry or omission in entry of B.S. khatian.
justice_names: Mr. Justice S M Kuddus Zaman

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Senior Advocate with S.K. Rezaul Haque, Advocate, instructed by Chowdhury Md. Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellants 
Kamal-ul-Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record ------For Respondent Nos. 30- 35 
Shamsul Alam, Advocate-on-Record ------ Respondent No.29 
Respondent Nos.1-28 ------Not represented.
parties:
Md. Bedarul Islam being dead his heirs: Kulsuma Khatun and others ------ Appellants.
Vs
Md. Zakaria and others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
4. The plaintiffs' case, in short, is that the suit land belonged to one Gani Mia, who sold the same land by a registered deed of sale dated 05.05.1925 to Lal Mia. After that, Lal Mia sold the same by a registered deed of sale dated 16.06.1925 to Najir Ahmed, the father of the plaintiffs. Subsequently, Najir Ahmed settled the said land with Abdur Rahman by a registered patta. Abdur Rahman used to stay in Burma. During the R.S operation, the R.S. Khatian for the suit land was recorded in the names of the plaintiffs father, Najir Ahmed and his four brothers, though they had no title to the suit land and they also did not possess the land on the basis of the wrong recording. Abdur Rahman sold the suit land to the plaintiff by a registered deed of sale dated 15.02.1975 and the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land. The recent B.S. Khatian was recorded in their names. Proforma defendant Nos.11 and 12 acquired 0.26 acre of land described in schedule 1(Ka) in L.A. Case No.13 of 1986-87. A Compensation Assessment Roll was duly prepared in the names of the plaintiffs. The principal defendants taking the advantage of the wrong recording of the land in R.S. and P.S. Khatians raised objection against the plaintiffs' right to get compensation for the acquired land and as such, the suit was filed to remove the cloud in the suit land. 

 5. Defendant Nos.2-8 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint of the suit. Their case, in short, is that the suit land belonged to C.S. recorded tenant Oli Mia, who by an amicable partition with Gani Mia was in possession of the suit land and subsequently, Oli Mia died leaving behind 5 sons namely, Najir Ahmed and his four brothers and the R.S. record was rightly made in their names. Abdur Rahman, son of Oli Mia, sold 0.08 acre of suit land to this defendant by a registered deed of sale dated 28.05.1986 and out of said land 0.05 acre was acquired by the Government and that mutation khatian in respect of 0.08 acre of suit land was prepared in the name of the defendant. The plaintiffs father, Najir Ahmed was entitled to get share in the suit land and that the alleged deeds of transfer and the deed of settlement are forged and ineffective and Najir Ahmed had never possessed the suit land. 

 13. The trial Court came to the finding that on consideration of evidence on record, it appeared that the plaintiff could not prove that at the time of R.S. operation, Abdur Rahman was in Burma (now Myanmar). The trial Court also came to the finding that the plaintiff could not prove that Abdur Rahman possessed the suit land himself or through 'bargader' and as such, the contention of the plaintiff-appellants that taking advantage of Abdur Rahman's staying in Burma, the R.S. khatian was wrongly prepared in the names of Nazir Ahmed and his four brothers. The trial court also found that exhibits-2, 2ka and 3 were never acted upon. The trial Court, therefore, concluded that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their title to and possession in the suit land. 

 14. The appellate Court, on the other hand, came to the finding that as per C.S. khatian Gani Mia (Guno Mia) was in exclusive possession of plot No.3182. The Appellate Court also found that in the C.S. khatian the four boundaries of the plot were clearly given which exclusively proved that Gani Mia, the C.S. recorded tenant was in exclusive possession of the suit plot No.3182. The appellate Court held that the suit land did not belong to Oli Mia but that it actually belonged to Gani Mia, who sold it to Lal Mia, who again sold it to Najir Ahmed. The Appellate Court also held that as Najir Ahmed had succeeded in proving his title by way of purchase on the basis of registered deed (exhibit-2ka) the initial presumption attached to R.S. khatian, exhibit-1(ka) was rebutted. The appellate Court also held that Najir Ahmed as tenure-holder in R.S. plot No.4429 (suit plot) was entitled to transfer the same by way of settlement which he did accordingly by executing patta exhibit-3 dated 18.07.1925, by which 18 gondas of land were transferred to Abdur Rahman. The appellate Court also held that the allegations of fraud by Najir Ahmed was not proved by cogent evidence and that the appellate Court also held that one who alleged fraud must bear the burden of proving it and the burden is comparatively heavier when it is against old registered documents. The appellate Court also held that by three documents (exhibits-2, 2ka and 3) no land of Oli Mia was attracted and that the chance of fraud in view of the given circumstances seemed to be too remote. Therefore, the appellate Court concluded that the plaintiffs had been able to prove their title to and possession in the suit land and accordingly, the appellate Court decreed the suit. 

 17. The plaintiffs claimed that land of C.S. khatian No.3182 belonged to Gani Mia who sold it to Lal Mia by a registered deed of sale dated 05.05.1925. Lal Mia also sold the land of the said plot to Najir Ahmed by a registered deed of sale dated 16.06.1925. Najir Ahmed settled the suit land to Abdur Rahman by a registered patta dated 18.07.1925. Abdur Rahman owned and possessed the suit land by paying rent to Najir Ahmed, the predecessor of the plaintiffs. But during S.A. operation, the land of said patta was wrongly recorded in the names of Najir Ahmed and his four brothers as Abdur Rahman at the relevant time was in Burma. Subsequently, Abdur Rahman sold the suit land as shown in schedule-Ka to the plaint to the plaintiffs by a registered deed of sale dated 15.02.1975. 

 18. On the other hand, the defendants claimed that their predecessor Oli Mia was the recorded tenant of C. S. khatian and that Oli Mia by amicable settlement with Gani Mia got the suit land as shown in the 1st schedule to the plaint and that he died leaving behind Najir Ahmed, Sadik Ahmed, Abdur Rahman, Abdul Khaleque and Md. Nasir. Subsequently, the suit land was correctly recorded in the names of Najir Ahmed and his four brothers. Najir Ahmed was the owner of 1/5th share of the suit land. In order to deprive his brothers, Najir Ahmed collusively created the deeds dated 05.05.1925 and 16.06.1925 and that those documents were not acted upon. The registered patta dated 18.07.1925 standing in the name of Abdur Rahman is also collusive. Therefore, the claim of the plaintiffs on the basis of registered deed of sale dated 15.02.1975 is void, collusive, inoperative and without any consideration. 

 19. Abdur Rahman, son of Oli Mia, sold .08 acre of land to the defendants by a registered deed of sale dated 28.05.1986. The 1st schedule land to the plaint has been recorded in C.S. plot No.3182 corresponding to R.S. plot No.4429. The C.S. record, exhibit-1 shows that the recorded tenants were Gani Mia, Oli Mia and Karimjan. The C. S. record (exhibit-1) reveals that the recorded tenants were in specific possession of the different plots of the khatian. Oli Mia was in possession of C.S. Plot Nos.3114 and 3380. Gani Mia was in specific in C.S. plot Nos.3182 and 3184 and the remaining plots were possessed by Karimjan. In the C.S. Khatian four boundaries of plots were clearly given so as to denote actual possession of each of the tenants. C.S. plot No.3182 exclusively stands in the names of the Gani Mia which is bounded on north by a road and on the south and east by Oli Miah and on the western side by Abul Hossain. Therefore, the aforesaid entry in C.S. khatian proved possession of Gani Mia, the C. S. recorded tenant exclusively in C. S. plot No.3182 and his title to the said plot would follow from the established possession. Gani Mia as an exclusive owner sold 18 gondas of land of C.S. plot No.3182 to Lal Mia by giving a defined boundary on 05.05.1925. Out of 96 decimals of the C.S. plot, 36 decimals of land were transferred which is proved by exhibit-2. While in possession of the said land, Lal Mia sold it to Najir Ahmed by a registered deed of sale dated 16.06.1925 (exhibit-2ka) and handed over possession thereof. 

 20. The aforesaid findings proved that the suit land did not belong to Oli Mia but it actually belonged to Gani Mia, who sold it to Lal Mia, who again sold it to Najir Ahmed. As Najir Ahmed has succeeded in proving his title by way of purchase on the basis of registered deed (exhibit-2ka) the initial presumption attached to the R.S. khatian exhibit-1(ka) was rebutted. Therefore, Najir Ahmed was legally entitle to settled the suit land to Abdur Rahman by exhibit-3, the registered patta dated 18.07.1925. The appellate Court on consideration of evidence on record found that the allegation of fraud was not proved in obtaining the suit land by the plaintiffs. The appellate Court also discussed the evidence adduced by P.Ws.1, 2 and 3 and found that they could prove that the Abdur Rahman was in actual possession of the suit land. The appellate Court also noted that P.Ws.2 and 3 were not cross-examined by the defendants in respect of their evidence as regards possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. The appellate Court also noted that the defendants did not adduce any oral or documentary evidence during the trial. The appellate Court also considered exhibits-4 and 4ka, the rent receipts in respect of the suit land and found that the plaintiffs paid rent before filing of the suit and that rent receipt not only proved possession of the plaintiffs but also proved as collateral evidence of title to the suit land. The appellate Court noted that respondent No.3 filed three rent receipts relating to P.S. plot No.3080 for an area of .08, .22, .10 and .05 acre of land and that from those rent receipts, the plaintiffs' claim of possession was not affected so far as regards the quantum of land in P.S. khatian No.3082. The appellate Court also held that the defendants had not come out with positive proof regarding exclusive possession of P.S. plot No.4429 and as such, their onus was not discharged.

full_judgment:
9. In deciding Issue Nos. 4 and 5 Learned Assistant Judge held that Plaintiff filed certified Copies of Heba-Bil-Ewaz Deeds dated 29.10.1948 and 30.10.1948 and Plaintiff proved those two Heba-Bil-Ewaz deeds in accordance with Law. Learned Assistant Judge further held that in accordance with Section 60 of Registration Act Ownership of Property conveyed by Two Heba-Bil-Ewaz. Deeds dated 29.10.1948 and 30.10.1948 (Exhibit 2 and 2 (ha) respectively) vested upon Plaintiff. Learned Assistant Judge, also, held that Plaintiff filed State Acquisition khatian which has been exhibited as Exhibit ka (K) and presumption of Law is that S.A. Khatian having been prepared in the name of Plaintiff, Plaintiff was found in possession on Suit Property during the period of preparation S.A. Khatian. Learned Assistant-Judge, also, rendered decision that from evidence, both documentary and oral it became manifestly clear that Plaintiff by way of two Deeds dated 29.10.1948 and 30.10.1948 became owner and possessor of Suit Property. In rendering decision Learned Assistant Judge duly considered evidence of P.WS 1, 3 and 4 who are tenants under Plaintiff since the year 1967-1968 and Defendant side could not bring out any sort of contradiction in versions supplied by P.W.s. Learned Assistant Judge, also, came to hold that Defendant failed to prove that Notice of Requisition and Acquisition had been served upon Plaintiff. Learned Assistant Judge taking into account provision embodied in Section. 4 of (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act 1948 and, also provisions contained in Section 7 of Act of 1948 and Section B and Sub-Section B and Section C and, also, relevant sections of Ordinance No. IX of 1969 held that Plaintiff having proved his ownership and possession on Suit Property is entitled to get reliefs prayed for. 

 12. Learned Additional District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka being the Last and Final Court of facts on consideration of Pleadings, evidence and other materials or record held that Plaintiff on calling two volumes of Heba-Bil-Ewaz Deeds lawfully proved two registered Deeds dated 30.10.1948 and 29.10.1948 and two Deeds had been exhibited as Exhibit 2 and 2 (ka). Learned Additional District Judge, also, came to hold that witnesses for Plaintiff-Respondent gave evidence in support of possession of Plaintiff-Respondent over Suit Property and preparation of SA Khatian, Exhibit 1 having been prepared in the name of Plaintiff, possession of Plaintiff on Suit Property had been proved. Learned Additional District Judge also, held that Government could not prove its claim of Requisition of Suit Property in L.A. Case No. 63 of 1959-1960 but Plaintiff acquired Suit Property by way of Heba-Bil-Ewaz Deeds before one decade i.e. in the year 1948 before alleged Acquisition of Suit Property by Government, and, as such, Notice was required to be served upon Plaintiff at the time of Requisition and Acquisition in accordance with Law and Rules. Learned Additional District Judge further held that Defendant-Appellant did neither deny the existence of Deeds of Plaintiff nor did take any lawful steps in respect of the Deeds, and, as such, lawful effectiveness of the Deeds remains unaffected. Learned Additional District Judge on consideration of evidence of Abdus Salam, witness for Defendant who in his testimony dial not at all state that Government or Railway have been in possession of suit property rather he admitted that he could not say in whose possession suit property has been, and, on the other had witnesses for Plaintiff-Respondent gave evidence in support of Possession of Plaintiff on suit property. Learned Additional District Judge found that finding reached by Trial Court on the issue of cause of 'action of Suit and Limitation are correct and just. Leaned Additional District Judge in conclusion came to hold that in light of discussion made above it transpired that Plaintiff-Respondent had been in possession of suit property and a prima facie Title had been established by Oral and Documentary .evidence and Judgment and Decree passed in favour of Plaintiff Respondent by Trial Court having been in accordance with law and procedure those are liable to be maintained. 

 18. The Point now may be discussed and answered. Exhibit 2 and 2 (ka) are two registered Heba-Bil-Ewaz Deeds dated 29.10.1948 and 30.10.1948 with respect to suit property i.e. 0.17 acres + 0.17 acres = 0.34 acres from C.S. Plot No. 1356 corresponding to S.A. Plot No. 4017 and 4019 and those two Heba-Bil-Ewan Deeds had been lawfully proved by Plaintiff by calling volumes of Deeds Exhibit I. Slate Acquisition Khatian prepared in the name of Plaintiff and there is presumption of correctness of the Record of Right, that is, S.A. Khatian prepared in the name of Plaintiff and this Presumption is attached under section 144 A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It appears that Defendant-Petitioner did neither deny existence of two Heba-Bil-Ewan Deeds nor take any steps against the Deeds. Plaintiff-Opposite Party No. 1 in order to prove the Deeds examined himself as P.W.1 and put on witness box PW-2, Deed Writer of two Heba-Bil-Ewaz Deeds who proved two Hcba-Bil-Ewaz Deeds which had been exhibited as Exhibit 2 and 2 (ka) and, also, PW-5 and PW-6 who being employees of Office of District Registrar brought volumes of two Deeds. Plaintiff-Opposite Party examined PW-3 and PW-4 to prove his Possession on suit property. PW-3 stated in his evidence that Plaintiff is the Owner and Possessor of Suit Property and on suit property there are three "Pucca" Houses and Twelve Thatched Houses and a Shop and Plaintiff possessed those through tenants. PW-3 stated that he constructed Ration Shop on Suit Properly and he is a tenant under Plaintiff. PW-4 in his evidence stated that on the suit homestead he is a tenant in two rooms under Plaintiff and he has been in the homestead since the Year 1967-1968 and Plaintiff inducted many persons on suit property as tenants and in all there are 20-25 tenants on suit property under Plaintiff. PW-5 is Record Keeper of the Office of District Registrar, Dhaka and he came to Court with Volumes and he proved the Deed dated 30.10.1948 which was exhibited as Exhibit 2 (ka). PW-6 in his evidence stated that he carried Volumes from the office of District Registrar. Dhaka and proved Deed dated 29/10/1948 and the said Deed had been exhibited as Exhibit-2. Credibility of evidences of PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, PW-4, PW-5 and PW-6 could not be shattered by way of cross examination from the side of Defendant- Petitioner.

vs

full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts for disposal of the Rule are that the plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 246 of 1987 in the Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Gaibanda praying for decree for partition to the extent of 2.11 acres of land appertaining to the jote of CS Khatian No. 79, 157 and 311 of Mouza Paschim Komarnai; jote of CS Khatian No. 407 of Mouza Purba Komarnai and to the jote CS Khatian Mouza Purba Komarnai stating inter alia that the schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha'  land to the plaint comprising the jote of CS Khatian No.79, 157 and 311 of Mouza Paschim Komarnai and CS Khatian No. 407 of Purba Komarnai and belonged to Mobarakulla in 4 annas share who used to possess the suit land in ejmali along with the other co-shares and the jote of CA Khatian No.79 and 311 of Mouza Paschim Komarnai belonged to Mobarakulla and Abarakullah in 2 annas share. Abarakullah there after, transferred his entire share from schedule 'Ga' and 'Gha' and to the plaintiffs in favour of Mobarakulla who used to possess the land in ejmali with the other co-sharers of the jote. Mobarakulla in all got an area of 2.93 acres of land from 'Ka' and 'Kha' schedule and an area of 1.22½ acres of land from schedule 'Ga' and 'Gha', in all total 4.15½ acres land. While in possession Mobarakulla died leaving 3 sons Jamat, Jinat and Anayet and a daughter Khuki Mai, accordingly, each son got 1.18½ acres of land. Jamat thereafter, transferred and his entire share by kabala dated 10-3-1949 in favour of Jinat and thus Jinat got in the schedule 'Ka' and 'Ga' land to the extent of 2.37 acres of land. Jinat thereafter, died leaving behind the plaintiffs as his heirs and that plaintiffs sold 0.37 acres of land and also purchased by kabala dated 2-5-1960 an area of 10 decimals of land and in this way the plaintiffs are in ejmali possession of 2.11 acres of land. The Other Co-shares Supjan, Rupjan, Kulupjan and Gendali sold their shares in favour of defendant No.19-22. The plaintiffs got their shares muted in the Government Sharasta and paid rent to the Government. The predecessor of defendant Nos.1-3 namely Anayetulla sold 0.70 acres of land in favour of different persons and the plaintiffs being in possession demanded partition to the co-shares on 15th Baishak, 1394 BS 

 7. Mr Golam Rabbani, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners has placed, the judgments, of both the Courts and also taken me through the plaint, written statement and evidence of the parties and submitted that the Appellate Court has not discussed and consider the evidence as contemplated under Order 41 rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and has committed error of law in passing the impugned Judgment and decree resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of Justice. The learned Advocate submitted further that in a suit for a partition the presumption of RS Khatian is immaterial inasmuch as Khatian cannot give title to the parties but the Courts below failed to consider the registered deed which is of more than 30 years and has not challenged its validity by anybody and on the face of such evidence, the findings and the decisions of the Courts below are not based on proper appreciation of evidence and law and, as such, committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate submitted that the Appellate Court failed to consider that the registered kabala dated 10-3-1949 executed by Jamat in favour Of Jinat has not been set aside by any competent Court of law and the plaintiffs having proved the existence of the document by filling certified copy as contemplated under section 65 of the Evidence Act and calling the volume from the concerned sub-registrar office and should have presumed that the document is a valid document as contemplated under section 114(E) of the Evidence Act and failing to hold that the registered deed dated 10-3-1949 has got presumptive value and in not holding, as such, the courts below committed error of law. The learned Advocate further submitted that the registered deed dated 10-3-1949 has got evidentiary value and the same is binding upon the defendants as they did not challenge the deed in any forum and, as such, both the Courts committed error of law in not giving decree on the basis of the said registered deed of more than 30 years old. The learned Advocate submitted further that the plaintiffs proved the genuineness of the deed dated 10-3-1949 calling for the volume and upon perusal of the Volume which was issued from the sub-registrar office and PW 4 proved the volume the Exhibit 3 and certified copy of the deed was marked as Exhibit 3 (Ka) by the Assistant Judge and thereby, judgments of both the Courts are not based on evidence on record and as such, are liable to be set aside as those Judgments have caused failure of Justice. The learned Advocate further submitted that the defendants could not produce any document to contradict the genuineness of the volume, the Exhibit 3 and 3(ka) and also did not prefer appeal against the judgment of the trial Court but the appellate Court failed to notice such genuine aspect of the case and passing the impugned judgment has committed error of law which is an decision in the occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate has submitted further, when secondary evidence in respect of the registered document produced and when no objection raised by the defendants or the learned Trial Judge rather the learned Assistant Judge marked the certified copy of the deed as Exhibit 3 and in view of such materials on record the Courts should have placed reliance on the evidence of PW 4 along with Exhibit 3(ka), the certified copy of the deed dated 10-3-1949 and should have decreed the suit. 

 9. The learned Advocate referring to the section 90 of the Evidence Act submits that a document of more than 30 years old, if it is produced with Certified copy of a document of more than 30 years as secondary evidence (section 65 of the Evidence Act) before the Court along with the volume from the sub registrar office and proved by the agent of the sub-registrar (PW 4) should have presumed that it is a genuine document but both the Courts below having not attached the presumption to the document of more than 30 years old and passing the impugned judgments committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of Justice. He then refers to a decision in the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) vs Md Reazuddin Pk reported in 5 BLC (AD) 76 where in, their lordships of the Appellate division held, 

 "Section 90—Presumption as to documents thirty years old : Where any document, purporting or proved to be thirty years old, is produced from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper, the Court may presume that the signature and every other part of such document, which purports to be in the handwriting of any particular person, is in that person's handwriting, and, in the case of a document executed or attested, and it was duly executed and attested by the persons by whom it purports to be executed and attested." 

 18. On further perusal of the evidence of the plaintiffs it appears that the Courts below have not discussed the documents of the plaintiffs inasmuch as Khatian exhibit 2 and rent receipts Exhibits 2(Ka) and 2(Kha) and also the oral evidence of PW 2 and PW 3 who deposed in order to prove the possession of the plaintiffs. On examination of the aforesaid Exhibits and oral evidence of PW 2 and PW 3 I am of the view that the plaintiffs could prove their possession covering the land of the document dated 10-3-1949 but the learned Judges have not recorded any findings with reference to those exhibits and oral evidence of PW 2 and PW 3.
