parties:
Mridul Kanti Sarder alias Mridul Sarder and others   ----- Petitioners
Vs
Krishna Charan Sarder and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule are that one Krishna Charan Sarder instituted the Other Suit No. 16 of 1990 on 20-1-1990 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Patiya, Chittagong against Mridul Sarder and 6 others, praying for a decree for declaration of title and confirmation of possession of the suit land, measuring an area of 4 sataks, i-e, 2 gandas of land in RS Plot No. 1377 under the RS Khatian No. 418, in Mouza-Dengapara, together with a decree for declaration of the BS Khatian recorded in respect of the suit property, is void, baseless and wrongly recorded, stating, inter alia, that one Uma Charan Sarder was in the right, title and possession of the suit land and the RS Khatian stood recorded in his name and after his death, Mathura inherited the right, title, possession and interest in the suit land. Mathura died leaving behind his daughter Khemlata and Khemlata with her son, Arun Sarder, inherited the same. Both Khemlata and Arun Sarder sold out the suit property to the plaintiff and handed over its possession. The defehdants have no right, title and possession in the suit land, but they are threatening the plaintiff of dispossession. The suit land is contiguous land to the homestead of the plaintiff and the BS Khatian has wrongly been recorded in the names of the defendants. 

 3. The defendant Nos. 1 to 6 have contested the suit by filing written statements, stating that Uma Charan had his 'Chakran' interest in the suit land and on his death, the suit property was restored to the Zamindar Sita Sundari Dutta and while she was in her khas possession, settled the suit land with Hirendra Lal Sarder, the predecessor of the defendants on 22-8-1956 under a registered Patta and handed over possession thereof and Hirendra Lal Sarder made a cowshed upon the suit land as the same is contiguous to his homestead and upon his death, the defendants have inherited it as his heirs and are in continuous possession in the suit land. The BS Khatian has rightly been recorded in the name of their predecessor and the purchase deed of the plaintiff has not been acted upon nor has he acquired any right, title and possession in the suit land by virtue of that deed, Since the plaintiffs vendor had no right, title, possession and interest in the suit land, the plaintiff too, has not acquired any such interest. The dispute being a long standing dispute, a local Shalish took place on 28-9-1980 between the plaintiff and the predecessor of the defendants and all the Arbitrators made an unanimous award in this respect and, according to the award, the plaintiff had no interest in the suit land. 

 4. After conclusion of the trial, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Patiya, has been pleased to dismiss the suit on his findings that the plaintiff has not disputed the registered Patta of the predecessor of the defendants and nothing has been mentioned about the Patta in the plaint and thus, the plaintiff has admitted the said Patta. The Patta was executed and registered on 22-8-1956 and the plaintiff claimed that it was not acted upon, and thereby also admitted that his vendors had no right, title and interest in the suit land and if, at all, the Patta made after 14-4-1956 was ineffective, in that case, the suit property will be khas land of the Government and, as such, the plaintiffs purchase is also not effective. The PW 1 has admitted in cross-examination that the BS record has rightly been prepared, which is Annexure-C, in the suit and, as such, the possession of the defendants has been proved in the suit land. Though the plaintiff claimed that he is in possession of the suit land from 8-9-1980, but could not mention the plot number of the suit land which is waste land and the PW 2 claimed possession of the plaintiff for 4/5 years, whereas the defendants claimed that they are possessing the same since the time of their predecessor having a cowshed and the Advocate Commissioner was examined in the suit as DW 2, who stated that he saw a cowshed in the suit land during his inspection made more than 7/8 years ago and from the Arbitration Award, Exhibit -F(1) also it appears that the defendants are in possession in the suit land. The plaintiffs with a view to prove his possession exhibited two rent-receipts, vide Exhibit-3-3(a) which are of much later time of the institution of the instant suit i-e, the suit was instituted on 20-1-1990 and the rent paid under these Dakhilas on 28-6-1990 and 10-6-1991 respectively and the defendants exhibited 6(six) rent-receipts vide Exhibit-E-E(5) and Chowkidari receipt, vide Exhibit-D in respect of the suit land showing that the defendants are paying rent right from 19-4-1974 and in view of the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 217 the rent-receipts are evidence of the possession, also may be used as a collateral evidence of title, thereby proving that the defendants are in exclusive possession of the suit land and, for argument's sake, if the Patta is not considered, still the possession of the defendants is for more than 12 years, and thereby creating possessory rights in favour of the defendants. In view of the case reported in 3 DLR 484 that if any person possesses any lane for 12 years is vested with the title of it and the person in possession became an owner' and that the plaintiff without instituting a suit for recovery of possession, cannot maintain his suit in its present form. The possession of the plaintiff in the suit land has not been proved and the BS Khatian has rightly been recorded. 

 5. On the other hand, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Patiya, Chittagong has been pleased to allow the Other Appeal No. 555 of 1991, preferred by the plaintiff against the said judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge in Other Suit No. 16 of 1990 setting aside the said judgment and decree and also to decree the suit declaring the right, title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land holding that at the time of hearing, the plaintiff appellant has produced the PS Khatian on 4-5-1993, which has also been considered in the appeal and the genealogy of Uma Charan given by the plaintiff has been proved and the plaintiff's purchase from Uma Charan's descendants, namely Khemlata and Arun Sarder, by a Saf-Kabala dated 8-9-1980 (Exhibit-2), is also proved, holding further, that since Uma Charan had his Chakran interest during the RS operation and subsequent PS record has also been recorded in the name of Uma Charan showing his Chakran interest, it is thus established, beyond reasonable doubt, that by operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, Uma Charan acquired his tenancy right under section 11 of the Act, since he was in possession of the suit land at the time when the said Act came into force and thus, became a tenant under the Government and the learned Assistant Judge has failed to consider this legal aspect of the case. The learned Appellate Court also held that the learned Advocates appearing for the defendants-respondents had admitted that the Patta in question has never been acted upon, since it was registered after 14-4-1956 and has argued on the right of the defendants by adverse possession, on the ground of possessing the suit land for more than 12 years. But the DW 3 Manindra Sarder has admitted the possession of the vendors of the plaintiff in his evidence admitting also that after the death of Mathura Sarder, Krishna Sarder is possessing the suit land and Krishna Sarder was the original plaintiff of this suit and since, the DW 3 himself admitted the possession of the plaintiff, the adverse possession of the defendants could not be held. 

 6. The defendants-respondents have thereafter preferred this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule with an order of maintaining status quo in respect of the suit property, on the grounds that the learned Appellate Court has committed a grave error of law in deciding the question of possession relying upon the confused statements of the DW 3 without noticing his clear evidence on record and the learned Appellate Court has wrongly construed the section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in view of the fact that Mathura died in 1943 and the Chakran interest was not heritable. The learned Appellate Court has erred in law in not holding that Khemlata and Arun Sarder did not acquire Chakran interest and also by relying upon the PS Khatian which was not filed and proved in accordance with law before the learned trial Court and the learned appellate Court has also committed an error of law in not holding that the plaintiff has failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land. 

 8. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate, appearing with Mr JN Deb and Mr Md Ekramul Hoque, the learned Advocates for the petitioners, by placing his reliance upon the case of Sakina Bibi vs Matra Bibi, reported in 1985 BCR (AD) 37 submitted that since Chakran interest is not heritable, Khemlata or her son Arun cannot be treated as in possession of the disputed land in the capacity of Chakran interest after the death of Uma Charan and that section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act gives protection only to those persons who are in possession of the lands in the capacity of Chakran interest at the time of operation. The learned Advocate thus submitted that the RS record tenant Uma Charan had his interest in the suit land as Chakran and so also in the unproved PS Khatian and since, according to law, the Chakran interest is not heritable, Khemlata and Arun Sarder have not inherited the interest of Uma Charan and, as such, they acquired no right, title interest and possession in the suit land to transfer it to the plaintiff. 

 11. From the RS Khatian No. 418, it appears that Uma Charan, son of Joyman Hori, got tenancy of 4 sataks of land under Chandra Mohan Dutta and Ramoni Mohan Dutta and others as “দখল কার চাকরান বাধ্যকর” and from the PS Khatian, produced before the learned Appellate Court, it also appears that 4 sataks of land was recorded in the name of Uma Charan, son of Joyman Hori, as his Chakran interest. 

 13. From Exhibit-B of the defendants, it appears that the Patta No. 4844 was registered on 22-8-1956 in respect of these 4 sataks of land by Sreemati Sita Sundari Dutta for settlement of land with Sree Khirendra Lal Sarder and the BS Khatian No. 736 (Exhibit-C) stood recorded in the name of Khirendra Lal Sarder in respect of these 4 sataks of land, and Exhibits-D and E series are the rent-receipts, showing rent paid by Khirendra also in the name of Uma Charan from the decade of seventies and the Exhibit-F is the Arbitration Award, where it was held that the vendors of the plaintiff had no possession of the suit land and also that the first party Krishna Kumar Sarder (plaintiff) had no possession in the land of dispute. The plaintiff produced 3 witnesses, including himself (Lalu Sarder, son of Krishna Sarder) and the stated, in gist that after the death of Uma Charan his son Mathura Sarder inherited the property and after the death of Mathura, Khemlata and her son Arungot it and the Amanat Kha stated that the plaintiffs father would possess the suit land and now the plaintiff is possessing it and the defendants have no possession in the suit land. The PW 3 is Khemlata, daughter of Mathura Sarder, stating that she had no brother and she along with her son Arun sold the suit property to the plaintiff and delivered its possession and they were in possession in the suit land. 

 14. DW 1 is Mridul Kanti Sarder who supported their Patta got through their father from Zamindar Sita Sundari also supporting the BS Khatian and the Award asserting their possession in the suit land. DW 2 is Md Ishaque who held the local inspection and proved his report stating that he found a cowshed in the suit land. The DW 3 is Monindra Sarder stating that there is a cowshed in the suit property and plaintiff or his vendors have never possessed the suit land and he saw the suit land in possession of Krishna Sarder after death of Mathura. Khemlata is his daughter and Arun grandson. After Mathura, Khemlata did not possess it. He did not know that Khemlata sold it to Krishna Sarder. It is not a fact that the plaintiff is in possession in the suit land. 

 24. Under the RS Khatian No. 418, Uma, son of Joyman Hori, had the Chakran interest in respect of the suit land. 

 26. In this portion, the vendor stated that at the time of death of Uma Charan, he had no other heir except the vendor No. 2, Khemlata and she was the granddaughter of Uma Charan. It also appears from the statement above, that her father Mathura Charan died some time before her grandfather, Uma Charan. Now if Uma Charan was alive on 16-5-1951, he acquired his right of occupancy in the land, recorded in the RS Khatian, If Uma Charan acquired the tenancy right, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, only after then, the sale deed of Khemlata and her son Arun Sardar may be operative. 

 33. Exhibit-F(1) is the Arbitration Award given by the 13 No. Shu-Chakradandi Union Parishad on 28-9-1980 holding the possession of Khirendra Sardar and finding no possession of Krishan Kumar Sardar. The BS Khatian No. 736 was recorded in the name of Khirendra Lal Sardar evidencing his possession, Khirendra Lal Sardar paid rent in the name of Uma Charan from the year 1974, vide Exhibit-E (series) and Lalu Sardar also paid rent in the name of Uma Charan for the years 1990 and 1991, vide Exhibit-3. 

 35. But there cannot be any adverse possession against the Government, in law. The land in question has been vested in the Government by operation of law on 2-4-1956. The possession could be adverse against Khemlata and her vendee. The Government has admitted possession of the defendants by receiving rent and by publishing the BS Khatian. 

 37. This collateral evidence may be taken with the BS Khatian for consideration. 

 38. In the case of Abdul Hamid vs Abul Hossain Mir, reported in 35 DLR 295 his Lordship held that "Presumption of Khatian loses its weight with the passage of time and that the entries in the subsequent khatian would be more acceptable to a Court than the entries in the earlier Khatian."

lawyer:
Amir Hossain with Farzana Hoque, Advocates ------ For the Appellants
Abdul Kuddus Mia, Advocate ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Mayurer Nessa and others ------ Appellants
vs
Julekha Khatoon and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Respondent Nos. 1-14 as plaintiffs filed the aforesaid suit of partition of the suit property claiming plaintiffs’ No. 1-13 as heirs of one of the recorded tenant Rahmat Ali whose name was recorded in the CS Khatian Ext. 2 as owner of 0.08 annas share of the jote. According to the plaintiffs, plaintiff No. 14 is the purchaser from the plaintiff No. 2. The plaintiffs claimed that other recorded tenant of the suit kharian was Alabuddin, predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 1-19, and defendant Nos. 20-23 are purchasers from the said defendants. Plaintiffs claimed partition On the ground that there was no partition by metes and bounds and taking advantage of wrong entry regarding possession in the CS khatian the defendants had been disturbing their possession. On such allegations plaintiff filed the suit on 27.1.63. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 8 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying material allegations and stating that the suit property originally belonged to their predecessor Alabuddin who took lease of the same from the landlord on tile basis of kabuliyat and patta from the landlord Gouri Pria Debi at an annual jama of Taka 16.00 and as the taluk of Gouripria Debi was purchased by Nabin Chandra Chakraborty said Alabuddin executed a kabuliyat in favour of the purchaser landlord who also executed a paua in his favour on 24th Kartick, 1310 BS Ext. 'A'. Since then Alabuddin was in possession of the entire suit property. Further case of the defendants was that the said Alabuddin had a brother named Sona Guzi who married mother of plaintiffs predecessor Rahmat Ali who came to the house of Sona Gazi and after the death of Sonagazi and his 2nd wife out of compassion Alabuddin allowed Rahmat Ali to possess the Suit plot Nos.160, 224 and 226. Taking advantage of old age and ignorance of Alabuddin the said Rahmat Ali during the CS operation wrongly recorded 0.08 annas share of the suit land in the suit khatian though he had no title in the suit property. Further case of the contesting defendants is that Yusuf Ali and Jinnat Ali, two sons of Alabuddin while in title and possession of the suit land executed a confirmatory kabuliyat in favour of landlord, Nabin Chakraborty on 4th Agrahayan 1331 BS and got a paua on the same date from the said landlord Ext. A(1) and since then they are in possession of the entire suit land except those three suit plots on payment of rents from before CS khatian in the name of Alabuddin and his heirs vide Ext. 'B' series. Their further case is that sons of Rahmat Ali relinquished possession of plot Nos. 224 and 226 in favour of Ishab Ali and Jinnat Ali after taking settlement of some land from them by a kabuliyat dated 3rd Chaitra, 1330 BS Ext. C. Their further case is that Alabuddin and after his death his heirs paid rent of the suit property to the landlord. 

 5. Mr. Amir Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, submitted that both the Courts below failed to hold that the presumption of correctness of the entry in the CS khatian Ext. 2 recording 8 annas share in favour of plaintiffs' predecessor Rahmat Ali was rebutted by the paua Ext. 'A' registered on 16.11.1903 long before the preparation of CS khatian Ext. 2 and the payment of rents alone by Alabuddin. 

 6. It appears that trial Court found that Alabuddin had 8 annas share and Rahmat Ali had 8 annas share in the suit tenancy although the original patta stood in the name of Alabuddin alone and that Rahmat Ali was in possession of about half of the tenancy. On the other hand Court of appeal below found that Alabuddin took lease on his own behalf and on behalf of his nephew Rahmat Ali and the plaintiffs have possession in the suit land. But none, of the Courts below found in which suit plots plaintiffs have exclusive or joint possession. It is not denied that only plot Nos. 160, 224 and 226 having an area of 50 acres were recorded in exclusive possession of plaintiffs' predecessor Rahmat Ali in the CS khatian Ext. 2 and other 10 plots except homestead plot No. 224 were recorded in exclusive possession of defendants predeceassor Alabuddin in the said khatian. Though the plaintiffs stated in para 7 of the plaint that Alabuddin and Rahmat Ali possessed the suit land in equal share and entry regarding exclusive possession in the CS khatian was wrong they did not state in which other plots they had possession. Plaintiffs adduced evidence to the effect that before compromise they possessed 7/8 plots and after compromise they possess 5 plots but none of the PWs could say in which plots plaintiffs possessed before compromise. Trial Court without considering the presumption of entry regarding possession in the CS khatian, failure of the PWs to state the plot numbers in which plaintiffs had possession and reliability of the PWs erroneously opined that plaintiffs previously possessed 7/8 plots. If the entry in the CS khatian Ext. 2 regarding share of plaintiffs' predecessor Rahmat Ali and defendants' predecessor Alabuddin is found to be correct the entry regarding exclusive possession of the said two persons cannot be found to be incorrect. As a matter of fact none of the Courts below specifically found the said entry regarding exclusive possession in the said CS khatian to be wrong or incorrect. I do not find any illegality in the finding of the Courts below regarding share of the parties in the suit property as recorded in the CS khatian inasmuch as both the Courts below considered the patta Ext. A and rent receipts Ext. B series in the name of Alabuddin along with other evidence on record for arriving at the said finding. But I fail to agree with the finding of the Courts below regarding possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land as the same suffers from non-consideration of material evidence on record and presumption arising from entry in the CS Khatian. 

 7. CS khatian Ext. 2 clearly shows that except homestead plot No. 234 all other plots were recorded in exclusive possession of the said Alabuddin and Rahmat Ali respectively. From the same it is clear that long before the CS operation they possessed the suit plots except plot No. 234 separately and exclusively and homestead plot No. 234 was only in their ejmali possession. From their above conduct it can easily be inferred that there was amicable partition between them in respect of those plots recorded in their respective exclusive possession. When CS khatian records a jote in the name of several persons having distinct share therein but the lands are recorded in exclusive possession of the respective co-sharers then there remains nothing to partition the lands unless the entry regarding exclusive possession is found to be wrong and incorrect. Had the entry regarding exclusive possession in the CS khatian been wrong Rahmat Ali or his heirs would not have remained silent for about fifty years from the date of final publication of the CS khatian. Such exclusive possession of a party in the land for a long period should not be easily disturbed on the flimsy allegation of a co-sharer in the jote unless he can prove by evidence that presumption of correctness of such entry is erroneous.

Vs.
Mongla Barman and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 filed the suit for permanent injunction for restraining the defendants from entering into CS Plots Nos. 784 and 802 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 125 of Mouza Galtoir, PS Chirirbandar, District Dinajpur. His case is that the suit land originally belonged to Dinomoni Barmani who sold the land to her son-in-law, Janaki Nath Barman, by a kabala dated 18.1.1938. (Ext. 1 (a). The plaintiff purchased that land by a kabala dated 1.4.1957 (Ext.1) and got his name mutated and obtained rent receipts (Exts 2(a) to 2(h)). On 15.5.1969 the defendants in collusion with each other attempted to dispossess the plaintiff. 

 3. The defendant-appellant's case is that the suit land belonged to Dinomoni Barmani and Lalit Chandra Barman in equal shares and their names were correctly recorded in the CS Khatian No. 125 (Ext. B); that by an exchange Lalit Chandra Barman got Plot No. 801 of CS Khatian No. 133 of mouza Galtoir (Ext. B(1) from defendant No. 3 Buli Barmani and transferred to her the disputed Plot No. 784 and that the fact of exchange was noted in the CS Khatian. Defendant No. 3 sold Plot No. 784 by a kabala dated 2.12.1968 (Ext. A) to defendant No. 4 who was in possession of that land through his bargadar. 

 5. After finding that Dinomoni inherited the land of CS Khatian No. 125 from her husband, and that her son-in-law Janaki looked after her properties and that there was no basis for the noting of the alleged exchange in the CS Khatian the trial Court held that Janaki got his son Lalit's name included in the CS Khatian fraudulently; that Dinomoni had title to all the lands including plot No. 784 and that the presumption of correctness of the record of right was rebutted. The trial Court further found that in the kabala dated 18.1.1938 executed by Dinomoni in favour of Janaki, there was a reference to two other, plots besides the two suit plots; that Janaki asserted his title and possession in the suit lands and executed Ext. 1 the kabala dated 1.4.1957 in favour of the plaintiff who after purchase got his name mutated and got rent receipts. The trial Court also accepted the evidence of PW 2 and 3 in support of the plaintiffs case and rejected the evidence of the defendants' witnesses. 

 8. In a simple suit for permanent injunction with regard to a disputed landed property the relief is available to a person who is in possession. The Court may enquire incidentally into the respective claims of the parties to the suit for determining whether the plaintiff has got a prima facie case i.e. whether he is in possession of the disputed property and entitled to the specific relief of permanent injunction. If the dispute involves complicated questions of title the plaintiff must establish his title by filing a regular suit for declaration of title. A simple suit for permanent injunction should not be allowed to be used as a testing device for ascertainment of title. In this case the plaintiff assails the presumption of the CS Khatian, a kind of exercise the Court in a simple suit for permanent injunction should ordinarily avoid. 

 9. By mere assertion of the plaintiff that the disputed holding originally belonged to Dinomoni the subsequent fact of exchange between Dinomoni's daughter Buli Barmani and her grandson Lalit Chandra, reflected in the CS Khatian, cannot be rebutted in view of the clear statement of the plaintiffs own witness, PW 3, that Dinomoni, Lalit and Janaki got the record prepared. After considering the evidence of PW 3 and other wises of boththe parties, and the fact that the plaintiff did not pursue his case under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the appellate Court held that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession in plot No. 784. The High Court Division reversed this finding of fact of the last court of fact without considering the oral evidence in the case. It did not consider that there was nothing on record to show that notice with regard to the mutation proceeding was served on Lalit Chandra. The plaintiff got the rent receipts on the basis of that mutation. The High Court Division wrongly held that the appellate Court ought to have presumed that the mutation proceeding was duly done as an official act, without considering that the proceeding was initiated at the instance of a private party and if it was concluded without serving notice on necessary parties it would not have any legal effect.

full_judgment:
2. Facts relevant are that the predecessor-in-interest of present respondent nos. 1(a)- 1(h) and respondent nos. 2 and 3 as plain-tiffs instituted Partition Suit No.57 of 1994 in thy Court of learned Subordinate Judge, 2na Court Bogra, impleading the petitioners herein alongwith the predecessor of present respondent nos.4(a)-4(f) and respondent nos.5-85 as defendants claiming saham of 1.48 1/6 acres of land out of the suit land measuring 13.35 acres, contending interalia, that the suit jote comprising 13.35 acres of land appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.10 of Mouza Khamarkandi under Police Station-Bogra, District-Bogra, originally belonged to Azim Uddin Mollah, Abdul Mollah and Sabu Mollah in equal share; During ejmali possession said Azim Uddin Mollah and Abdul Mollah transferred their shares to the extent of two third measuring 11 bighas and 17 kathas infavour of Asmat Ullah and Jasmat Ullah both sons of C.S. recorded tenant Azim Uddin Mollah by registered deed dated 09.06.1917 on condition that they would pay vendor's debt . of Tk.450/- to the ex-landlord; Since the sale was a conditional one, the vendors retained possession of the land; The said sale deed was never acted upon for non-payment of the debt to the ex-landlord in compliance with the condition stipulated in the deed; Azim Uddin Mollah died leaving three sons namely Asmat, Jasmat and Najem alongwith two daughters solebi and Sawabi; Sabu Mollah died leaving three sons namely Korban, Muslim and Moyez; Jasmat died leaving full brother Asmat; Said Abdul Mollah died leaving wife Amiron and three sons namely Kashem, defendant no.1 Chand, defendant no.2 Farid and 3 daughters namely Shukimon, defendant no.3 Rupban and Janina; Amiron died leaving two sons Ayetullah and defendant no.2 Farid and daughter defendant no.3 Rupban; Asmat Ullah died leaving two sons namely olam and Nasir and two daughters Toiron and Gendi; Najem died leaving a son plaintiff no.1 Jashim and daughter Lalbibi; Sawabi died leaving a son defendant no,6 Kuranu; Nasir died leaving a son plaintiff no.2 Khairuzzaman Mollah and daughter plaintiff no.3 Shahera; Golan died leaving wife defendant no,7 Kochimon and two daughters namely Jahanara, Jobeda and two sisters Gendi and Toiron; Salebi died leaving two sons Md. Nabir Uddin and Kalim Uddin, defendant nos.10 and 11 respectively; Korban died leaving three sons namely Buhl, Riaz and Kawser; Said Riaz died leaving four sons namely Md. Biraz Uddin, Md. Azizer Rahman, Md. Hafizar Rahman and Md. Abdur Rahman, defen-dant nos.13-16 respectively; Kawser died leaving only daughter defendant no.17 Mosammat Asma and brother Bulu; Moyez died leaving wife Fuljan, a son defendant no. 18 Md. Mojam Uddin and two daughters Most. Kallaton Nesa and Most. Potol Bibi; Fuljan died leaving husband defendant no.10 Md. Nabir Uddin, a son Mojam Uddin and three daughters Kallaton, Potol and Golapi, defendant nos.19-21 respectively; Moslem died leaving a son Samsul and three daughters Borki Bibi, Bull and Momijan, defendant nos. 22-25 respectively; Kashem died leaving a son Futu Mollah, defendant no.26 and three daughters Sonaban Bibi, Fatema Bibi and Rahima Bibi, defendant nos.27-29 respectively; Shukimon died leaving four sons namely Kazem, Sukra, Azo and Kachua alongwith one daughter Atopjan; Said Kazem died leaving defen-dant no.30 Kodban and Atopjan died leaving a daughter defendant no.31 Sharifon and three brothers Sukra, Azo and Kachua; Said Sukra died leaving wife defendant no.32 Hamidon and three sons namely Md. All Fakir, Md. Hachen Fakir and Md. Hamid Fakir alongwith daughter Shurjoban, defendant nos.33-36 respectively; Azo died leaving a son Yousuf Ali and two daughters Momena and Ayjon, defendant nos.37-39 respectively; Jarina died leaving two sons Rabia and Bacha; Said Bacha died leaving wife defendant no. 40 Achiron and brother Rabia; Said Rabia died leaving wife defendant no.41 Maim n, and five sons namely Abul Hossain, Gaffer, Hobibar, Sekander and Nur Hossain and three daughters Asarban, Nurbanu and Asma Khatun, defendant nos.42-49. respectively. Toiron died leaving five sons namely Asgar, Ahab, Dhalu, Bulu and Tutu and two daughters' Jarina and .lamina, defendant nos.50-56 respectively; Gendi died leaving a son defendant no.57 Dilbor and a daughter defendant no.58 Sahera; Kachu died leaving wife Kanchi and two sons Sobhan, Montu alongwith daughter Mariam, defendant nos.59-62 respectively; Defendant nos.1-62 are the co-sharers by inheritance to the suit jote and defendant nos.63-66 are the co-sharers by purchase to the suit jote; The plaintiffs are in ejmali possession; The plaintiffs demanded partition of the suit land from defendant no.26 on 15.06.1992 but he denied; Hence, the suit. 

 5. The case of the defendant nos. 67 and 68 are that the suit jote appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.10 originally belonged to Abdul Azim Mollah, Abdul Mollah and Sabu Mollah; During ejmali possession Azim Mollah and Abdul Mollah transferred their share to the extent of 11 bighas and 17 kathas in the year 1917 to Asmat and Jasmat but the C.S. record was not prepared accordingly; Azim Mollah, Abdul Mollah, Sabu. Mollah, Asmat and Jasmat transferred 22 bighas and 6.75 kathas of land to Shushila Shundari Gbosh, predecessor of the defendants, vide registered deed no.11.2 dated 05.01.1923 prior to the C.S. operation but C.S. record was prepared and published wrongly in the name of Azim Mollah, Abdul Mollah and Sabo Mollah; Though C.S. record was published wrongly but Shushila Sundari Ghosh possessed the purchased land through borgadars; Abdul Pramanik transferred 1.17 acres of land to Rajani Kanta Ghosh, husband of Shushila Sundari vide registered kabala dated 18.12.1928; Both Shushila Sundari and Rajanii. Kanta Ghush gave barga of the suit land infavour of Abdul Pramanik for 7 years by barga deed dated 02.04.1929; Shushila settled .55 acre of land to different persons and the rest to the extent of 10.59 acres was recoraed in the M.R.R. Khatain in her name Rajani Kanta died prior to publication of M.R.R. Khatian; Shushila Sundari died leaving two daughters Radharani and Raj lakshmi, defendant nos.67 and 68 respectively; During the war of liberation Shushila Sundari and her successors engaged Chand Miah son of Abdul Ariz as bargadar in respect of their share and left for India; On their return after liberation when they demanded usufructs from Chand Miah, he denied to give the same and then they filed Title Suit No. 2 of 1974 against Chand Miah which was decreed on compromise in their favour; Rajlakshmi transferred .24 acre of land by registered deed dated 25.06.1989 infavour of defendant no.22 son of defendant no.2; Rajlakshmi also transferred some lands to different persons; After transfer, the defendants retained possession to the extent of 7.43 acres of land; The defendants filed Case No.3713192 under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against defendant no.26 and others which was disposed of in their favour on compromise; Plaintiffs are not entitled to get any saham/relief in the suit and the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 11. Mr. Sk. Md. Morshed, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the High Court Division committed an error by not considering that Azim, Abdul, Sabu alongwith Asmat Ullah and Jasmat Ullah executed registered deed dated 05.01.1923 infavour of Shushila Sundari Ghosh, mother of the defendant-appellants, which shows that Asmat Ullah and Jasmat Ullah, purchaser of the land vide registered deed dated 09.06.1917, had been the owner and possessor of the land purchased and which also proves that the registered deed dated 09.06.1917 was duly executed. He also submits that the plaintiffs failed to prove their claim that the debt due to ex-landlord to the extent of Tk.450/- was not paid; He again submits that the document being ancient one clearly establish right, title, interest and possession of the defendant-appellants and their predecessor. He further submits that the defendant-appellants by adducing evidence proved that the respondent-plaintiff's predecessors cultivated the land as bargadar of Shushila Sundari and that the M.R.R. Khatian was prepared duly in the name of defendants' predecessor i.e. Shushila as such the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set-aside. He also submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the defendant-appellants relayed the land through Advocate Commissioner which is apparent from Advocate Commissioner's report as such the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set-aside. He lastly submits that the High Court Division wrongly shifted the onus of proof of payment of debt to the ex-landlord by the vendees of kabala dated 09.06.1917 on the defendant-appellants though in view of the kabala dated 05.01.1923 the onus was squarely falls upon the respondent-plaintiffs to prove the non-payment of the dues of ex-landlord by the vendees and as such the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set-aside. 

 12. On the other hand Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent nos.1(a)- 1(h), 2-3 submits that the deed dated 09.06.1917 executed by Md. Azim Mollah and Md. Abdul Mollah infavour of Asmat Ullah and Jasmat Ullah was a conditional sale and the condition not being complied with, it was not acted upon and accordingly C.S. Khalian was prepared in the name of original owners but the trial court erroneously shifted the onus upon the plaintiffs as such the impugned judgment and decree shall sustain. He also submits that C.S. Khatian has presumption of its correctness which is suit rebatable by proper evidence but no evidence was adduced by the contesting defendants to discharge their onus which lawfully lies on them and the trial court failed to appreciate the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs and thus erroneously holding title and possession of the defendants. He again submits that Khatian has no presumptive value as such the impugned judgment and decree shall sustain and the appeal is liable to be dismissed. He lastly submits that the plaintiffs categorically stated in the plaint that: 

 "Considering the evidence adduced by the defendant-respondents it does not appear that the consideration money for the deed dated 09.06.1917 i.e. exhibit 'Ica' was paid to the ex-landlord. It appears that trial court courageously fixed the onus of such proof on the plaintiff-appellants. The rebuttal onus always lies with the other side who wants to repudiates the presumption as the C.S. record of rights hold. 

 22. As per provisions of Section 90 of the Evidence Act there is a presumption infavour of a thirty years old original copy of a registered deed which is submitted in the court from proper custody. For proper appreciation Section 90 of the Evidence Act is reproduced below: 

 "90. Presumption as to documents thirty years old: Where any document, purporting or proved to be thirty years old, is produced from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper, the Court may presume that the signature and every other part of such document, which purports to be in the handwriting of any particular person, is in that person's handwriting, and, in the case of a document executed or attested, that it was duly executed and attested by the persons by whom it purports to be executed and attested. 

 23. From the provisions of above mentioned Section of the Evidence Act it appears that the exhibited copy of thirty years old registered document dated 05.01.1923 is being an original copy and produced before the court from proper custody as such the presumption infavour of deed no.112 dated 05.01.1923 is that the said deed is a genuine one. In such a situation the onus of proof of the allegation of the plaintiffs regarding lending money by taking signature in blank stamp and thereafter used the same to create forged document by the predecessor of the defendant nos.67 and 68 lies upon the plaintiffs. 

 30. From the aforementioned discussions, we are of the view that since the suit land was purchased by Shushila Sundari before C.S. operation, the C.S. record should have been prepared in her name. Again, on perusal of exhibit-'neo' i.e. M.R.R. khatian no.15 it appears that said khaitian was prepared in the name of Shushila Sundari in continuation of kabala dated 09.06.1917 and 05.01.1923 which are marked as exhibit-la' and ‘kha' respectively, as such said M.R.R khatian was prepared correctly. From the contents of kabala dated 18.06.1080 (exhibit-'pa') and another kabala also dated 18.06.1980 (exhibit-' fa' it appears that defendant no.69 purchased portion of the suit land from the heirs of Shushila Sundari. Thus Trial Court justly arrived at a finding that plaintiffs have failed to prove their title in the suit land.
