Hriday Ranjan Dey and another ------ Appellants
Vs.
Niranjan Dey and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The appellants as the plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession or in the alternative for recovery of possession if found to be out of possession stating, inter alia, that the suit land comprising of Schedules 1 and 2 recorded in CS Khatian No. 2 and 2A originally belonged to one Baisnab Chandra Dey who was succeeded by son Abhoy Charan Dey. After the death of Abhoy Charan Dey his son Ananda inherited the same. But Ananda being the minor boy possessed the same through his maternal uncle one Jogesh Chandra Dey. Thereafter for legal necessity and maintenance of minor Ananda his uncle transferred the land to the predecessor of the plaintiffs by a kabala Exhibit 1 dated 7-12-1926. Since then the plaintiffs were in exclusive possession of the suit land. The plaintiffs also purchased some land situated to the western side of Schedule 1 property from the principal defendants and predecessors of other defendants by a registered kabala on 20-11-1930. The proforma defendant No. 8 Ananda after attaining majority affirmed the aforesaid sale of the suit land. During the PS operation Ram Kumar, the maternal uncle of Abhoy Charan Dey fraudulently got schedule 2 land recorded in his name. Since the defendants threatened to dispossess, the plaintiff instituted the suit. 

 5. On perusal of the judgment of the trial Court it appears that the trial Court found that CS Khatians Exhibits 2 and 2(a) stand in the name of Baishnab Charan Dey original raiyat in respect of the suit land on the basis of an oral Bandabasti and that the defendant could not prove that the suit land belonged to Jituram. The defendant though sought to allege an unregistered Muktinama (Annexure-C) executed by Ananda but the trial Court on evidence found that all person concerned wrote in the Muktinama with the same pen and ink whereas the body of the same shows otherwise and would lead a prudent person to believe that it is a fabricated document. The trial Court also believed that during the minority of Ananda the burden of recording the suit land was with Jituram who had fraudulently entered his name as there was nothing on record to show that the suit land originally belonged to Jituram. The trial Court also found that Ram Kumar, maternal uncle of Abhoy Charan fraudulently got Schedule 2 recorded in his name. 

 7. The Court of appeal below found that the schedule 1 land recorded in CS (Khasra) Khatian No. 267 (Exhibit 2A) and the schedule 2 land recorded in CS (Khasra) Khatian No. 260 in the name of Baisnab in raiyat right was taken lease from one Ram Krishna Chowdhury and others and that the defendants could not acquire any title or possession of the suit land in schedule 2 recorded in the name of Ram Krishna in RS Khatian No. 239 Exhibit D 1 and in the name of Nikunja and others in PS Khatian No. 185 Exhibit E(1) as no basis could be shown for such recording. In view of the plaintiff's case that during RS Khatian Ram Kumar, maternal uncle of Abhoy Charan, fraudulently got schedule 2 land recorded in his name, the Court of appeal below on consideration of evidence on record arrived at a finding of fact that "RS Khatian 239 in the name of Ram Kumar Exhibit D(1) and RS Khatian 185 Exhibit D and the PS Khatian Exhibit E(1) in the name of Ram Kumar and Nikunja and others are fabricated documents and cannot be accepted as genuine as they had no basis to be so recorded." Similarly, "PS Khatian 23 Exhibit E(2) in the name of Niranjan, Nikunja and others has no basis at all as admittedly the RS Khatian 17 Exhibit 3 was prepared in the name of Ananda under the supervision of Ram Kumar and there is no basis for the preparation of PS Khatian 23 Exhibit E(2) in the name of Nikunja and others in respect of schedule 1 land." The Court of appeal below concurred with the trial Court as regards Exhibit C Muktinama which could not confer the defendant with any title in respect of the suit property. The Court of appeal below also did not find the suit land originally possessed by Baisnab was succeeded by his son Abhoy Charan and Anancla and thus Jituram or his successive heirs have any interest nor had possession in the suit land. Apart from PWs supporting the possession of the plaintiffs DW 1 Niranjan himself admitted the possession of the plaintiffs. 

 9. Mr Abdus Salam Khan, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, has assailed the impugned judgment submitting that the High Court was incompetent to disturb the finding of fact arrived at by the final Court of fact on consideration of evidence on record inasmuch as it erred in law in disturbing the finding as to adverse possession arrived at on the basis of the evidence and that disturbing the finding of fact arrived at by the Courts below that the Baisnab admitted that the original owner was in possession and the possession of the suit land was correctly recorded in his name in CS Khatian and that the plaintiffs also acquired right by adverse possession on the basis of the purchase from Jogendra maternal uncle of Ananda and that the Courts below on consideration of evidence on record found that the record of schedule 2 land in RS in the name of Ram Kumar and subsequent PS Khatian has no basis and accordingly, erred in law in disturbing the concurrent finding of fact based on evidence on record arrived at by the Courts below. 

 10. Mr Sharifuddin Chaklader, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the respondents, submitted that the said schedule 2 having been recorded in the name of Ram Kumar in the RS Khatian who is son of Jitu Ram, the owner of the suit land but part of the land recorded in the name of domesticated son-in-law did not acquire any right, title and possession. The learned Advocate-on-Record further submitted that in the absence of any issue as to adverse possession the Court of appeal below erred in law in holding that the plaintiffs have acquired title on the basis of adverse possession. 

 11. Admittedly the land in suit of the schedules were recorded in the name of Baisnab in CS (Khasra) Khatian No. 267 (Exhibit 2A) and CS . (Khasra) Khatian No. 260. The plaintiffs have led evidence to show that the, suit land so recorded belonged to Baisnab Chandra Dey who has acquired raiyat right taking lease from the landlord Ram Krishna Chowdhury and others and the tenancy in (Nal land) Exhibit 2 has been taken lease by Baisnab from Khas Mahal, Patiya at a rental of Rs 1/4 and the Empress of India the rent free tenancy in schedule recorded in Exhibit 2(a) (Bhiti land) in raiyati right was taken lease of by Baisnab from one Ram Krishna Charan and others. The presumption of the CS Khatian under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is that every entry in a record of rights finally published shall be the evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. Reference may be made in this regard to the case of Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Kari and others. 30 DLR (SC) 81. 

 12. The respondents claimed that settlement Khatians namely, RS and PS Khatians have been made in the name of Ramkumar and in the name of his heirs on succession. The plaintiffs had no interest in the suit land far less possession therein referring to RS Khatian No. 239 Exhibit D(I), RS Khatian Exhibit D in the name of Nikunja and others and RS Khatian 185 Exhibit E(I) in the name of Nikunja and others but the defendants could not produce any basis of the said recording so as to nullify the entries in CS Khatian and in the absence. of any evidence on record to show that either Ramkumar or Nikunja became the owner of the property recorded in CS Khatian Exhibit 2 or there was any settlement by the landlords in the name of Nikunja or Ramkumar. The learned District Judge being the final court of fact on consideration of the evidence on record concurrently arrived at the finding of fact that RS Khatian 239 in name of Ramkumar, Exhibit D(I) and RS Khatian 185 Exhibit D and the PS Khatian Exhibit E (I) in the name of Ramkumar and Nikunja and others are fabricated documents and cannot be accepted as they had no basis to be so recorded. Similarly, RS Khatian No. 17 Exhibit 3 in the name of Ananda in respect of schedule 1 land and corresponding PS Khatian 23 Exhibit E (2) in the name of Nikunja and others had no basis at all as admittedly RS Khatian 17 Exhibit 3 was prepared in the name of Ananga under the supervision of Ram Kumar without any basis. 

 13. The trial Court found that the Muktinama Exhibit C was a fabricated and forged document prepared for the purpose of the suit and the court of appeal below observed that the defendants gave a go-bye to Exhibit C to prove his case. Thus, there is no basis for PS Khatian Exhibit E2. Exhibit 1 is the kabala by Jogendra, maternal uncle of Ananga which was ratified by Ananga, attaining majority as he did never claim the property back from the plaintiffs.

Akhtar Hossain Shariff And Others ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Munshi Akkas Hossain & Ors ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
4. The suit was contested by defendants 1, 2, 10, 12 and 14 by filing a joint written statement. They denied all the allegations made in the plaint and their case, inter alia, was that the Ka schedule lands were the khas lands of the landlords; that the interests of the original owners in respect of other Schedule lands were auction sold in execution of certificate cases for arrears of rent and the landlords auction purchased the same and after possessing the lands for some years, leased out the lands to the defendants, who are in possession of the same since their lease, that the plaintiff obtained Kabala without any consideration, from the heirs of the original tenants taking advantage of the wrong entry in the R.S. Khatians and the plaintiff acquired no title by virtue of the Kabala which was for no consideration. 

 6. The learned Subordinate Judge on retrial dismissed the suit of the plaintiffs and held that though the R.S. Khatians recorded the names of the plaintiffs and their predecessors the presumption arising out of the record of rights had been rebutted by the defendants by adducing evidence. He found the dakhilas filed by the plaintiffs to have been manufactured after the criminal proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C. He also found that the suit lands were auction purchased by the landlords and that they entered into khas possession of the same after taking delivery of possession and being in possession they settled the schedule lands in favour of the defendants. He found that the Kabuliyats executed by the defendants were acted upon and that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the suit lands. 

 7. On appeal by the plaintiffs, the teamed Additional District Judge, Faridpur, reversed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and decreed the suit. The learned Additional District Judge held that vendors of the plaintiff Mujibur Rahman, were the original tenants in respect of the disputed lands; that the landlords could not go into possession of the lands in question by evicting the tenants pursuant to their purchase in certificate proceeding, that the presumption arising out of the record of rights had not been rebutted; that the rent receipts filed by the defendants did not contain the particulars of the lands to indicate that these referred to the suit lands. He also held that the plaintiffs had all along been in possession of the lands and the plaintiffs had been able to prove their title to the lands detailed in the schedule to the plaint. 

 12. Dr. Kamal Hossain, the learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants argued that the lower appellate Court having found that plaintiffs were out of possession before the institution of the suit, the onus as to possession required under Article 142 of the Limitation Act had not been discharged by the plaintiffs. He further argued that the plaintiffs not being in possession of the suit lands at the time of institution of the suit, the presumption of R.S. Record is deemed to have been rebutted by the defendants and the onus shifted upon the plaintiffs to prove that they were continuously in possession for 12 years before dispossession. The learned Counsel submitted that the judgments of Criminal Court in 145 Cr.P.C. proceeding Est. J(2) and in the theft case Ext. J(3) had established defendants possession in the suit land before the institution of the civil suit. 

 14. The learned Counsel further argued that the lower appellate Court had found on a consideration of evidence that the plaintiffs had been all along in possession of the disputed lands and the landlords could not evict them and this being a question of fact, the learned Judge of the High Court Division did not rightly interfere with the findings of the lower appellate Court He further submitted that while remanding the case to the trial Court the High Court Division directed that the defend-ants would produce and prove the landlords papers with regard to their settlement but the defendants had failed to do so. Mr. Jane Alam further argued that the Courts below had come to the finding on consideration of evidence on record that the presumption of correctness of the records of right had not been rebutted. He submitted that judgments in criminal cases are not admissible in civil proceeding and its findings are not binding on the civil court. 

 15. This Court granted leave to consider whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in dismissing the second appeal without noticing the apparent inconsistency between the finding on possession of the plaintiffs and the decree for eviction of the defendants from the suit lands, due to obvious misreading of evidence oral and documentary and total omission on the part of the lower appellate Court in reversing the judgment of the trial Court, to consider as to whether presumption of correct recording of the R.S. Khatians (Ext. 4 series) was duly rebutted as found by the trial Court. 

 19. It is the positive findings of the lower appellate Court, which findings have been affirmed by the High Court Division, that the plaintiffs have all along been in possession of the schedule lands and that the presumption of the R.S. record could not be rebutted by the defendants.

Joynal Abedin (Md) and others ----- Petitioner
vs
Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Jamalpur ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
3.1. The suit property measuring 48 decimals of land appertaining to CS Khatin No. 1539 was originally recorded in the names of Shashi Mohan and his four (04) brothers in equal shares. The same land was recorded in SA Khatian Nos. 1828 and 1948 comprising of 34 decimals and 14 decimals respectively in the lone name of Dhirendra Mohan Dey, the son of Sree Sasi Mohan Dey. Thereafter, recent B.R.S Khatian No. 5023 was finally published incorporating the said suit land in the name of Abdul Aziz, the predecessor of writ petitioner Nos. 2-8 and Md. Zoynal Abedin, petitioner No. 01. Regarding the suit land, relevant government authority instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1974 for correction of BRS Khatian No. 5023 and Abdul Aziz and Zoynal Abedin instituted Other Classes Suit No. 136 of 1976 for declaration of title to the said land. Both suits were disposed of analogously by the then Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh vide judgment dated 31-5-1977 decreeing the Other Classes Suit in part declaring plaintiffs' title to 1 anna 12 gondas only of the suit land and the rest to be in the category of enemy property and thereupon, ordering to correct the BRS Khatian No. 5023 accordingly in the name of relevant government authority. The decree dated 31-5-1977 was challenged by the plaintiffs before the High Court Division in Appeal No. 74 of 1977 which due to establishment of Arpito Sampotti Prottarpon Tribunal under the Arpito Sampotti Prottarpon Ain, 2001 got abated in view of section 13 of the Ain. Be it noted, the entire quantum of suit land has been enlisted as vested property in Schedule-Ka vide gazette notification published on 9-4-2012. 

 4.1. There was no reason to enlist the suit land as vested property as the petitioners have been althrough in peaceful possession thereof since 1975. The entire quantum of the suit land belonged to Dhirendra Mohan Dey by means of amicable partition amongst the co-sharers and, consequently, the Khatian No. 1948 and 1828 were published in his sole name. Dhirendra Mohan Dey transferred vide two registered sale deeds dated 1-10-1975 bearing No. 25175 and dated 5-11-1975 bearing No. 28129 incorporating 34 decimals and 14 decimals respectively in favour of the predecessors of these petitioners. Post-transfer necessary legal actions including mutation and payment of up to date land tax, holding tax etc. have been duly completed; even BRS Khatian No. 5023 also has been correctly prepared and published in the names of the recipients of the sale deeds. Those deeds and updated Khatian are still in force in petitioners' favour. They are the real owners or 'malik' of the land in question and the government authority never had possession in and control over the land by virtue of any title vested in it. Resorting to tricky device some colourable lease documents have been created and a sham lease has been shown to have been granted in favour of one Laxmi Rani, who, in fact, had been the tenant under Dhirendra Mohan Dey. The suit land during recent revisional survey was recorded in khas Khatian No. 01 which upon being challenged by the petitioners under Rule 30 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 was ordered to be released from khash Khatian and to open separate khatians also in their names. The tribunal or the appellate tribunal without appreciation of evidence adduced, whether documentary or testimonial, in its appropriate perspective, dismissed the Arpito Sampotti Prottarpon Case and the appeal upon misconception of law. Hence, both the judgments and the decrees passed by both the tribunal and appellate tribunal as mentioned hereinabove are nullity and are liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 

 6.1. First of all, petitioner's learned counsel Mr. Md. Bodruddoza, referring to an undisposed of local inspection application by the tribunal, submits that the same was brought to substantiate the existence of petitioners' having buildings on the suit land but neither of the tribunals below, trial or appellate, ever addressed the said application or the aspect of petitioners' possession over the suit land, rather both the tribunals disbelieved the factum of possession despite stronger basis thereof remaining present. The learned counsel further submits that the positive evidence of possession, both oral and documentary, .appearing in the testimonies of PW 1 and PW 2 was not appropriately analyzed in the judgments in its correct approach. The learned counsel emphasizes that the tribunal deliberately skipped DWI 's failure to substantiate government's case on evidence. He also underscores that unnecessarily emphasizing more on the CS Khatian while SA Khatian was finally published in 1962 in petitioners' predecessors favour was a futile and an uncalled for exercise. Since under the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance, 1965, government was only vested with the power of controlling the abandoned property, no title or ownership was created in favour of the government in respect of the vested and non-resident property. The learned counsel underscores that since the suit land has finally been published in BRS Khatian in the names of the petitioners, its inclusion in the vested property in 'Ka' scheduled list is a blatant illegality and a manifest indicia of executive high-handedness. Be it mentioned that the Government also lost in the proceedings under Rule 30 and 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 and the title deeds dated 1-10-1975 and 5-11-1975 cited by petitioners in the avbove proceedings were relied on upon by the survey authority. The learned counsel reiterates that petitioners' title document, being duly registered kabalas unless cancelled by competent Court and, a variety of legal documents of possession including finally published khatian and payment of land tax and holding tax etc. were adequate inter-woven evidence to pass an order of releasing the suit land from the impugned vested property list. But the tribunal and the appellate tribunal upon misconception of facts and of law concurrently arrived at a fallacious decisions which are liable to be set-aside. Learned counsel further submits that a construction plan has already been approved by proper authority at the instance of this petitioners upon a certain quantum of suit land. The learned counsel submits that Dhirendra Mohon Dey died in Bangladesh, and since then the petitioners have been in peaceful possession of the suit land by mutating their names and on payment of up to date rent to the government. It is stated that during enjoyment of peaceful possession of the predecessor of the petitioners, Abdul Aziz transferred certain quantum of land to petitioner No. 4 by way of registered sale deed bearing No 12363 of 1992 and thereafter, petitioner No. 04 by mutating his name has been paying rent to government regularly and enjoying its peaceful and uninterrupted possession therein. Learned counsel further submits that after the death of Abdul Aziz (predecessor of the petitioners), petitioner No. 08 inherited some quantum of land from the suit land as per his share and after having inherited the same he also has been enjoying peaceful possession and ownership by mutating his name and paying rent regularly. In view of the above facts and features of the circumstances, the learned counsel, however, urges the Rule to make absolute. 

 6.2. Per contra, Mr. Md. Mohaddes-ul-Islam, learned Deputy Attorney-General on being assisted by Mr. Ashique Rubaiat, learned Assistant Attorney-General, frankly submits on behalf of respondent No. 01 that the SA Khatian in the lone name of Dhirendra Mohon Dey to the extent of whole of suit land and the subsequent BRS Khatian in the names of the petitioners have been wrongly prepared and published. The alleged deeds of sale dated 1-10-1975 and 5-11-1975 did not operate to create title to petitioners' predecessors or to the instant petitioners, as the case may be, to the extent of entire suit land; it only creates title in respect of Dhirendra Mohon Dey's proportionate share of 12 gondas only. Thus petitioners' claim to the entire 48 decimals of suit land does not bear any basis but a ficticin simpliciter. The Deputy Attorney-General further submits that in the case before tribunal the petitioner intentionally concealed the lineage of CS recorded tenants simply for apprehension of losing in the case. The learned counsel concludes that the tribunal upon detailed evidence and hearing disposed of and dismissed the Arpi to Sampotti Prottarpon Case No. 75 of 2013 which had been rightly affirmed in appeal. 

 7.2. It, however, appears that the tribunal while adjudicating the contentions raised in the Arpito Sampotti Tribunal Case held, Annexure-B-3, that the petitioners were not entitled to acquire title to the whole of suit land since their vendor, Dhirendra Mohon Dey, had no title to the whole amount of land as there were other co-sharers also as per CS Khatian. We find a specific case to have been demonstrated by the petitioners that Dhirendra Mohon Dey by way of amicable partition owned the suit land in the whole. Admitted publication of SA Khatian Nos. 1948 and 1828 in Dhirendra Mohon's single name including the suit land in its entirety excluding other co-sharers therein appeared to be prima facie evidence of his possession at the relevant time. None of the co-sharers ever challenged the correctness of the SA Khatians or the validity of the family partition as being never done by them. It is evident from the impugned Gazette dated 9-4-2012 that the suit property was enlisted as enemy property vide Case No. 71/6970. Till 1969-70, no other co-sharers came forward to resist the claim of Dhirendra Mohon and to refute sole possession of 48 decimals of CS recorded land in Dhirendra Mohon's name alone. But before the enemy list was done, the SA Khatian got finally published attributing thereto the presumption of possession in Dhirendra Mohon's favour. The incorporation of suit land in SA Khatians in Dhirendra Mohon's name reflects the initial basis of amicable family partition particularly when the Khatians continued to operate till further Khatian under new survey operation was published in ultimate conformity with the earlier Khatians. It appears from the lower court record that a number of co-sharers of Dhirendra Mohon Dey were impleaded as defendants in the Other Classes Suit No. 136 of 1976 which was analogously disposed of with Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1974. None of the co-sharers entered appearance to resist the family partition claim raised by Dhirendra Mohon Dey, rather impliedly allowed by their unopposed acts being ever raised in any legal action whatsoever. Unless a claim is controverted by persons directly affected or likely to be affected thereby, particularly when such claim is adjudicated with opportunities being provided to all concerned, such claim cannot be unilaterally deprecated on a mere hypothesis unattended by necessary surrounding circumstances. The exclusive and continued possession of one co-sharer over the land of other co-sharers for an unobjected and uninterrupted period of 12 years or more creates title by adverse possession in favour of the co-sharer possessing the land of such other co-sharers without material opposition. In the premises, the decision held either by learned erstwhile Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh in the said analogous judgment of Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1974 and Other Classes Suit No. 136 of 1976 or the decision held by the trial tribunal (Annexure-B-3) in Arpito Sampatti Case No. 75 of 2013 or by the appellate tribunal, (Annexure-B-1), in Arpito Appeal No. 02 of 2018, whichever may be, that the basis of SA Khatians in the sole name of Dhirendra Mohon Dey to be absolutely wrong do not appear to us to be in any way logically acceptable. 

 7.3. On the contrary, contesting respondent No. 01 states in the affidavit-in-opposition that only the respective share of Shailendra Mohon Dey to the extent of 12 gondas of suit land was considered as evacuee property after his migration to India with family members after the partition of India in 1947. The respondent althrough assailed to impair the credibility of the title of Dhirendra Mahon Dey as well as that of the petitioners claiming through Dhirendra Mohon relating to suit land but the respondent undertook no effort as to how, when and in what manner the government acquired title to the entire suit land or how that land of 48 decimals came under the control and management of the government. We are unable to detect any full-fledged legal proceedings at government's instance to claim the suit land, except the reference to the case bearing No. 71/69-70 appearing in the relevant column (No. 02) of the impugned Gazette notification dated 9-4-2012. The existence of registered title deeds dated 1-10-1975 and 5-11-1975 (Annexure-D and E), comprising of the suit land in petitioners'/their predecessor's name, the preparation and final publication of BRS Khatian No. 5023 in the names of the recipients of theses deeds (Annexure-G), acknowledge-ment of land tax, (Annexure-I-I series), and holding tax, (Annexure-M series), by the government, the striking out of the suit land from khas Khatian No. 01 and ordering the same to be recorded in separate Khatian in petitioners' name (Annexure-F), etc, are not liable to be knocked down by a simple and solitary assertion of fact that the suit land had been rightly included in the vested property list.

full_judgment:
2. Facts, leading to filing this civil appeal, in short, are that the respondent No.1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.191 of 1993 against the defendant No.1 and others in the Court of 2nd Assistant Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession stating, inter alia, that Hari Charan Rishi was the original owner of the suit property along with other properties and during the Cadastral Survey (in short, C.S.) operation the suit land and other properties were correctly recorded in C.S. Khatian No.497 in the name of Hari Charan Rishi who had been enjoying the suit land by erecting tin shed house thereon and used to reside with his family members in the suit land on payment of rents to the Zaminder. While Hari Charan Rishi had been possessing the suit land, State Acquisition (in short, S.A.) operation started and the suit land bearing C.S. Plot No.1230 was recorded in his name in the S.A. Khatian No.754. During S.A. operation 0.05 acres of the suit land was wrongly recorded in his name instead of 0.06 acres. After about two years of S.A. operation, Hari Charan Rishi died leaving behind two sons namely, Paban Chandra Rishi and Ram Chandra Rishi to inherit the properties including the suit land. Thereafter, while two brothers had been enjoying and possessing the suit land by inheritance, Paban Chandra Rishi died about two years before liberation of Bangladesh leaving behind only son namely, Pulin Chandra Rishi to inherit his father portion including the suit land. Thereafter, Ram Chandra Rishi died in the year 1977 leaving behind one son Shushil Chandra Rishi to inherit the share of his property. Pulin Chandra Rishi and Shushil Chandra Rishi who got the suit land by way of inheritance and while they had been enjoying the same, left the locality for the good of their business. They went to Jurain Rishi Para under Demra Police Station and were settled there. Before leaving of the locality Sukdeb Rishi, a neighbor of Pulin Rishi and Shushil Rishi was requested to look after the suit land on their behalf. After some time Pulin Chandra Rishi left for Jurain Rishi Para and went to the village Kuthai under Keranigonj Police Station and settled there. However, frequently both of them used to visit the suit land. Pulin Chandra Rishi and Shushil Chandra Rishi had been enjoying the suit land through Sukdeb Rishi sold the suit land to the plaintiff by executing a saf-kabala registered deed dated 13.03.1986 bearing deed No.2513 and handed over the possession of the suit land to the plaintiff on the same date. After purchasing of the above suit land the plaintiff was enjoying the suit land by mutating his name in the khatian and by paying rents to the Government. He constructed the pucca boundary wall surrounding the suit land. While he was peacefully possessing and residing in the suit land with his sister, another family member, the defendant Nos.1-7, in the first part of the month of September, 1991 claimed the suit land as their own and threatened to hand over the possession of the suit land in their favour on 20.02.1992 and they tried to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land but they could not succeed. Being disappointed they threatened the plaintiff with dispossession from the suit land at any time and, as such, the plaintiff has filed a suit for permanent injunction against the defendant Nos.1-7 in the Court of Second Assistant Judge, Dhaka being Title Suit No.52 of 1992. However, on 08.10.1992, the defendants dispossessed him from the suit land. Thereafter, he filed the instant suit withdrawing the Title Suit No.52 of 1992. 

 3. The defendants contested in the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint, contending, inter alia, that the suit is false, groundless and barred by limitation; neither it was evaluated properly nor adequate Court fees were paid. It is bad for defect of parties, hence, not maintainable in its present form and nature. The C.S. recorded holding owner Hari Charan Rishi died circa 55 years ago leaving behind only son Paban Chandra Rishi who died leaving behind two sons namely Pulin Chandra Rishi and Ram Chandra Rishi as his legal heirs. They left the suit land Mouza after their father’s death and start residing in the village named Utail belonged to Keranigonj Thana. Ramchandra Rishi and his mother Rotimonjuri sold half of suit plot no. 1230 to one Dr. Monoruddin. Monoruddin sold the same to Shashimohon Rishi through registered Kabala dated on 29.11.1948. Among them Shashimohon Rishi solely possessed the same through mutual arrangement and died leaving behind his mother Oishsorja Bala as the only heir. Pulin Rishi sold and handed over the possession of his portion of the suit land to Oishsorja Bala through Sale deed no.13261, dated on 22.10.1960. Oishsorjo Bala sold and handed over the possession of the entire land to one Totazuddin on 23.04.1969 and he then sold and handed over the possession to one Habibullah on same day. Habibullah died leaving behind Md. Shafiullah as his legal heir. After his death, his heirs sold the same to the defendant no.7 through registered deed nos. 4683/1990 and 7402/1990. As the Khatian number was wrong recorded in the suit land and Totazuddin rectified it through registered deed on 22.08.1990. On 14.01.1993 the suit property was mutated and separate holding was prepared in the name of Md Shahidullah. The plaintiff purchased from one Sukhdeb Rishi’s C.S. plot no. 1238 adjacent to the suit land. Sukhdeb was never the caretaker of Shusil and Ramchandra. Shusil and Ramchandra never sold the suit land through registered Kabala no. 2513 of 1986. It is a forged deed and was not acted upon. Defendant no.7 is possessing the suit land by erecting semi pukka building, tin shed houses and tube well with boundary wall around it. The suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 20. The plaintiffs-Respondent’s mode of ownership and possession over the suit land as made out in their written statement were that Hari Charan Rishi was the original owner of the suit property and the same were correctly recorded in CS Khatin No. 497 and during the SA operation the suit land bearing Plot No.1230 was recorded in his name, Hari Charan Rishi died after 02 years of SA operation leaving behind two sons namely, Paban Chandra Rishi and Ram Chandra Rishi. Paban Chandra Rishi died about two years before liberation leaving behind only son Pulin Chandra Rishi. After that Ram Chandra Rishi died in the year 1977 leaving behind one son Shushil Chandra Rishi to inherit the share of the property. Pulin Chandra Rishi and Shushil Chandra Rishi left the suit land for the good of their business and they went to Jurain Rishi Para under Demra Police Station and were settled there. Before leaving of the suit land Sukdeb Rishi, a neighbor of Pulin Rishi and Shushil Rishi, was requested to look after the suit land on their behalf. After some time Pulin Chandra Rishi left for Jurain Rishi Para and went to the village Kuthai under Keranigonj Police Station and settled there and occasionally both of them used to visit the suit land. Thereafter, since 1977 Pulin Chandra rishi and Shushil Chandra Rishi were enjoying the suit land through Sukdeb Rishi and thereafter they sold the suit land to the plaintiff by executing a saf-kabala registered deed dated 13.03.1986 bearing deed No. 24513 and handed over the possession of the suit land to the plaintiff on the same dated. After purchased of the suit land the plaintiff was enjoying the suit land by mutating his name in the khatian and by paying taxes to the Government. He constructed the pucca boundary wall surrounding the suit land. While he was peacefully possessing and residing in the suit land with his sister the defendant Nos.1-7, in the first part of the month of September, 1991 claimed the suit land as their own and threatened to hand over the possession of the suit land in their favour on 20.02.1992 and they tried to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land but they could not succeed. Being disappointed they threatened the plaintiff with dispossession from the suit land at any time and, as such, the plaintiff has a suit for permanent injunction. However, during pendency of the suit the defendants dispossessed them on 08.10.1992. 

 21. The plaintiff side was duty bound to prove the genealogy of their forerunner and mode of their possession and dispossession over the suit land. However, they skipped the burden of proving the chain of ownership upto 1977 that is prior to their deed of purchase. No certificate of death or inheritance of the concerned, Voter list, Nationality certificates were submitted and reliable oral evidences too were not adduced to establish their chain of title over the suit land. As the defendants made out their own chain of title with registered deeds alongwith possession over the suit land it was imperative on the plaintiffs to prove all of the facts relevant for the sake of establishing title, possession and dispossession alleged. On weighing the evidences it transpires that they were failed to discharge the duties. Nonetheless, the learned Judge of the trial Court decreed the suit ignoring these facts and drawn some irrelevant and self explanatory presumptions as to the aliveness of the CS owner during SA operation, awarding presumptive value of correctness of SA Khatians and inferring some sort of title from SA Khatian in favour of CS owner. Moreover, the trial Court strangely bypassed deeds of the defendants registered prior to the deeds of the plaintiffs without any convincing findings. High Court Division too relied on these grounds in decreeing the suit without considering the legal process and material on record of the suit, we are, therefore, of the view that it has committed Legal error. 

 “A record of rights has been described by Sir Henry Maine as a detailed statement of all rights in land drawn up periodically by the functionaries employed in setting the claims of the Government to its shares of the rental........Though it does not create a title, it gives rise to a presumption in its support, which prevails until its correctness is successfully impugned.” 

 33. Under the Chapter X of Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 such the presumption as the correctness of the entries in the CS Record of rights arose by virtue of sub-section (5) of section 103B of the Act. However, there is no such presumption of correctness was available in respect of SA Khatians as the same were prepared on the tables instead of field cadastral survey. This notion were ratified by various decisions of this Division such as in case of Abdul Aziz vs. Hindu Deity Luxmi Gobinda Jew and others and Abdul Gafur and others Vs. Md Abdur Razzak and others reported in 58 DLR(AD) (2006) 206 and 62 DLR(AD) (2010) 242 respectively. 

 “Presumption as to genuineness of certified copies 79. The Court shall presume every document purporting to be a certificate, certified copy or other document, which is by law declared to be admissible as evidence of any particular fact and which purports to be duly certified by any officer of the 28[Government] to be genuine: Provided that such document is substantially in the form and purports to be executed in the manner directed by law in that behalf.

3. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to Golok Nath who died leaving behind 5 (five) sons, namely, Lok Charan, Sundari Mohon, Romesh Chandra Nath, Shoshi Mohan Nath and Suresh Chandra Nath. The SA Khatian in respect of the suit land was correctly prepared in their names in equal share and by way of amicable partition, 3 (three) brothers, namely, Romesh Chandra Nath, Suresh Chandra Nath and Mohan Nath got the suit land. They offered to sell the suit land and one Yasin Ali, a predecessor of the plaintiffs, wanted to purchase the same. The talk of sale took place and the consideration was fixed at taka 20,000.00 and on 24.08.1972 an agreement of sale was executed by the said 3(three) brothers after receiving taka 16,000.00 and delivered the possession of the suit land in favour of Yasin Ali. After execution of the said Bainapatra, Yasin Ali died leaving behind his wife, plaintiff No.1, six sons, plaintiff Nos.2-7, two daughters, plaintiff Nos.8-9, who have been possessing the suit land. During Revisional Survey, the plaintiffs went to the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Office, Rajnagar for mutation of the suit land in their names claiming title on adverse possession but the Mutation Case was rejected on 02.12.2000. After that, the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.3 of 2001 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Moulvibazar praying for title on the basis of adverse possession and the said suit was decreed exparte on 01.07.2001 declaring the plaintiffs' title. While the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land peacefully, the defendants on 31.10.2001, in collusion with each other attempted to dispossess the plaintiffs by taking away ripe paddy from the suit land forcibly and as such, the plaintiffs were constrained to institute the instant suit for perpetual injunction. 

 4. Defendant Nos.1-5 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegation made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs had no cause of action to file the suit; that the suit was barred by limitation and that the suit being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act was not maintainable in the present form. The defendants also con-tended that Md. Yasin Ali, predecessor of the plaintiffs, never purchased the suit land and the alleged deed of agreement is nothing but a false and forged document and the plaintiffs obtained the ex-parte decree dated 01.07.2001 in Title Suit No.3 of 2001 by practicing fraud upon the Court. The defendants further contended that the suit land belonged to Golok Chandra Nath, who died leaving behind 5(five) sons and the last SA Khatian was correctly prepared in their names. Three sons of Golok Chandra, namely, Lok Charan, Sundari Mohon Nath and Shoshi Mohon Nath got the entire suit land by way of amicable partition and they sold out the suit land in favour of defendant Nos.1 and 2 by a registered deed dated 26.02.1982 and since then they have been possessing the suit land. Three sons of Golok Chandra Nath, namely, Romesh Chandra Nath, Suresh Chandra Nath and Shoshi Mohan Nath left this country before the liberation war and no notice of Title Suit No.3 of 2001 was served upon them and the plaintiffs obtained the ex-parte decree in Title Suit No.03 of 2001 by practicing fraud upon the Court. The plaintiffs have no title and possession in the suit land and as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 14. Admittedly, the suit land originally belongs to one Golok Nath who died leaving behind five sons namned Lok Charm, Sundari Mohon, Romesh Chandra Nath, Shoshi Mohon Nath and Suresh Chandra Nath and that SA Khatian in respect of land in suit was correctly prepared in their names to the extent of equal share. 

 "In a simple suit for permanent injunction with regard to a disputed landed property, the relief is available to a person who is in possession. The Court may enquire incidentally into the respective claims of the parties to the suit for determining whether the plaintiff has got a prima facie case, i.e., whether he is in possession of the disputed property and entitled to the specific relief of permanent injunction. If the dispute involves complicated questions of title, the plaintiff must establish his little (title) by filing a regular suit for declaration of title. A simple suit for permanent injunction should not be allowed to be used as a testing device for ascertainment of title. In this case, the plaintiff assails the presumption of the CS Khatian, a kind of exercise, the Court in a simple suit for permanent injunction should ordinarily avoid."(sic)

full_judgment:
Abu Bakar Siddiquee, J: This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated the 24th day of November, 2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3505 of 2007 discharging the Rule and affirming the judgment and decree dated 17-7-2007 passed by the Joint District Judge, Brahmanbaria in Other Appeal No.53 of 2006 allowing the appeal and reversing those dated 10-5-2006 in Other Suit No.71 of 2005 of trial Court. 2. The facts relevant to dispose of the appeal, in short, are that respondent No. 1-9 as the plaintiffs instituted Other SuitNo.71 of 2005 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Brahmanbaria for declaration of title and for recovery of khas possession. The case of the plaintiffs was that CS Khatian No.114 in respect of the disputed land was prepared in the name of their predecessor-in-interest. CS recorded 'Ka' group tenants, Zalfur Uddin, Patchu, father of Kala Miah and Kalfur Uddin, father of Lai Mahmud, were full brothers. Zalfur Uddin died issueless leaving two full brothers: Patchu and Kalfur Uddin as his heirs and accordingly, they inherited the share of Zalfur Uddin in the suit plots. Subsequently, Patchu died leaving behind his son, Kala Miah and Kalfur Uddin died leaving behind his son, Lai Mahmud. The CS recorded tenants. Bashu .Miah died leaving behind plaintiff No.9 as his heir and Seraj Ali died leaving behind his three sons: plaintiff Nos.6 and 7 and Sultan Meah, father of plaintiff No.8. Kala Miah died leaving behind his two sons and two daughters: plaintiff Nos.4, 5, 10 and 11. Lal Mahmud died leaving behind his son named Abdul Khaleque. Thereafter, Abdul Khaleque died leaving behind his three sons and three daughters: plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and 12-14. Thus, the plaintiffs became the owners of the suit land and some other lands. The suit land was correctly recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and in the name of their predecessor-in-interest during the SA operation. The plaintiffs had been possessing the suit land for a long time through their bargader, defendant No. l. Since the plaintiffs had to stay outside the area in connection with their business, defendant No.1 was entrusted to get the suit land recorded in their names during Bangladesh Survey. The plaintiffs recently came to know that defendant No.1 had been planning to construct houses on the suit land by filling it up with earth. Thereafter, the plaintiffs made a search of their khatian in the survey office and found that defendant No.1 had got DP Khatian No. 1107 in respect of the suit land along with some other lands recorded in his name. The plaintiffs asked defendant No.1 on 28-1-2005 to quit the possession of the suit land, but defendant No.1 refused to do so and instead, he claimed his title over the same. Thus, a cloud was created on the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land hence, they filed the suit for the relief as aforementioned. 

 3. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that he was never a bargader in the suit land under the plaintiffs. He took settlement of some portion of the suit land from one Abdul Malek Haji and that he had been possessing the same. One Jogendra Mohan Chowdhury being the owner had been possessing 121/2 decimals land in Suit Plot Nos.434, 435 and 436 by way of purchase from the CS recorded tenants and sold the same to Kashem Ali and Sadir Meah by a registered kabala being No.7791 dated 6-10-1984. Besides Abdul Khaleque, the plaintiffs' father sold 2½ decimals land from Plot No.434 by registered deed No.37094 dated 3-4-1961. Sadir Meah sold 6¼ decimals land from the suit plots to Tuku Meah, Abu Bakar, Bazlu Meah and delivered possession thereof to them. SA Khatian No.112 was prepared in the names of Tuku Meah and other sons of Kala Meah. Tuku Meah, Abu Bakar, Nurul Huq and Bazlu Meah by a registered exchange deed bearing No.6973 dated 28-10-1958 exchanged 6¼ decimals land of the suit plots with Kashem Ali and delivered possession and thus, they became disinterested in the suit plots. Kashem Ali became owner of the entire suit land and he being in possession thereof sold the same to Zaher Meah by a registered deed being No.224 executed on 9-1-1977 and registered on 18-1-1977 and delivered possession of the transferred land to him. Zaher Meah exchanged the suit land with defendant No.1 by a registered exchange deed dated 13-6-1988. In this way, defendant No.1 became the owner of the suit land and had been possessing the same by growing crops thereon and by paying rents regularly to the Government. The plaintiffs having no right, title and possession in the suit land were not entitled to get any relief in the suit and the same was liable to be dismissed. 

 8. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Counsel, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the Appellate Court below being the last Court of fact failed to appreciate that the appellant is the purchaser of the land from the true owner of the suit land and they are not the Borgadar under the present respondent whereas the trial Court rightly held the aforesaid fact and dismissed the suit. He further adds that the positive findings of the trial Court were not adverted by the Appellate Court below who wrongly held that the appellants are liable to be evicted from the suit land although DP Khatian has been prepared in the name of the defendant-appellants on the basis of their title and possession for more than 12 years and, as such, the defendants acquired statutory right by way of adverse possession. He further adds that the revisional Court also failed to appreciate the aforesaid fact of right, title and possession of the defendant- appellants and wrongly supported the Appellate Court below which are the product of mere non-consideration, misreading and non-appreciation of the evidence on record. 

 10. He further adds that the trial Court failed to appreciate the evidentiary value of CS and SA Khatian which created an unrebuttable presumption in favour of the plaintiff and also that Jogendra Mohan Chowdhury had no saleable interest in the suit land and the defendants have failed to prove the very basis of preparation of the DP Khatian. He further adds that the DP Khatian and the rent receipt conferred no title. 

 12. It is admitted by the parties that CS Khatian No.114 in respect of the disputed land was prepared in the name of plaintiffs predecessor-in-interest. CS recorded "Ka" group tenants Zalfur Uddin, Patchu, father of Kala Miah and Kalfur Uddin, father of Lai Mahmud were full brothers and that Zalfur Uddin died issueless leaving two full brothers, Patchu and Kalfur Uddin as his heirs and accordingly, they inherited the share of Zalfur Uddin in the suit plots. It is not denied that subsequently, Patchu died leaving behind his son, Kala Miah and that Kalfur Uddin died leaving behind his son, Lai Mahmud. It is also undisputed that the other CS recorded tenants, Bashu Miah died leaving behind plaintiff No.9 and Seraj Ali died leaving behind of plaintiff Nos.6 and 7 and Sultan, father of plaintiff No.8 and Kala Miah died leaving behind his two sons and two daughters, plaintiff Nos.4, 5, 10 and 11 and that Lai Mahmud died leaving behind his son, Abdul Khaleque. It is also not denied that Abdul Khaleque died leaving behind his three sons and three daughters: plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and 12-14 and in this way, the plaintiffs claimed to have acquired the suit land and some other lands. It appears that the suit land was recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and in the name of their predecessor-in-interest during the SA operation. The plaintiffs also claimed that they had been possessing the suit land for a long time through their bragader, defendant No. l. It is also contended that since the plaintiffs had to stay outside the area in connection with their business, defendant No. 1 was entrusted to get the suit land recorded in their names during Bangladesh Survey and that the plaintiffs recently came to know that defendant No. l had been planning to construct house on the suit land by filling it up with earth. 

 13. The plaintiffs (respondents) have come with an allegation that they made a search of their khatian in the survey office and found that defendant No. 1 got his name recorded in DP Khatian No.l 107 in respect of the suit land along with some other lands. The plaintiffs asked defendant No.1 on 28-1-2005 to vacate the possession of the suit land, but defendant No.1 on the event of refusal to do so and instead of vacating, he claimed his title over the same. 

 14. On the other hand, the present appellants (defendants) filed RoR Khatian No.1 12 (Exhibit-Gha') from which it is seen that the name of Bazlu Mia, Nurubaksha, Tuku Mia and Abu Bakar son of Kala Gazi are the recorded tenants who are the successive heirs of CS tenant Bashu. The present, plaintiffs filed an exchange deed being No.6973 dated 28-10-1956 (Exhibit-Gail) from which it revealed that the aforesaid successive heirs of Bashu (who appears to be RS tenant) exchanged the suit property with one Kashem Ali and the suit property has fallen in the share of the second party, Kashem Ali through this exchange deed. The appellants (defendants) has filed another kabala dated 9-1-1977 executed by Kashem Ali (Exhibit-Ga) from which it appears that the suit property has been sold by Kashem Ali in favour of Zaher Mia (DW 3). Thereafter, the present appellants (defendants) filed another deed of exchange dated 13-6-1988 (Exhibit-Kha) from which it is seen that aforementioned Zaher Mia exchanged the suit property with Shahidul Haque who is the present defendant. On perusal of those registered deeds, it appears that the successive heirs of Bashu transferred their share in favour of the present defendants. It is admitted by the respondents (plaintiffs) that they have been possessing the suit land through their borgadar, defendant No. 1 which has been denied by defendant No. 1. But the said defendant claimed that he has been possessing the suit land for more than 17/18 years and thereby he has acquired a statutory right by way of adverse possession. 

 17. Defendant No.1 while deposing as DW 1 stated that certain portion of the suit land belonged to one Jogendra Mohan Chowdhury who granted settlement of such land to one Haji Khaleque and he transferred the said land to One Kashem Ali in the benami of Tawkin Mia and Shadek Mia who exchanged the same in favour of Zaher Ali and he subsequently exchanged such land with him (defendant No. 1). Aforesaid Zaher Mia while deposing as DW3 slated that he transferred the land in favour defendant No.1, but he could not say as to which land he has transferred. The learned Judge of the trial Court held that the defendant filed a RoR porcha. But there is no record which Jogendra Mohan Chowdhury was CS recorded tenant. The RoR is not a document of title. The Appellate Court observed that the name of Jogendra Mohan Chowdhury does not appear as the recorded tenant either in CS Khatian No.114 or kabala dated 6-10-1984. If Jogendra Mohan Chowdhury's title and possession in the suit land remained unproved, the purchaser (defendant) has acquired no title and possession. This observation made by the Appellate Court below has been approved by the revisional Court. We also find that Jogandra Mohan Chowdhury was not CS record tenant. The appellant (defendant) thus acquired no right and title in respect of such portion of land. Excepting such portion of land which defendant No.1 claimed to have been acquired from Jogendra Mohan, the appellant acquired other portion of the suit land as has been discussed by us earlier. In that case, we are of the view that the present appellant and respondent appears to be co-sharers in the suit jams and in that case, the respondent may be allowed to remain in joint possession with defendant No. 1.

Md. Ruhul Amin, J :- These appeals, by leave, are against the order dated June 30, 1997 of a Division Bench of the High Court Division passed in Civil Order Nos. 3230, 3231, 3232, 3233 and 3234 of 1997 rejecting the 5 revisional applications summarily. The revisional applications were filed against the judgment and order dated 10.4.1996 of the 1st Court of Additional District Judge, Sylhet, passed in Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 76, 77, 78, 79 and 80 of 1994 allowing the same upon reversing the judgment and order dated August 31,1994 in Miscellaneous Case (Preemption) Nos. 179, 180, 181, 182, and 183 of 1989 allowing the same. The Miscellaneous Cases were filed under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 seeking pre-emption in respect of the sale by 5 different kabalas dated 5.9.1988. The claim of pre-emption was made on the assertion that by inheritance the pre-emptors the co-sharer of the land of lot Nos. 2183 and 2184 of khatian No. 450. 

 2. The pre-emptor claimed to have inherited the land of khatian No. 450 from his father late Abdul Mogni and uncle Abdul Ghani who died leaving only daughter, Respondent No. 2 Panda Begum. It was the case of the pre-emptor that Panda Begum as co-sharer of the Khatian in question sold parcels of land by five registered kabalas dated September 5, 1988 to Mehfzur Rahman, the Respondent No.1 in each of the appeal. It was also averred by the pre-emptor that a suit for partition, partition Suit No. 111 of 1988, is pending before the 2nd Court of Joint District Judge, Sylhet as regard the land of khatian No. 450 filed by one of the co-sharers by name Abdul karim. 

 3. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed upon assertion that there was amicable partition of the land of khatian in question amongst the co-sharers and the pre-emptor and other co-sharers of the khatian had separated their jamas and have recorded their names in respect of their respective saham got by amicable partition in separate khatians, that the pre-emptor in respect of his share separated the jams and has got his name recorded in khatian No. 450/2 and as such pre-emptor ceased to be the co-sharer of the land of the case khatian. The preemptees, contended that they had effected improvement of the disputed land. 

 4. The trial Court allowed the prayer for pm emption on the finding that the pre-emptor and the seller opposite party are co-sharers of the khatian and that preemptees failed to establish there had been partition of the land of khatian by the decree of the Court or by a registered deed of partition. The trial Court also held that the Miscellaneous Cases were not barred by limitation and further held that opening of khatian No. 450/1 and 450/2 do not establish that the jama of the khatian No. 450 was separated. The trial Court while allowing the prayer for preemption awarded Compensation of Tk. 1,00,000/- to the pre-emptees. On appeal the judgment and order of the trial Court was reversed and the Miscellaneous Cases were dismissed. The appellate Court held that upon amicable partition amongst the co-sharers the pre-emptor splitting fame got his name recorded in khatian No. 450/2 and as such pre-emptor was not entitled to pre-empt the sale held on September 5, 1988. 

 5. Thereupon the pre-emptor moved the High Court Divisions in revisional jurisdiction. The High Court Division by common order, as stated hereinabove, rejected the revisional applications summarily upon observing "Since in the instant Cases the holding in question has been separated or sub divided upon opening a new khatian at the instance of the pre-emptor, the preemptor ceased to be a co-sharers in the holding in question". 

 7. The learned Counsel for the appellant, in all the appeals, submitted that amicable partition of the land of the khatian No. 450 alleged by the preemptees being not partition in the eye of law and thus there being no ceasing of co-share ship in the land of the khatian by the so called amicable partition the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court were in error in holding that pre-emptor ceased to be a co-sharer of the land of libation No. 450 and as such he was not entitled to seek preemption in respect of the purchase made by the preemptees. The learned counsel also submitted that in fact by the opening of khatian No. 450/1 and 450/2 in the name of the heirs of late Abdul Mogni and the pre-emptor there was no separation of jams or sub division of the holding as contemplated by section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, rather the same were updating of the record of right i.e khatian No. 450 as per provision of Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 . The teamed Counsel continued since there was no legal partition i.e partition by metes and bounds by the decree of the Court or by a registered instilment of partition and consequent thereupon there was no separation of title of the recorded tenants of khatian No. 450 and as by amicable partition title is not separated but only possession is separated and it being the case of the pre-emptees that there was a amicable partition amongst the co-sharers of the khatina no.450 and as thereby there had been no separation of title the High Court Division as well as the appellate Court below were in error in holding that pre-emptor ceased to be a co sharer in respect of the land of khatian No. 450 and consequent thereupon in rejecting the prayer for preemption, that ratio decadent of the decision reported in 35 DIR(AD) 230 being that by a legal partition co-sharer of a holding ceases to be co-sharer of the original holding and in the instant case there being no legal partition, rather partition suit being pending, the High Court Division and the lower appellate Court were in error in rejecting the prayer for pre-emption upon holding that the pre-emptor ceased to be a Co sharer in the background of the assertion made by the preemptees that there had been amicable partition of the land of khatian No. 450 amongst the co-sharers and that in the light of the amicable partition the pre-import got his share recorded in khatian No. 450/2, that the ratio dividend of the decision reported in 35 DLR(AD) 338 has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. 

 8. The learned Counsel for the Respondent No.1 submitted that the very fact of opening of khatian No. 450/1 clearly shows that after amicable partition amongst the co-sharers of khatian No, 450 the heirs of late Abdul Mogni got the aforesaid khatina opened in their names in respect of the land inherited from their father and their late uncle, Abdul Gani and that opening of the said khatian No. 450/1 and later on opening of khatian No. 450/2 in the name of the preemptor as there has been ceasing of co share ship of the heirs of late Abdul Mogni in respect of the land of khatian No. 450 the High Court Division and the Court of appeal below were quite correct in rejecting the prayer for pre-emption upon arriving at the finding that the pre-emptor ceased to be the co-sharer in respect of the land of khatian No. 450. The learned Counsel also submitted that after opening of the new khatian in the name of the pre-emptor he is claiming the land separately from the land recorded in khatian No. 450/1 and that in the light of amicable partition separate Municipal holding has been opened in respect of the land of respective co-sharers. he also submitted that the contention of the pre-emptor that since there was no legal partition or that there was no partition by registered instrument and consequently there having no partition of the land 0f khatian No. 450 in the eye of law and that a suit the partition is being pending and as such the High Court Division and the appellate Court were not correct in holding that pre-emptor ceased to be a co sharer is no merit since the fact of opening of khatian No. 450/1 as clearly manifest there has been a partition among the co-sharers of the khatian No.450 and that the said partition was given effect by opening of the aforesaid khatian and as such as in fact there had been partition of the land of khatian No. 450 the High Court Division and the appellate Court below were quite correct in rejecting the prayer for pre-emption on the finding that pre-emptor ceased to be the co-sharer. 

 12. Facts of the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230, in short, are that the land of C.S Khatina No. 214 was owned by Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Chowdhurani Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 for partition and by the decree passed in the suit Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik got sham and Rangubala Chowdhurani got share. Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik sold his share to Nafisa Khatun by the sale deed dated 19.7.1952 and thus she became the co sharer of Rangubala. Rangubala Chowdhurani created a lease in respect of her Share in favour of Ayesha Khatun by a registered lease deed dated 23.12.1953. Nafisa Khatun sold her share to the Respondent No.1 (preemptor) by the sale deed dated 18.4.1972 . Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant (preemptees) by a registered sale deed dated 10.9.1973. This sale was sought to be pre-empted claiming to be the co-sharer of the holding primarily on the plea that on the acquisition of rent receiving interest under raiyat being up graded to raiyat and thereupon only one S.A. khatian having been prepared recording the names of the persons who acquired interest in the land of C.S. khatian No. 214. 

 13. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed contending that seller Ayesha khatun (Respondent No. 2) was not a co sharer in the tenancy, because the land of the tenure was partitioned by the decree in Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 between Akshoy Kumar and Rangubala and that a separate tenancy was created in favour of the Respondent No.2 by Rangbala by granting permanent lease reserving to herself annual rent of Tk.1/- and that Ayesha Khatun paid the rent to the lessor till the rent receiving interest was acquired by the Government. It was also the case of the preemptees that S.A. khatian was not correctly prepared because neither preemptor (Respondent No.1) nor his vendor was co sharer of Respondent No.2 and that he (preemptees) after purchase applied for mutation of his name and accordingly his name was mutated in the S.A. khatian and the jama was separated. The trial Court allowed the prayer for pre-emption and the appeal by the pre-emptees was dismissed preempted went on revision before the High Court Division but did not have the desired result. 

 Facts of the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 1 338, in short, are that pre-emption was sought in respect of an auction sale in Certificate Case No. 408 of 1967-1968 clamming to be the co-sharers by purchase of the land of plot No. 107 and 87 of Khatian No. 14 from recorded tenant H.E. Percival by the kabala dated 29.12.1965. It was the case of the preemptors that their names were mutated in khatian No.14. It may be mentioned H.E. Percival was the owner of the land of khatian Nos. 14,18,20, and 24. plot No.108 originally was listed in khatian No.14 . At one stage of the certificate proceeding the land of the aforesaid 4 khatian were amalgamated in khatian No.18 comprising plot Nos. 108, 116, 117, 119 and 121 and finally in the certificate   case land of khatian No.18 was put to auction and the same was purchased by the preemptees. 

 18. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed contending, inter alia, that though the pre-emptors were co-sharers of khatian No .14 but they ceased to be the co sharers of the said khatian while the different plots of khatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24, as owned and possessed by H.E. Percival were amalgamated and consolidated in one khatian, namely khatian No.18, land of which was sold in auction and where in the preemptors were not co-sharers of the certificate debtor. 

 20. The Appellate Division by majority decision restored the judgment of the trial Court holding that although at one point of time the pre-emptors were the co-sharers of the khatian No. 14 by purchasing land of plot Nos. 107 and 87 and plot No. 108 was in the said khatian, but when the land of the different Khatians, i.e khatian Nos. 18, 20, 24 as well as the land of plot No. 108 of Madan No. 14 was consolidated in one khatian i.e . in khatian No. 18, the pre-emptors ceased to be the co-sharers of the recorded tenant RE Percival in respect of the land of khatian No.18. Pre-emptors prayer for pre-emption was riot allowed since on the consolidation and amalgamation of the land of H.E. Percival in a new khatian i.e. khatian No. 18, the preemptors ceased to be the co-sharers of the recorded tenant of the said khatian. So it is seen that a tenant though at one time was the co-sharer in a particular tenancy alms, with the co-sharer in a particular tenancy along with the person who acquired interest subsequently in the land of the tenancy, but when the land of the original tenant or tenants of the said holding wherein purchaser-tenant(s) has no right, is listed in a different khatian and thus leaving the land of the tenant (s) who became the co-sharer in the tenancy either by purchases or by some other mode(s) in the old tenancy them exists no co-share-reship in respect of the land so listed in two (2) different khatians and as such prayer for pre-emption by one of the recorded tenant of the original tenancy is not available in respect of the land of the new tenancy or khatian and vice-versa. 

 21. It may be mentioned the second point in the leave was left undiscussed. The admitted position in the instant case is that appellant's predecessor Abdul Mogni and appellant's uncle, Abdul Ghani along with others were the tenants of khatian No. 450. It is the case of the preemptor appellant that his uncle Abdul Ghani died leaving no male issue and as such Abdul Ghani and for that matter his heirs also inherited the property of Abdul Mogni along with his daughter. It is seen from the materials on record that heirs of Abdul Mogni some time in 1985 upon splitting up jams separated their share whatever they had in plot Nos. 2180-2184 of khatian No. 450 by opening new khatian No. 450/1 and that later on upon splitting up the jama the appellant in the year 1995 separated Iris share in plot Nos. 2183 and 2184 of khatian No. 450/1 by opening new khatian no. 450/2. 

 22. It is the case of the preemptees-respondent that there has been a amicable partition of the land of khatian No. 450 between the heirs of Abdul Ghani and Abdul Gani. As against this it was the contention of the appellant that there was no partition by metes and bounds amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani. In the background of the aforesaid contention of the appellant it has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the pre-emptor appellant that in the absence of a 'legal partition' that is partition by Metes and bounds through a decree of a court, and in the absence of any partition by any legal installment of partition there had been no separation of title, as such pre-emption sought by the appellant was very much available and that amicable partition is no partition in the eye of law. 

 24. In the instant case it was contended from the side of the preemptees-respondent that there was amicable partition of the land of khatian No. 450 amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gain. This contention appears to be correct in the background of the fact of the opening of khatian No. 450/1 in the name of the heirs of Abdul Mogni. In the aforesaid state of the matter it is seen that jointness of possession of the land of khatian No. 450 among the hens of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani ceased. The preemptees purchased the land of khatian No.450 from the heirs of Abdul Gain. The preemptor prior to the transaction under pre-emption got opened separate Khatian, khatian No. 450/2, taking out his share from the land of Khatian No. 450/1. In our opinion in the afore state of the matter there being to jointness of possession between the pre-emptor and the preemptees in respect of the land of khatian No. 450 and jointness of possession or co-sharer ship in the land transferred being the requirement for seeking pre-emption in respect of non-agricultural land and the said legal requirement being absent in the instant case, pre-emptor's prayer for pre-emption is not legally available to him. 

 25. The finding of the trial court that by the disputed alleged separation of jama the pre-emptor in view of his inheritance from his uncle retained his status as a co-sharer in the land of khatian No. 450 appears to be not well funded in that no material has been brought is record to establish that khatian No. 450/1 in the name of heirs of Abdul Mogni was opened only in respect of the property they inherited from Abdul Mogni or in other words in the khatian No. 450/1 property inherited from Abdul Gani was not listed. 

 26. As the law is now settled that pre-emption under Section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act can be sought for by a person who is a co -sharer of the land sought to be preempted. It has already been mentioned Abdul Mogni's heirs taking out the land whatever they inherited from Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani in the land of khatian No.450 got recorded their share in khatian No. 450/1 with new jama on in other words upon splitting up of the original jama and this step of Abdul Mogni's heirs reflects that whatever quantity of land they got by inheritance in the land recorded in khatian No.450 and were possessing got the same recorded in the new khatian i.e khatian No. 450/1. This shows said step was taken by the heirs of Abdul Mogni by the Division/partition amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani of the land whatever they had in the said khatian. In the background of the partition/division heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani brought to an end of joint possession of the land inherited by them in khatian No. 450. It is also seen that later on the appellant whatever share he acquired in the property of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani he got said share recorded in a new khatian i.e khatian No. 450/2 with a new jama. This shows that whatever quantity of property he got from his father and also from Abdul Ghani he got that quantity of property recoded in khatian No. 450/2. This fact demonstrates that he is in possession of the property recoded in khatian No. 450/2 and thus he ceased to be a co possessor or joint possessor of the property of khatian No. 450. The very fact of opening of khatian by the appellant in his name shows that he is in exclusive possession of the land of his share in plot Nos. 2183 and 2184. On the opening of new khatian No. 450/1 in the names of the heirs of Abdul Mogni comprising the land of aforesaid two plots and some other plots inherited by them from Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani and later on upon opening of the khatian No. 450/2 comprising the share of appellant in plot Nos. 2183 and 2184. in other words in respect of the share which he had in the land of khatian No. 450/1, he ceased to be a co-sharer in the land of khatian No. 450, or in other words in respect of the land whatever left in the share of heirs (s) of Abdul Ghani in khatian No. 450. Thus the appellant being not the recorded tenant of khatian No. 450 and that being not the co-sharer of the land as recorded in khatian No. 450 or in other words appellant being the tenant of the tenancy as in khatian No. 450/2 and consequently not being the co-sharer of the tenancy or the land as in khatian No.450 as such was not entitled to seek preemption of the land sought to e preempted since the land so sought of be preempted is of khatian No.450. The jointeness of possession amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani in respect of the land on khatian No.450 has been served by the fact of opening of khation No. 450/1 in the name of the heirs of Abdul Mogni in respect of the land which they inherited from Abdul Mogni and Abdul gani. The opening of new khatian in their names by the heirs of Abdul Mogul shows that they are in specific possession of the land of the plots listed in the said khatian and further opening of khatian No. 450/2 with separate jama comprising land of plot Nos. 2183 and 2184 by the appellant in his name in respect of the quantity of land he got by inheritance out of the land of khatian No. 450/1 shows that he is in specific possession of the land of the plots listed in the said khatian. 

 27. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that opening of khatian No. 450/1 and khatian No.450/2 are not in fact separation of jama or creation of new tenancy with separate jama upon splitting up of tenancy of khatian No. 450, but in fact is correction of record of right making the same up to date as contemplates by section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or in other words the learned Counsel wants to say that there is more mutation of the names of the heirs of Abdul Mogni. The Submission no made is not well founded in that had the steps that were taken by the heirs of Abdul Mogni were in fact making the record of right upto date there was no earthly reason for starting a new khatian with different jama i.e khatian No. 450 /1 in the name of the heirs of Abdul Mogni and later on khatian No. 450/ 2 in the name of the appellant, In our opinion mutation of the names because of transfer or inheritance would be certainly noting down the names of the transferee (s) or the names of the heir (s) of original recorded tenant (s) in the record of right as stands at that particular moment and that not to open a separate khatian with separate jama as in the instant case has happened, It is also seen from the I record that heirs of Abdul Mogni paid rent as  against the khatian No. 450 /1. This fact shows that heirs of Abdul Mogni ceased to be the tenants of khatian No. 450. 

 28. In the background of the materials on record and the discussions made hereinabove it is seen that jointness of possession of the land of khatian No. 450 amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani ceased on the opening of a khatian No. 450/1 by the heirs of Abdul Mogni in respect of the land they got by inheritance   from Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani and that later on upon the opening of khatian No. 450/2 in the name of the appellant and as in respect of non agricultural land pre-emption is available only to a non-agriculture tenant who is a co-sharer of the land so transferred i.e co-sharership in the land transferred is the sole criterion for the purpose of seeking pre-emption when a part of the non-agricultural land held by a on-agricultural tenant is Transferred to a stranger i.e a person who is not a co-sharer tenant in the land to transferred and as in the instant case it is seen that appellant is not a co-sharer tenant in the land sought to pre-empted, as such he is not entitled to seek pre emption of the land transferred by the heir of Abdul Ghani to the preemptees.
