2. Facts, in short, are that land sought to be preempted along with some other land belonged to Abdur Rahman who died leaving sons Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Gafur. Abdul Gafur filed Title Suit No. 18 of 1954 seeking partition of the land inherited from Abdur Rahman. After the final decree Abdul Gafur got in his share 335 aurjuthansa and Abdur Razzaque got in his share 1005 aurjuthansa. Decree in the partition suit was made final (subject matter of the partition suit was land measuring 1340 aurjuthansa listed in CS Khatian No. 8282, the corresponding SA Khatian No. 3232). Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land recorded in a separate khatian being Khatian No. 3232/1. Abdul Gafur's heirs, pre-emptors, purchased 335 aurjuthansa of land on 16-6-1981 from Hannan's heirs. ie heirs of Abdur Razzaque's son. Abdur Razzaque's daughter Rowshan Akhter sold 167 aurjuthansa of land to Alfazuddin Ahmed pre-emptee on August 24, 1981. This sale has been sought to be pre-empted by Abdul Gafur's sons claiming to be co-sharers of the land. 

 3. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed contending, inter alia, that in the light of the decreein the partition suit filed by the pre-emptor's predecessor Abdul Gafur, his brother Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land separated upon opening separate SA Khatian No. 3232/1 by filing Mutation Case in the year 1977 and that after purchase by the pre-emptors they got the purchased land recorded in separate Khatian No. 3232/1/1 by filing Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1/81-82 of the office of Circle Officer (Revenue) Kotwali, Dhaka and thus ceased to be the co-sharer. It was also the contention of the pre-emptee that pre-emptors were aware of the transfer from the time of sale and that the land sought to be pre-empted being recorded as nishkar, section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act has no manner of application. 

 4. The Court of 1st instance rejected the prayer for pre-emption with the findings that pre-emptors were not co-sharers and that the prayer for pre-emption was barred by limitation. The said Court based its finding as to pre-emptors of not being co-sharers on Exhibit B(3) which later on was re-numbered as Exhibit A ie Khatian No. 3232/1 /1 opened in respect of the purchased land measuring 335 aurjutansha of Abdul Gafur's heirs from Abdur Razzaque's heirs. The said Khatian was started by the order dated 13-8-1981 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1/81-82 of the office of Circle Officer (Revenue), Kotwali, Dhaka. 

 5. On appeal, the appellate Court allowed the prayer for pre-emption on the finding that the claim of pre-emption is not barred by limitation since no notice under section 24(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was served on the pre-emptors and that the pre-emptors are co-sharers and that pre-emptee opened in his name separate Khatian in respect of the land sought to be pre-empted without serving notice on the co-sharers and, as such, by the said separation of Jama the pre-emptors did not cease to be the co-sharers of the land measuring 1005 aurjutansha ie land that Abdur Razzaque got in his share pursuant to the decree in the partition suit filed by Abdul Gafur. The appellate Court also held that Khatian No. 3232/1/1 in the name of the pre-emptors is in respect of the land allotted in the share of Abdul Gafur in the partition suit. 

 6. The pre-emptee moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction as against the judgment and order of the appellate Court allowing pre-emption. The High Court Division on the finding that pre-emptee separated the Jama in respect of his purchased land without compliance of the provision of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and, as such, appellate Court did not commit any error in holding that the pre-emptors are the co-sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted. The High Court Division further held that in spite of the opening SA Khatian No. 3232/1/1 the pre-emptors remained co-sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted since the said khatian was opened in respect of the land pre-emptors' predecessor Abdul Gafur got pursuant to the decree in the partition suit and that the said khatian is not in respect of the land purchased from Abdur Razzaque's heirs by the pre-emptors. 

 7. The pre-emptee as against the judgment and order of the High Court Division obtained leave contending, infer alia, that the High Court Division overlooked that the Court of appeal below without noticing and considering Exhibit B(2) Khatian No. 3232/1 relied upon by the trial Court came to an erroneous finding that the pre-emptors were the co- sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted, that the High Court Division erred in law in not considering that the Court of appeal below was wholly wrong in holding that Khatian No. 3232/1/1, standing in the name of the pre-emptors, was in respect of the land got pursuant to the final decree in the partition suit though there was no such evidence. Leave was also obtained for consideration whether the decisions reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323; 1987 BLD (AD) 122 and 33 DLR (AD) 309 have been properly interpreted in the instant case. 

 8. The admitted fact is that, property of holding No. 45(1) belonged to Abdur Rahman who died leaving sons Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Gafur. Abdul Gafur filed partition suit No. 18 of 1954 and in view of the decree therein got in his saham land measuring 335 aurjuthansa. The decree in the partition suit was made final is an admitted fact. Abdur Razzaque who was defendant in the partition suit got 1005 aurjuthansa in his share. Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land measuring 1005 aurjuthansa recorded in a separate khatian, being No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3). It may be mentioned land measuring 1340 aurjuthansa which was subject matter of partition was recorded in CS Khatian No. 8282 and later on the said land was recorded in SA No. 3232 (Exhibit B 1). Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land pursuant to decree in partition suit recorded in the separate khatian No. 3232/l as back as in June 1977. Heirs of Abdul Hannan (son of Abdur Razzaque) sold 335 aurjuthansa of land to the sons (pre-emptors') of Abdul Gafur in June 1981. The pre-emptors got the land purchased recorded in Khatian No. 3232/1/1 by order dated 13- 8-1981 in Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1/81-82. On August 24, 1981 Abdur Razzaque's daughter Rowshan Akhter sold 167 aurjuthansa of land to the pre-emptee. This transfer sought to be pre-empted by Gafur's heirs under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, hereinafter in short, the Act, claiming to be the co-sharers of the land so transferred. 

 10. The land sought to be pre-empted along with the other land belonged to Abdur Rahman and on his death his 2 sons Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Gafur inherited the same. Abdul Gafur had the 4 annas share. He filed Partition Suit No. 18 of 1954 and got his saham to the extent of 335 aurjuthansa. The partition decree was made final. Thus Gafur got his share being partitioned by metes and bounds by the decree in the partition suit. The land which was the subject matter of the partition suit was undoubtedly non-agricultural land. So, after partition by metes and bounds Abdul Gafur ceased to be the co-sharer of the land allotted to the other co-sharer or, in other words, as regards the other quality of land. This is one aspect of the matter as to the situation of co-sharership between Abdur Razzaque, the heirs of Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Gafur or the heirs of Abdul Gafur. Pursuant to the decree in the partition suit Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land measuring 1005 aurjuthansa recorded in khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3). The pre-emptors are not challenging legality of the fact of opening of this khatian or, in other words, opening of new khatian upon splitting of the original khatian No. 3232 (Exhibit B (1)) in the names of the heirs of Abdur Razzaque. After the purchase by the pre-emptors from the heirs of Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque, they opened in their names separate khatian, khatian No. 3232/1/1 by the order dated 13- 8-1981 in Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1 of 81-82. The appellate Court considered this khatian as of in respect of land measuring 335 aurjuthansa got in the partition suit by Abdul Gafur and after his death inherited by the pre-emptors. The revisional Court concurred with the said finding of the Court of appeal without taking into consideration the materials on record. It may be mentioned trial Court held that khatian No. 3232/1/1 was in respect of the land purchased by the pre-ernptors from the heirs of Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque. The High Court Division as well as the appellate Court on the view that khatian No. 3232/1/1 is in respect of the land allotted to Abdul Gofur in the partition suit held the pre-emptors being the co-sharers were competent to pre-empt the land sought to be pre-empted, while the trial Court held that because of opening of khatian No. 3232/1/1 in respect of land purchased by the pre-emptors from the heirs of Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque they ceased to be the co-sharers and, as such, were not entitled to pre-empt the land sought to be pre-empted. The fact that khatian No. 3232/1/1 was not as regard the land got by Abdul Gafur pursuant to decree in the partition suit but relates to the land purchased by the pre-emptors from Abdul Hannan's heirs is evidenced by the certified copy of the petition whereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1 of 81-82 was started for separation of jama upon splitting up the khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heir. It is seen that after the transfer by Hannan's heirs and by Rowshan Akhter (who sold to the pre-emptee land measuring 167 aurjuthansa) the quantity of land stands at sail? aurjuthansa in Khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit B (2). The endorsements made therein clearly show pre- emptors in respect of their land purchased from Abdul Hannan's heirs got the said purchased land recorded in khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A). Had the Khatian No. 3232/1/1 been in respect of the land got by Abdul Gafur pursuant to the partition decree there was no occasion for deduction of the said land from the khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) prepared in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs. If Gafur's heirs would have got the land which Gafur got by the decree in the partition suit ie land measuring 3535 aurjuthansa listed in a khatian other than 3232 (Exhibit B (1), then the said land would have been deducted from the khatian No. 3232, and not from the split khatian 3232/1 opened as back in 1977 in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs. So, it is seen that the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court upon total misconception that khatian No. 3232/1/1 was opened in respect of the land Abdul Gafur got by the decree in partition suit were in error in holding that pre-emptors are the co- sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted and entitled to pre-empt the land transferred by Rowshan Akhter to the pre-emptee. 

 11. Leave was also granted to consider whether the principle of law enunciated in the cases reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309; 1987 BLD (AD) 122 and 33 DLR 320 was properly interpreted by the High Court Division in view of the case of the (pre-emptee that prayer for pre-emption was not maintainable since after purchase pre-emptors separated the jama of their purchased land and he also separated jama of his purchased land by opening a separate khatian. It was urged before the High Court Division that since the pre-emptee has got a separate holding in respect of his purchased land by opening a separate khatian and that no appeal having been filed as against the order of the Revenue Officer allowing splitting of the jama the validity thereof cannot be opened in a collateral proceeding ie in a pre-emption proceeding, before the Civil Court and that Civil Court is not competent to ignore the order. In support of the aforesaid contention cases reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309 and in 1987 BLD (AD) 122 were referred to. In refusal of the aforesaid contention and in support of the contention that an order passed under section 117 (1)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 by the Revenue Officer without notifying the co-sharer and consequently, the same totally being violative of the provision of law, legality of such order can very much be seen by the Civil Court in collateral proceeding ie in pre-emption proceeding, from pre-emptor's side case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323 was referred to. 

 13. The question of legality of order of the Revenue Officer splitting up the jama and opening in the name of pre-emptee separate khatian on the oasis whereof there was the contention that by the opening of the said khatian pre-emptors ceased to be the co-sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted has lost its importance and relevancy because of the fact that pre-emptors got their purchased land from Hannan's heirs listed in a separate khatian being No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) upon splitting up the jama of khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) and consequently, the question of competency of Civil Court to examine legality of the order of Revenue Officer passed under section 117 (c) of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the collateral proceeding as well as question of proper interpretation of the principle of law enunciated in the above mentioned 3 cases in the background of the fact of the instant cases are not necessary. The pre-emptors obtained order of the Revenue Officer on August 13, 1981 in Miscellaneous Case No. 198 'G1' P-1/81-82 for opening a separate khatian in respect of their purchased land from Hannan's heirs and this splitting up of the jama and opening of separate khatian, being No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A), in the name of the pre-emptors in respect of the land purchased from Hannan's heirs was before the transfer to the pre-emptee. The transfer by Rowshawn Akhter, daughter of Abdur Razzaque, to the pre-emptee was made on August 24, 1981. In this background of the facts it is seen that the pre-emptors ceased to be the co-sharers of the land recorded in Exhibit 3 ie khatian No. 3232/1, listing name of heirs of Abdur Razzaque. 

 14. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that in respect of non-agricultural land on the opening of separate khatian upon splitting up of the jama of the land sought to be pre-empted in the name of the per-emptor disentitles him from exercising right of pre-emption in respect of the land whereof he ceased to be a co-sharer because of splitting up of jama and starting of a separate khatian in his name. In support of the aforesaid submission he has referred to the observation in the case of Begum Khodeza Akhter vs Hajera Khatun and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 212. In the said case the question of separation of jamaby pre- emptors was raised contending that pre-emptors after purchase filed an application before the Revenue Officer for separation of their jama and thereupon, a Separation Case was started and the same ended in an order separating the jama and thereupon the parties paid rent separately. In that background it was observed "If this is a fact then, certainly the pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharers and are debarred from claiming pre-emption". Since the pre-emptee in support of his contention that pre-emptors separated their jama relied upon the statement made in the petition for pre-emption and as there was no other evidence as to separation of jama and the lands were recorded under separate khatian and that as there was also no material as towhether the proposal for opening separate khatian was finally accepted resulting in separation of jama and payment of rent separately by the 2 co-sharers and that as it was contended by the pre-emptors that they filed application for mutation of their names in place of original owner and that proposal for mutation was erroneously referred to as separation of jama and that the said case did not reach its finality and consequent thereupon they continue to be co-sharers, the case was sent back to the lower appellate Court to determine the question as to separation of jama. Since in the instant case there are materials on record to show that pre-emptors after their purchase from Hannan's heirs land measuring 335 filed an application for separation of the jama and the same was allowed by the Revenue Officer and thereupon separate khatian, being No. 3232/1/1, in respect of the aforementioned quantity of land has been opened evidenced by Exhibit A and, as such, we feel there is no necessity of sending back the case to the court below for determination of the fact of separation of jama by the pre-emptors in respect of the land purchased from Hannan's heirs. The pre-emptors by opening separate khatian in their names in respect of the land purchased from Hannan's heirs ceased to be the co-sharers of the land recorded in khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) that stands in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs. 

 15. The learned Counsel for the respondents has submitted that because of the decree in partition suit same ipso facto would not constitute separation of jama or mutation in the background of the provision of section 117(1)( c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and that for the said one of the purposes ie for separation of jama or mutation, there shall have to file an application seeking separation of jama or for mutation. The question of ceasing of co-sharership in non-agricultural land upon partition by metes and bounds pursuant to a decree in partition suit and question of ceasing of co-sharership in the land on separation of jama and opening of Khatian are two different aspects of ceasing of co-sharership. The two modes of ceasing of co-sharership are two distinct and different modes. The question of ceasing of co-sharership by metes and bounds partition pursuant to a decree in partition suit is now a settled question. In the instant case there was ceasing of co-sharership twice first, because of decree in the partition suit filed by pre-emptors' father and second, by separation of jama or splitting up of jama and opening of separate khatian by the pre-emptors. The contention of the learned Counsel for the respondent that in the absence of application under section 117(1)( c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act there cannot be separation of holding or mutation can hardly be disputed, rather it is the requirements of provision of law that an application for separation of holding or mutation has to be filed and thereupon the Revenue Officer is authorised for separation of the jama or mutation prayed for upon due service of notice to the other co-sharers, 

 16. As seen from the materials on record the pre-emptors after their purchase from Hannan's heirs land measuring 335 aurjuthansa filed application seeking separation of jama and thereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 198 (u) P-1/81-82 was started and that the Revenue Officer allowed separation of jama by the order dated August 13, 1981 and thereupon separate khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) has been opened in the name of the pre-emptors. So, it is evidenced that khatian (Exhibit A) has been opened in the name of the pre-emptors on their application filed under section 117(1)( c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It is seen from the, judgment of this Division reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 and the case reported in 52 DLR (AD) 41 that upon partition of the non-agricultural land by metes and bounds by a decree in a partition suit there occurs ceasing of co-sharership among the separate specific saham holders. From the respondent's side we have not been referred to any case to take a view different from the ratio of the cases reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 and 52 DLR (AD) 41 that in case of partition of non-agricultural land in pursuant to a decree in a partition suit co- sharership among the specific saham holders ceases. 

 17. Learned Counsel for the respondents has submitted since Abdul Gafur who" got land measuring 3535 arjutansha pursuant to the decree in the partition suit did not file any application for separation of the land he got by the partition decree by opening separate khatian and, as such, he remained a co-sharer and that 'after his death his heirs remained co-sharers of the land recorded in SA khatian No. 3232 and in support of the said contention has referred to the case reported in 36 DLR 193. This contention is of merit since en the basis of the final decree in the partition suit Abdur Razzaque's heirs splitted up the jama of Khatian SA No. 3232 and get opened in their names separate Khatian, being No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3), Abdul Gafur remained a tenant in khatian No. 3232 in respect of the land he get in the light of the decree in the partition suit filed by him. There is no reason to take a view different from the view expressed in the case reported in 36 DLR 213 that for sub-division of holding as per provision of section 117(c) of SAT Act there shall have to make an application to the Revenue Officer by one or more co-sharer tenants and order for sub-division of holding shall be made after notice to. the parties concerned to appear and upon hearing the party concerned, if appears. No. exception has been taken by Abdul Gafur's heirs as regard splitting of jama of khatian No. 3232 at the instance of Abdur Razzaque's heirs and opening of separate khatian, being No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) in respect of land measuring 1005 arjutansha they get pursuant to the decree in the partition suit. 

 18. The contention of the learned Counsel for the respondents that as Gafur did not seek for separation of jama in respect of the land he got by the partition decree; as such, he remained to be a co-sharer and that only if Gafur, or for that matter, his heirs would have filed application seeking separation of the jama in respect of the land got in pursuant to the decree in the partition suit and the land purchased from Hannan's heirs or if would have prayed for listing of the land got by the partition decree and by purchase from Hannan's heirs in one khatian only, in that case it could have been said that there has been ceasing of ce-sharership as regard the land recorded in SA Khatian No. 3232. This contention of the learned Counsel for the respondents appears to be of no merit in the background of the materials on record. The undenied position is that Abdur Razzaque's heirs in the light of the partition decree sought separation of jama upon splitting of the jama of SA khatian No. 3232 and on the application of Abdur Razzaque's heirs seeking separation of jama separation proceeding was started and that Revenue Officer made the order on June 1, 1977 for separation of jama and thereupon khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) was opened in respect of the land measuring 1005. This quantity of land Abdur Razaaque got in his share pursuant to partition decree in Partition Suit No. 18 of 1954 wherein final decree was made on May 20, 1967. After the opening of separate khatian in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs pre-emptors purchased 335 aurjuthansa of land from the heirs of Abdul Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque and thereupon pre-emptors approached the Revenue Officer for separation of jama of their purchased land upon splitting up of the jama of khatian No. 3232/1 by filing separation case No. 198 (u) and that the same was allowed by the Revenue Officer by the order dated August 13, 1981 and on the basis thereof khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) has been opened in the name of the pre- emptors fer 3535 arjutansha of land. The pre-emptors contention is that Khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) is in respect of the land Abdul Gafur got pursuant to the decree in the partition suit. This contention is of no merit since after opening of khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs, Abdul Gafur remained the recorded tenant in respect of his share in khatian No. 3232 and, as such, there was no occasion or necessity to go for having a khatian in respect of the land he got pursuant to the partition decree. The fact that khatian No. 3232/1 opened in respect of the land purchased by the pre-emptors from Abdur Razzaque's heirs is seen from the material on record ie petition filed by the pre-ernptors seeking separation of jama and whereupon Separation Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1-81-82 was started and pursuant to an order allowing the said separation case separate khatian No. 3232/1/1 has been opened. In the aforesaid background of the facts the pre-emptors' claim of remaining co-sharers since their predecessor Abdul Gafur did not apply for separation of the jama in respect of the land he got on the basis of partition decree and that if Abdul Gafur or for that matter his heirs would have gonefor separation of jama there would have been one khatian for the purchased land as well as for the land got by the decree in the partition suit is of no merit. The notings in the khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit B2) (after listing of the land purchased by pre-emptors and the pre-emptee in new khatians) clearly show that khatian No. 3232/1/1 text A) was open upon separation or splitting upon jama of khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3). 

 19. In the background of the discussions made hereinabove we are of the view that because of the decree in the partition suit as there has been ceasing of co-sharership between the plaintiff and the defendant of the partition suit that ended in final decree upon allotment of separate saham to respective parties and that as the pre-emptors got the jama of khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) split up in respect of their land purchased from the heirs of Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque and go to separate khatian opened in their names before the transfer to the pre-emptee and consequent thereupon as they ceased to be the co-sharers ofkhatian No. 3232/1 or, in other words, land of the said khatian pre-emption sought for on the basis of purchase of land made from the heirs of Abdul Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque against the pre-emptee who purchased the land sought to be pre-empted from heirs of Abdur Razzaque was not available. The High Court Division as well as the appellate Court in disregard of the materials on record as discussed above wrongly assumed that khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) was started in the name of pre-emptors in respect of the land Abdul Gafur got pursuant to the decree in partition suit and thereupon erroneously allowed pre-emption.

full_judgment:
2. Maran Mondal, predecessor-in-interest of the petitioners as plaintiff, instituted a suit in the 3rd Court of Munsif Dhaka being Title Suit No. 732 of 1981 subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 153 of 1984 before Munsif. Savar for declaration of his title in the suit land measuring 0.82 acre of nal land as recorded in CS Plot No. 787 under CS Khatian No. 137/24 corresponding to SA Plot No. 198 under SA Khatian No. 198 and RS Plot Nos. 1194 and 1204 under RS Khatian No. 225 of Mouza Barakakar, PS Savar, District Dhaka. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to Lakshman Mondal, full brother of plaintiff Maran Mondal and the same was correctly recorded in the CS and SA Khatians in the name of Lakshman MondaI. Lakshman Mondal eventually died as a childless widower at his native village Kakabo PS Savar District Dhaka leaving the plaintiff as his only heir to succeed him and since then he has been owning and possessing the suit property peacefully on payment of rent to the Government Acquired Estate. The plaintiff’s further case is that while he has been in rightful possession of the suit property the same has been correctly recorded in his name in the finally published RS Khatian No. 225 following which he has been paying rent to the Government in his own name in respect of the suit property. It was in late 1975 that at the instance of some greedy and unscrupulous persons the defendants illegally tried to treat the suit property as a vested property and threatened to oust him from possession by sheer force and under threats of imminent forcible dispossession he was constrained to pray for yearly lease of the suit property under protest but at the same time he filed an application before the appropriate authority for releasing the suit property from the list of vested property. It has further been contended by the plaintiff that the SDO. Dhaka who is defendant No. 2 in the suit after proper enquiry clearly found in his order dated 5-10-76 Ext. 5 that the original tenant Laksham Mondal had died 15 years ago at his native village Kakabo, Savar leaving plaintiff Maran Mondal as his brother and only heir to succeed him. The learned SDO in his order dated 5-10-76 further found that there was no occasion to treat the suit property as vested property and recommended the release of the suit property from the list of the vested property. The learned ADC (Rev) Dhaka eventually rejected the said recommendation of the SDO Dhaka illegally and arbitrarily and this necessitated the filing of the suit for declaration that the suit property is not vested property and the plaintiff is the absolute owner of the same. 

 4. The learned Munsif by his impugned judgment dated 12-1-85 dismissed the suit without discussing any evidence oral or documentary. It is evident from the impugned judgment that the learned Munsif dismissed the suit in a most casual manner without discussing and considering any evidence adduced by the plaintiff and the legal incidence of the documents exhibited in the case in support of the plaintiff’s case. It also appears from Ext. 4 and 5 that these do not contain any khatian number but the learned Munsif appears to have discovered a khatian number in the said exhibits, the basis of which is not available on record arid discarded the plaintiff’s case with reference to the baseless khatian purported to have been mentioned therein. 

 5. Mr SR Karmaker the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners submits that the learned Court of appeal below seriously erred in law in holding that the suit property is a vested property without any basis at all. The learned Advocate further submits that in the face of cleat assertions by the plaintiff and evidence led to substantiate the same to the effect that his brother Lakhman Mondal never left this country to settle in India and he died at his native village Kakabo leaving the plaintiff as his only heir and since then he has been owning and possessing the suit property and his name has duly been recorded in the finally published RS Khatian and he has been regularly paying rent to the Government Acquired Estate, there is absolutely no basis for treating the suit property as vested property on the basis of a VP Case started in late 1975. The learned Advocate further submits that in the face of the clear finding recorded by defendant No. 2 SDO Dhaka in Ext. 4 that the admitted tenant Lakshman Mondal had died in this country leaving the plaintiff to succeed him as his only heir and in the face of the unchallenged evidence of the plaintiff as PW 1 to the said effect the learned Court of appeal below evidently erred in law in arbitrarily ignoring the said evidence both oral and documentary by illegally shifting the onus of proof regarding the death of Lakshman Mondal and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Karmaker further submits that from Exhibit 4 it is evident that the learned SDO Dhaka who is defendant No. 2 in the suit and himself conducted an enquiry in the VP Case himself found on local enquiry that Lakshman Mondal had died in this country as a citizen of the erstwhile East Pakistan and he never migrated to India and since Lakshman's death plaintiff Moran Mondal has been owing and possessing the suit property on payment of rent to the Government Acquired Estate and on such findings recommended the realse of the suit property from the list of the  vested property. the learned Court of appeal below evidently erred in law in completely ignoring these pieces of material evindence convincingly proving the plaintiffs case and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 6. Mr Karmaker has drawn my attention to Ext. 5 and the order dated 17-8-88 passed by the learned ADC (Rev) Dhaka wherein he called for opinion of the legal Adviser of Vested Properties in respect of release of the suit property from the list of vested properties. It also appears from Ext. 5 that before the opinion of the Legal Adviser of the Vested Property could be obtained as ordered by the learned ADC (Rev) the Superintendent of Vested Properties who is a much lessor officer and subordinate to the SDO could wishfully throwaway the definite recommendation of the SDO for release of the suit property by substituting the satisfaction of the SDO by his own satisfaction without any further material before him and the learned ADC (Rev). Dhaka simply acted mechanically at the bidding of the Superintendent of Vested Properties in rejecting SDO's definite recommendation and positive finding and completely ignoring the legal incidence of the finally published RS Khatian in the name of the plaintiff-Ext. 3 and the Government rent receipts Ext. 2 series in favour of the plaintiff. 

 8. In support of his submissions Mr Karmaker has placed before me the case of Abul Khair vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 29 wherein their Lordships held that before a property could be treated as a vested property the authority concerned must prove that the original tenant migrated to India before the Enemy Property laws came into force in 1965. In the instant case there is absolutely no material on record to prove that Lakshman Mondal migrated to India at any point of time and settled there permanently but on the contrary there is convincing documentary and oral evidence to prove that the admitted tenant Lakshman Mondal had died in this country as its citizen leaving the plaintiff as his only heir to succeed him. The casual exercise made by the defendants in treating the suit property as a vested property without any legal basis whatsoever ostensibly at the instance of an irresponsible Tashilder who is accountable to none and an overzealous Superintendent lightly setting at nought the definite finding and recommendation of the SDO Dhaka must be held to be acts of malfeasance and witch-hunting at the cost of a citizen of the country whose name has duly been recorded in the finally published RS Khatian and from whom rent is being regularly accepted by the Government treating him as a tenant in respect of the suit property. 

 9. In the face of the SA Khatian standing in the name of Lakshman Mondal and the finally published RS Khatian standing in the name of plaintiff Maran Mondal and the Government regularly accepting rent from the plaintiff treating him as a tenant and there being no material basis and legal foundation for treating the suit property as an enemy property subsequently vested property on the basis of a case started in late 1975 the learned Courts below evidently erred in law in passing the impugned judgments on erroneous view of law. 

 20. There is yet another special feature of the case which has been overlooked by the learned Courts below. Admittedly the finally published RS Khatian stands in the name of the plaintiff and the Government is regularly accepting rent from him thereby recognising him as the tenant in respect of the suit land. A finally published record of rights revised under section 114A of the SAT Act has a presumption of correctness and that presumption continues till it is otherwise rebutted by reliable evidence. Nothing has been done by the contesting defendants to dispel the legal presumption that attaches to the finally published RS Khatian in the name of the plaintiff. Recognition of the plaintiff as a tenant in respect of the suit property by the Revenue Authority of the Government is binding upon the Vested Property Department and the latter cannot claim the suit land as a vested property summarily discarding the finally published RS Khatian in the name of the plaintiff. The action of the ADC (Revenue) Dhaka who is the de facto head of the Vested Property Department of the District indulging in oppressive litigations must be deprecated. The case of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Narayanganj vs. AKM Latiful Karim and others reported in 17 BW (HCD) 249 lends instant support to this view. The impugned judgment cannot be sustainable on that ground as well.
